15186.m: Portuguese expansion began with the capture of Ceuta in 1415.

15187.q: Which Portuguese prince systematically promoted voyages of exploration along the African coast in the 15th century?
15187.e: Prince Henry the Navigator financed and organised many expeditions to West Africa. He himself hardly ever went to sea; his nickname comes from a later time.
15187.m: Henry the Navigator made the exploration of Africa a state project of Portugal.

15188.q: Who was the first European to sail round the southern tip of Africa, around 1488?
15188.e: Bartolomeu Dias reached the Cape of Good Hope and proved that it was possible to sail round Africa. This brought the sea route to India within reach.
15188.m: By rounding the Cape, Bartolomeu Dias opened the way into the Indian Ocean.

15189.q: What was Portugal’s main economic aim with the sea route to India?
a: Direct spice trade without Arab and Italian middlemen
Selling potatoes and maize to Asia
Land for Portuguese farmers to settle
15189.e: Spices such as pepper brought high profits in Europe. A sea route of its own was meant to cut out the expensive middlemen of the Mediterranean and Eastern trade.
15189.m: The wish for direct spice trade drove the search for the sea route to India.

15190.q: How did Spain and Portugal divide the newly discovered lands in the Treaty of Tordesillas in 1494?
a: By a line 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde Islands
15190.e: Land west of the line was to belong to Castile, land east of it to Portugal. The interests of the people living there played no part.
15190.m: The Treaty of Tordesillas divided the world between Spain and Portugal.

15191.q: Which pope, in the bull “Inter caetera” of 1493, granted the lands discovered by Columbus to Castile?
15191.e: Pope Alexander VI issued the bull “Inter caetera” in 1493. Its unclear borderline led to direct negotiations between Spain and Portugal a year later.
15191.m: In 1493 the pope claimed the right to dispose of newly discovered lands.

15192.q: Which Portuguese navigator reached the coast of Brazil in 1500?
15192.e: Cabral was on his way to India and landed on the Brazilian coast in 1500. He took possession of the area for Portugal, as it lay east of the Tordesillas line.
15192.m: From Cabral’s landing in 1500, Brazil became Portuguese.

15193.q: How many men returned to Spain on the “Victoria” in 1522 from the first circumnavigation of the world?
15193.e: The fleet had set out in 1519 with five ships and about 240 men. Only the “Victoria” under Juan Sebastián Elcano returned in September 1522, with 18 men.
15193.m: Only a small part of the crew survived the first circumnavigation of the world.

15194.q: Where did Ferdinand Magellan die in 1521 during the first circumnavigation of the world?
a: On the island of Mactan in the Philippines
While passing through the Strait of Magellan
On the Spice Islands of the Moluccas
At the Cape of Good Hope
15194.e: Magellan fell on 27 April 1521 in a fight with local people on Mactan. The voyage then continued without him.
15194.m: Magellan himself did not live to see the end of his circumnavigation.

15195.q: Which manoeuvrable type of ship, thanks to lateen sails, allowed the Portuguese to sail against the wind too?
15195.e: The caravel was small and fast and, with triangular lateen sails, could tack against the wind. This was vital for the return voyage along the African coast.
15195.m: The caravel was the typical explorers’ ship of the 15th century.

15196.q: Which trading company, founded in 1602, dominated large parts of the Asian trade in the 17th century?
15196.e: The VOC was founded in 1602 and was allowed to make treaties, build forts and wage war in the name of the Netherlands. It is seen as an early joint-stock company.
15196.m: With the VOC, private trading companies took over state power overseas.

15197.q: Why did Martin Waldseemüller name the new continent after Amerigo Vespucci on his world map of 1507?
a: Because Vespucci described the land in reports as a separate new continent
Because Vespucci was the first European to land in America
Because Vespucci paid for Columbus’ voyage
Because Vespucci was viceroy of New Spain
15197.e: Columbus believed until the end that he had been in Asia. Vespucci’s reports spread the idea of a “New World”, so Waldseemüller put the name America on the map.
15197.m: America bears the name of Amerigo Vespucci because he spoke of a new world.

15198.q: Why did Christopher Columbus sail west in 1492?
a: He wanted to reach Asia by a western sea route and underestimated the Earth’s circumference
He deliberately wanted to discover an unknown continent
He wanted to prove that the Earth is round
He was looking for a sea route round the southern tip of Africa
15198.e: Columbus reckoned with a much smaller Earth and Asia close by. Educated people had long known that the Earth is a sphere. On 12 October 1492 he landed on an island in the Bahamas.
15198.m: Columbus was looking for Asia and came across America.

15199.q: In which year did Hernán Cortés and his indigenous allies conquer Tenochtitlan?
15199.e: After a siege of several months, Tenochtitlan fell on 13 August 1521. Mexico City, the capital of New Spain, was built on its ruins.
15199.m: The fall of Tenochtitlan in 1521 ended Aztec rule.

15200.q: Which indigenous people was Cortés’ most important ally in conquering the Aztec Empire?
15200.e: The Tlaxcalans were enemies of the Aztecs and provided Cortés with thousands of warriors. Without indigenous allies the few Spaniards could not have conquered the empire.
15200.m: The Spanish conquest of Mexico succeeded only with indigenous allies.

15201.q: What role did La Malinche play in the conquest of Mexico?
a: She was Cortés’ interpreter and an important adviser
She led the uprising on the “Noche Triste”
She was the wife of Moctezuma II
15201.e: La Malinche had been handed over to the Spanish as a slave in 1519. She spoke Nahuatl and a Maya language and became an indispensable go-between for Cortés.
15201.m: La Malinche made it possible for Cortés to communicate with the peoples of Mexico.

15202.q: Where did Francisco Pizarro capture the Inca ruler Atahualpa in 1532?
15202.e: Pizarro captured Atahualpa in Cajamarca in November 1532. Despite a huge ransom in gold and silver, the Spanish had him executed in 1533.
15202.m: The capture of Atahualpa in Cajamarca began the downfall of the Inca Empire.

15203.q: What was the main cause of the massive population decline of the indigenous peoples of the Americas after 1492?
a: Diseases brought in, such as smallpox and measles
Great volcanic eruptions in the Andes
15203.e: The people of the Americas had no immunity to diseases from Europe. On top of this came violence, forced labour and hunger. Together they led to a dramatic fall in population.
15203.m: Imported epidemics contributed most to the population collapse in the Americas.

15204.q: What was an encomienda in the Spanish colonial empire?
a: A right to the labour of indigenous people
A landed estate given as a gift
15204.e: The encomendero received labour or tribute from a group of indigenous people and was supposed to protect them and teach them Christianity in return. In practice the system often led to exploitation.
15204.m: The encomienda combined a duty to convert with the exploitation of indigenous labour.

15205.q: Which laws did Emperor Charles V issue in 1542 that, among other things, banned the enslavement of indigenous people?
15205.e: The Leyes Nuevas (“New Laws”) banned the enslavement of indigenous people and restricted the encomiendas. In Peru they triggered a revolt by the encomenderos, and parts were withdrawn.
15205.m: The New Laws of 1542 were meant to protect the indigenous population better.

15206.q: Which Dominican friar denounced the violence of the conquerors in his “A Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies”?
15206.e: Bartolomé de las Casas wrote the account in 1542 and published it in 1552. For decades he campaigned for the rights of the indigenous population.
15206.m: Bartolomé de las Casas became the best-known critic of the Spanish conquest.

15207.q: What was the Valladolid debate of 1550/51 between Las Casas and Sepúlveda about?
a: Whether war against and subjugation of indigenous people were justified
How Brazil should be divided between Spain and Portugal
Whether the heliocentric view of the world was correct
Who should run the silver mining in Potosí
15207.e: Sepúlveda considered the violent subjugation just; Las Casas firmly disagreed. No clear verdict was reached, and both saw themselves as the winner.
15207.m: At Valladolid, people argued for the first time about the right to conquer as a matter of principle.

15208.q: Why must the account by Las Casas be read critically as a source, even though it is very valuable?
a: It is a passionate indictment that exaggerates and sometimes gives very high numbers
It was only written in the 20th century
It was written by an Aztec general
It contains no information at all about the conquerors’ violence
15208.e: Las Casas wanted to move the king to act and therefore wrote in a deliberately forceful way. Spain’s opponents later used the text for the so-called “Black Legend”.
15208.m: Even justified accusations must be checked as sources for their purpose and exaggeration.

15209.q: Which city in today’s Bolivia became one of the largest cities in the world through silver mining after 1545?
15209.e: Potosí was founded in 1545 at the silver mountain Cerro Rico and had about 150,000 inhabitants around 1611. Thousands of indigenous people had to do forced labour there in deadly conditions.
15209.m: The silver of Potosí financed the Spanish world empire at the expense of indigenous forced labourers.

15210.q: Which settlement, founded in 1607, is seen as the first permanent English colony in North America?
15210.e: Jamestown in Virginia was founded in 1607 by the Virginia Company. After years of hunger, tobacco growing became the economic basis of the colony.
15210.m: Permanent English settlement of North America began with Jamestown in 1607.

15211.q: What was the main reason the Pilgrim Fathers emigrated to America on the “Mayflower” in 1620?
a: To be able to live their faith freely as religious separatists
To look for gold in America
Because they had been banished as convicts
To set up sugar cane plantations
15211.e: The Pilgrim Fathers had separated from the Anglican state church, were harassed in England and at first lived in Leiden in the Netherlands. In 1620 they founded Plymouth Colony in New England.
15211.m: Religious freedom was an important motive of the settlers in New England.

15212.q: Which colonial power founded the city of Quebec in 1608?
15212.e: Samuel de Champlain founded Quebec for France in 1608. New France lived largely from the fur trade with indigenous peoples.
15212.m: Quebec was the centre of the French colony of New France.

15213.q: What does the term “Columbian Exchange” mean?
a: The transfer of plants, animals and diseases between the Americas and the rest of the world
The barter between Columbus and the Taíno in 1492
The exchange of prisoners after the conquest of Mexico
The division of the colonies between Spain and Portugal
15213.e: Maize, potatoes and tomatoes came to Europe; horses, cattle and wheat came to the Americas. But the exchange also included germs, often with devastating consequences.
15213.m: The Columbian Exchange changed diets and nature on both sides of the Atlantic.

15214.q: Where was the Aztec capital Tenochtitlan?
a: On islands in Lake Texcoco in the Valley of Mexico
On the Pacific coast of Peru
In the rainforest of the Yucatán Peninsula
At the mouth of the Mississippi
15214.e: Tenochtitlan lay at about 2240 metres above sea level on islands in Lake Texcoco. Causeways linked the city to the mainland. Today it is almost completely built over by Mexico City.
15214.m: Tenochtitlan was an island city in the middle of a highland lake.

15215.q: According to their founding legend, which sign showed the Aztecs where to build Tenochtitlan?
a: An eagle on a cactus fighting a snake
A jaguar coming out of a cave
A condor circling over a volcano
A white feather on a rock in the lake
15215.e: According to the legend, the Mexica were to settle where an eagle sat on a prickly pear cactus. This image can be seen today on the coat of arms of Mexico. It is a legend, not a proven account.
15215.m: The founding legend of Tenochtitlan lives on in Mexico’s coat of arms.

15216.q: What were the chinampas of the Aztecs?
a: Artificial fields built in shallow lake water
Stone step pyramids for sacrificial rituals
Ballgame courts in the temple districts
15216.e: Chinampas were long, narrow beds made of mud and plant material in marshy areas. They often allowed several harvests a year.
15216.m: With chinampas the Aztecs won fertile land from the lake.

15217.q: Which three cities formed the Aztec Triple Alliance?
15217.e: After the victory over Azcapotzalco, Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan formed an alliance in the 15th century. The alliance secured dominance over the Valley of Mexico.
15217.m: The Aztec Empire was based on an alliance of three city-states.

15218.q: To which two gods was the Templo Mayor in Tenochtitlan dedicated?
15218.e: The double temple was dedicated to the war and sun god Huitzilopochtli and the rain god Tlaloc. Its remains have been excavated in the middle of Mexico City since 1978.
15218.m: The Templo Mayor was the religious centre of Tenochtitlan.

15219.q: What does the Quechua name of the Inca Empire, “Tawantinsuyu”, mean?
15219.e: The empire was divided into four regions whose borders met in the capital Cusco. Hence the name “the four parts”.
15219.m: Tawantinsuyu means the Inca Empire divided into four regions.

15220.q: What were quipus used for in the Inca Empire?
a: Recording numbers and data with knotted cords
As irrigation channels on the terraces
As signal fires along the roads
15220.e: Quipus were coloured knotted cords with which specialists recorded population figures, supplies and dues. The Inca had no writing in the European sense.
15220.m: With quipus the Inca ran their empire without writing.

15221.q: Under which ruler did the great expansion of the Inca Empire begin from about 1438?
15221.e: Pachacútec, whose name means roughly “world-changer”, made the empire a great power. The exact dates are uncertain. According to a widespread interpretation, he also had Machu Picchu built.
15221.m: Pachacútec turned the Inca Empire into a great power of the Andes.

15222.q: What was the mit’a in the Inca Empire?
a: A labour duty owed to the state as a tax
A religious festival at the solstice
A troop of messengers on the imperial roads
A court for disputes between villages
15222.e: Instead of money, subjects paid with labour, for example in road building or in the army. The Spanish later abused this system for forced labour in the silver mines of Potosí.
15222.m: The mit’a was a tax in the form of labour.

15223.q: Which internal crisis weakened the Inca Empire just before Pizarro arrived?
a: A war of succession between the brothers Atahualpa and Huáscar
A Maya revolt in the north of the empire
A famine after the eruption of Chimborazo
15223.e: After the death of Huayna Cápac, his sons fought for power. Atahualpa had just won when Pizarro arrived in 1532. The split made the conquest easier.
15223.m: The brothers’ war over the throne made it easier for the Spanish to conquer the Inca Empire.

15224.q: Why do only parts of four Maya manuscripts survive today?
a: Spanish missionaries such as Diego de Landa had Maya writings burned
The Maya only wrote on perishable sand
The Inca destroyed the Maya libraries
An earthquake destroyed the archive of Tikal
15224.e: In 1562 the Franciscan Diego de Landa had Maya writings and religious objects burned at Maní. Many other manuscripts were lost in this way or through decay.
15224.m: Much Maya knowledge was lost through the destruction of manuscripts.

15225.q: How was the world of the Classic Maya organised politically?
a: Into a single great empire with Tikal as its capital
Into an empire under a Sapa Inca
Into an alliance led by Tenochtitlan
15225.e: Cities such as Tikal, Calakmul or Copán had their own rulers and often waged war on each other. There was never a united Maya empire.
15225.m: The Maya lived in many independent city-states.

15226.q: Which causes are discussed for the decline of many Maya cities in the southern lowlands around 900?
a: Droughts, overused soils and wars between city-states
The plague brought in from Europe
15226.e: Researchers name population pressure, soil exhaustion, long droughts and wars. The Spanish only arrived centuries later.
15226.m: The decline of the Classic Maya had several causes, mainly ecological and political.

15227.q: How long did it take the Spanish to conquer all the Maya areas?
15227.e: The conquest began in the 1520s. The last independent centre, Tayasal in today’s Guatemala, did not fall until 1697.
15227.m: The Maya resisted the Spanish conquest until 1697.

15228.q: According to current estimates, how many Africans were forced onto ships in the Atlantic slave trade?
15228.e: Researchers estimate that about 12 to 13 million people were shipped from the 16th to the 19th century. The estimates are based mainly on analysed ship lists and port registers.
15228.m: The Atlantic slave trade carried off more than twelve million people from Africa.

15229.q: Which area was the most important destination of the Atlantic slave trade?
a: The English colonies in North America
15229.e: Rio de Janeiro and Salvador da Bahia were the largest ports of arrival. Portuguese and Brazilian traders transported almost half of all those carried off.
15229.m: No country took in as many enslaved people as Brazil.

15230.q: How did the so-called triangular trade work?
a: Goods from Europe to Africa, enslaved people to the Americas, plantation products to Europe
Spices from Asia to Africa, gold to the Americas, silver to Asia
Goods from the Americas to Africa, enslaved people to Europe, sugar to the Americas
Furs from the Americas to Asia, silk to Africa, salt to Europe
15230.e: Ships brought goods such as cloth, weapons and alcohol to West Africa and exchanged them for captives. These were carried off to the Americas, and sugar, tobacco or cotton went to Europe.
15230.m: The triangular trade linked Europe, Africa and the Americas in a system of exploitation.

15231.q: What do historians usually call the voyage of the slave ships from Africa to the Americas?
15231.e: The “Middle Passage” was the middle section of the triangular trade. People were crammed together below deck, and many died of disease and mistreatment.
15231.m: The Middle Passage was the deadliest part of the triangular trade.

15232.q: According to estimates, how many people died during the crossing of the Atlantic?
15232.e: Estimates suggest about 1.5 to 2 million deaths at sea. In addition, many died during capture in Africa and after arrival.
15232.m: The crossing alone cost millions of those carried off their lives.

15233.q: Which European sea power was the first to carry off people from West Africa, from the 1440s?
15233.e: In 1441 Portuguese sailors first brought captives from the West African coast to Portugal. From the 16th century this grew into the transatlantic trade.
15233.m: Portugal was at the beginning of the European slave trade with Africa.

15234.q: What was an “asiento” in connection with the slave trade?
a: A licence from the Spanish Crown to deliver enslaved people to its colonies
A revolt of enslaved people in the Caribbean
A type of ship for crossing the Atlantic
A law to free enslaved children
15234.e: The Spanish Crown granted asientos to traders and companies, giving them the right to sell people in the Spanish colonies. These contracts were highly sought after.
15234.m: Through the asiento the Spanish Crown also earned money from the slave trade.

15235.q: For which plantation product were especially many enslaved people carried off to the Caribbean in the 17th and 18th centuries?
15235.e: Sugar was in great demand in Europe and brought high profits. Work on the sugar plantations was extremely hard, and the death rate among the enslaved was correspondingly high.
15235.m: Demand for sugar drove the slave trade to the Caribbean.

15236.q: In which year did Great Britain ban its subjects from the slave trade?
15236.e: The British Parliament passed the Slave Trade Act in 1807. Slavery itself was only abolished in the British Empire in 1833.
15236.m: Great Britain banned the slave trade in 1807 and slavery in 1833.

15237.q: Which state was created in 1804 by a successful revolution of enslaved people?
15237.e: In the French colony of Saint-Domingue, the enslaved rose up from 1791. On 1 January 1804 Haiti declared its independence.
15237.m: Haiti was the first state founded by freed enslaved people.

15238.q: Which country, with the “Golden Law” of 1888, was the last in the Americas to abolish slavery?
15238.e: The Lei Áurea of 13 May 1888 ended slavery in Brazil. In the USA it had already been banned in 1865 by the 13th Amendment.
15238.m: In 1888 Brazil was the last country in the Americas to end slavery.

15239.q: At which congress in 1815 did European powers condemn the slave trade in a joint declaration?
a: At the Peace Congress of Westphalia
At the Paris Peace Congress of 1856
15239.e: In 1815 the Congress of Vienna adopted a declaration condemning the slave trade. The ban, however, was only enforced much later.
15239.m: In 1815 the European powers condemned the slave trade in Vienna.

15240.q: How were people from Switzerland involved in the Atlantic slave trade, even though Switzerland had no colonies?
a: As investors, merchants, bankers and plantation owners
Not at all, there were no links whatsoever
Only as sailors in a Swiss war fleet
As a colonial power with its own ports in West Africa
15240.e: Swiss trading houses and private individuals invested in slave ships, supplied trade goods such as printed cotton cloth or owned plantations. Researchers have been examining these links more closely in recent years.
15240.m: Swiss people also profited from the Atlantic slave trade.

15241.q: Which formerly enslaved man published an autobiography in 1789 that strengthened the British movement against the slave trade?
15241.e: In “The Interesting Narrative”, Olaudah Equiano described how he was carried off and enslaved. The book is an important source from the point of view of someone affected.
15241.m: Olaudah Equiano gave enslaved people a voice of their own in the abolition movement.

15242.q: On which day did Martin Luther send his 95 Theses to Archbishop Albrecht of Mainz?
15242.e: Luther sent the theses to Albrecht of Mainz on 31 October 1517. This date is now seen as the start of the Reformation and is celebrated as Reformation Day.
15242.m: 31 October 1517 is seen as the starting point of the Reformation.

15243.q: What were Luther's 95 Theses mainly directed against?
15243.e: Luther criticised that indulgences sold people a false certainty of salvation. True repentance could not be bought with money.
15243.m: Luther's theses mainly attacked the sale of indulgences.

15244.q: Among other things, what was the indulgence renewed by Pope Leo X in 1515 meant to raise money for?
a: For rebuilding St Peter's Basilica in Rome
15244.e: In 1515 Leo X renewed an indulgence, half of whose proceeds went into rebuilding St Peter's Basilica. Albrecht of Mainz used his share to repay debts to the Fuggers, who had lent him money for fees to the Curia.
15244.m: Indulgence money helped pay for rebuilding St Peter's Basilica.

15245.q: Which order did Martin Luther belong to as a monk?
15245.e: In 1505 Luther joined the order of Augustinian Hermits in Erfurt. As a monk and professor of theology in Wittenberg he developed his criticism of the Church.
15245.m: Luther was a monk in the order of Augustinian Hermits.

15246.q: Why is the famous nailing of the theses to the door of the Castle Church in Wittenberg disputed by researchers?
a: It was only recorded in writing after Luther's death
The Castle Church did not yet exist in 1517
The theses were only presented orally
15246.e: What is certain is the letter to Albrecht of Mainz of 31 October 1517. The posting on the church door is only reported by Philip Melanchthon after Luther's death, which is why historians examine it critically.
15246.m: The posting of the theses was only recorded late and is therefore disputed.

15247.q: What consequence did the Edict of Worms of May 1521 have for Luther?
a: He was placed under the imperial ban and declared an outlaw
He had to leave the empire within three days
He received safe conduct for life
15247.e: With the Edict of Worms Emperor Charles V placed Luther under the imperial ban. Anyone could now arrest him, and his writings were banned.
15247.m: The Edict of Worms made Luther an outlaw in 1521.

15248.q: What did Luther do on 18 April 1521 at the Diet of Worms before Emperor Charles V?
a: He refused to recant his writings
He knelt and begged the emperor's forgiveness
He burned the Pope's bull there
15248.e: After asking for time to think the day before, Luther refused to recant unless he was proved wrong by Holy Scripture or clear reasons. In doing so he put conscience above the authority of Church and emperor.
15248.m: At Worms in 1521 Luther refused to recant his teaching.

15249.q: Where did Luther translate the New Testament into German in 1521 and 1522?
a: In the Castle Church in Wittenberg
15249.e: After the Diet of Worms Luther was taken to the Wartburg for his protection. There he translated the New Testament in about eleven weeks.
15249.m: Luther translated the New Testament at the Wartburg.

15250.q: In which year did Luther's New Testament appear as the so-called September Testament?
15250.e: The September Testament appeared in September 1522 in around 3,000 copies. The edition sold out within about three months.
15250.m: The September Testament of 1522 was Luther's first printed New Testament.

15251.q: In which year did the first complete Luther Bible with the Old and New Testaments appear?
15251.e: After the New Testament of 1522, Luther and helpers also translated the Old Testament. In 1534 the first complete Luther Bible was published in Wittenberg.
15251.m: The first complete Luther Bible appeared in 1534.

15252.q: How did Luther react in December 1520 to the papal bull threatening him with excommunication?
a: He travelled to Rome to apologise
He fled to the Swiss Confederacy
15252.e: Luther burned the bull Exsurge Domine on 10 December 1520 in front of the Elster Gate in Wittenberg. In January 1521 he was then finally excluded from the Church.
15252.m: In 1520 Luther burned the bull that threatened him with excommunication.

15253.q: What position did Luther take in 1525 towards the rebelling peasants?
a: He called on the princes to take tough action
He led a peasant army himself
He supported all the peasants' demands
He stayed completely neutral and silent
15253.e: Luther condemned the violent uprising in his pamphlet against the robbing and murdering hordes of peasants. He saw it as the duty of the secular authorities to restore order.
15253.m: In the Peasants' War Luther sided with the princes.

15254.q: Which principle of the Reformation says that the Bible alone is the standard for faith?
15254.e: Sola scriptura means ‘by Scripture alone’. With it the Reformers rejected Church tradition as an equal source of faith.
15254.m: Sola scriptura means that the Bible alone counts for faith.

15255.q: Which event of 1529 does the name ‘Protestants’ go back to?
a: The Protestation at the Diet of Speyer
15255.e: In April 1529 a minority of princes and imperial cities in Speyer protested against a majority decision against the Reformation. The name Protestants comes from this.
15255.m: The Protestation of Speyer in 1529 gave the Protestants their name.

15256.q: Whom did Luther marry in 1525, openly breaking with celibacy?
15256.e: On 13 June 1525 in Wittenberg Luther married the former nun Katharina von Bora. The vicarage with a family became a model for Protestant clergy.
15256.m: In 1525 Luther married the former nun Katharina von Bora.

15257.q: In which village in the Toggenburg was Huldrych Zwingli born in 1484?
15257.e: Zwingli was born on 1 January 1484 in Wildhaus in the upper Toggenburg. The village now belongs to the canton of St Gallen. Later he worked as a priest in Glarus and Einsiedeln and died near Kappel in 1531.
15257.m: Zwingli came from Wildhaus in the Toggenburg.

15258.q: Which Church rule was deliberately broken at the Zurich sausage eating in 1522?
15258.e: After Ash Wednesday sausage was eaten in the house of the printer Christoph Froschauer. Zwingli was there and did not eat himself, but afterwards defended breaking the fast in a pamphlet.
15258.m: The sausage eating of 1522 deliberately broke the rule of fasting.

15259.q: Who declared Zwingli the winner after the First Zurich Disputation in January 1523?
a: The council of the city of Zurich
The Federal Diet of the Confederacy
15259.e: About 600 people took part in the disputation of 29 January 1523. The fact that the city council decided on matters of faith shows the close link between the Reformation and the authorities in Zurich.
15259.m: In Zurich the secular council decided on the Reformation.

15260.q: How many theses, the so-called Schlussreden, did Zwingli present at the First Zurich Disputation in 1523?
15260.e: Zwingli summed up his teaching in 67 articles. They formed the basis of the debate before the Zurich council.
15260.m: In 1523 Zwingli defended his teaching in 67 articles.

15261.q: Which topics were debated at the Second Zurich Disputation in October 1523?
a: Images in churches and the Mass
15261.e: From 26 to 28 October 1523 there was argument about the veneration of images and the Mass. Afterwards the images were to be removed from the churches within six months.
15261.m: The Second Zurich Disputation dealt with images and the Mass.

15262.q: Which experience made Zwingli a sharp critic of the mercenary system?
a: As an army chaplain he witnessed the defeat at Marignano in 1515
He was wounded himself as a mercenary in Rome
He lost his brother in the Burgundian Wars
He saw the Sack of Rome in 1527
15262.e: Zwingli went with troops from Glarus to Italy as an army chaplain and witnessed the costly Battle of Marignano in 1515. Afterwards he criticised mercenary service and foreign pensions.
15262.m: Marignano in 1515 turned Zwingli against mercenary service.

15263.q: What made the agreement between Luther and Zwingli fail at the Marburg Colloquy in 1529?
a: Their understanding of the Lord's Supper
The number of books in the Bible
15263.e: Luther held on to the bodily presence of Christ in the Lord's Supper, while Zwingli interpreted it symbolically as a meal of remembrance. As a result no joint Protestant alliance came about.
15263.m: The dispute over the Lord's Supper divided Luther and Zwingli at Marburg.

15264.q: When and where did Zwingli die?
a: In 1531 at the Battle of Kappel
In 1531 at the Battle of Marignano
In 1536 during the conquest of Vaud
15264.e: On 11 October 1531 Zwingli marched with the people of Zurich into the Second War of Kappel. He was captured and killed at the Battle of Kappel am Albis.
15264.m: Zwingli died in 1531 at the Battle of Kappel.

15265.q: Who took over the leadership of the Zurich church as Antistes after Zwingli's death?
15265.e: Heinrich Bullinger became Antistes about two months after Zwingli's death and remained so until 1575. He strengthened the Zurich Reformation and built international links for it.
15265.m: Heinrich Bullinger continued Zwingli's work in Zurich.

15266.q: How did Reformed Zurich treat the Anabaptist Felix Manz?
a: He was drowned in the Limmat
He was made pastor of the Fraumünster
He was elected to the council
15266.e: The Anabaptists rejected infant baptism and were persecuted in Zurich. Felix Manz, a former companion of Zwingli, was drowned in the Limmat; a memorial plaque has only marked this since 2004.
15266.m: Zurich persecuted the Anabaptists harshly; Felix Manz was drowned.

15267.q: Which Zurich printer published a richly illustrated complete edition of the Zurich Bible in 1531?
15267.e: The Zurich Bible was translated between 1524 and 1529 and printed by Froschauer. In 1531 the illustrated complete edition appeared, even before Luther's full Bible.
15267.m: The Zurich Bible was published by Christoph Froschauer in 1531.

15268.q: Where did Zwingli work as a people's priest from 1516 before he came to Zurich?
a: At the Abbey of St Gallen
15268.e: From 14 April 1516 Zwingli was people's priest in Einsiedeln. There he was already preaching against abuses on pilgrimages and against indulgence preachers.
15268.m: Before Zurich, Zwingli worked as a priest in Einsiedeln.

15269.q: Which humanist influenced Zwingli especially strongly?
15269.e: Zwingli read the writings of Erasmus intensively and adopted his return to the Greek text of the Bible. Erasmus's criticism of war also shaped him.
15269.m: Erasmus of Rotterdam was an important model for Zwingli.

15270.q: Which country did John Calvin come from?
15270.e: Calvin was born on 10 July 1509 in Noyon in Picardy. As a persecuted Protestant he fled France and later worked in Geneva.
15270.m: Calvin was a Frenchman from Noyon in Picardy.

15271.q: In which city did the Reformer John Calvin mainly work?
15271.e: Calvin came to Geneva in 1536 and shaped the city from 1541 until his death in 1564. As a result Geneva became the ‘Protestant Rome’.
15271.m: Calvin made Geneva a centre of the Reformation.

15272.q: Where did Calvin go after he was expelled from Geneva in 1538?
15272.e: After disputes about the Lord's Supper and church discipline Calvin had to leave Geneva in April 1538. In Strasbourg he taught theology and looked after a French refugee congregation.
15272.m: After his expulsion in 1538 Calvin worked in Strasbourg.

15273.q: Which teaching of Calvin says that God has decided in advance who will be saved?
15273.e: According to Calvin, God alone decides on a person's salvation. Many believers therefore looked for signs of being chosen in the way they lived.
15273.m: Calvin's doctrine of predestination says that God decides salvation in advance.

15274.q: Which four offices did Calvin's Geneva church order provide for?
15274.e: Calvin derived the four offices from the New Testament. The elders worked with the pastors on church discipline, and the deacons looked after the poor and the sick.
15274.m: The Geneva church had pastors, teachers, elders and deacons.

15275.q: Which body supervised the citizens' conduct and church discipline in Calvin's Geneva?
15275.e: The Consistory was made up of pastors and elders. It warned and punished citizens who broke the church rules, for example by gambling or swearing.
15275.m: The Geneva Consistory watched over the citizens' morals.

15276.q: Which critic of the doctrine of the Trinity was executed in Geneva in 1553?
15276.e: Michael Servetus was burned in Geneva on 27 October 1553. Calvin had provided theological opinions for the trial, which is why the case is still seen as a dark chapter.
15276.m: The execution of Michael Servetus in 1553 harms Calvin's reputation.

15277.q: Who was the first rector of the Geneva Academy founded by Calvin in 1559?
15277.e: Calvin founded the Geneva Academy in 1559 to train pastors and teachers. Its first rector was Theodore Beza, who after Calvin's death in 1564 also succeeded him at the head of the Geneva church.
15277.m: Theodore Beza was the first rector of the Geneva Academy.

15278.q: What did Calvin and Heinrich Bullinger agree on in 1549 in the Consensus Tigurinus?
a: On the understanding of the Lord's Supper
On a military alliance against Savoy
15278.e: With the Consensus Tigurinus the Zurich and Geneva Reformations found a shared teaching on the Lord's Supper. It is seen as an important step towards the Reformed denomination.
15278.m: The Consensus Tigurinus of 1549 united Zurich and Geneva on the Lord's Supper.

15279.q: Which sociologist put forward a thesis in 1904/05 about the link between Calvinist ethics and capitalism?
15279.e: In his work on the Protestant ethic and the spirit of capitalism, Max Weber interpreted the hard work and thrift of Calvinist believers as a driving force of the modern economy. The thesis is still disputed today.
15279.m: Max Weber linked Calvinist ethics with the rise of capitalism.

15280.q: What were Calvin's followers in France called?
15280.e: The French Calvinists were called Huguenots. They were persecuted for a long time, for example in the St Bartholomew's Day Massacre of 1572.

15281.q: During which period did the Council of Trent meet?
15281.e: With long breaks, the council met in three phases from 1545 to 1563 in Trent. It was the Catholic Church's answer to the Reformation.
15281.m: The Council of Trent lasted, with breaks, from 1545 to 1563.

15282.q: Which pope called the Council of Trent?
15282.e: Paul III called the council to respond to the Reformation. It was concluded under Pius IV, who confirmed its decisions in 1564.
15282.m: Pope Paul III called the Council of Trent.

15283.q: How did the Council of Trent define the relationship between the Bible and Church tradition?
a: Scripture and tradition count as equal sources of faith
15283.e: The council placed tradition on an equal footing with Holy Scripture. In doing so it deliberately set itself apart from the Reformation principle of sola scriptura.
15283.m: For Trent, Scripture and tradition are equal sources of faith.

15284.q: Which edition of the Bible did the Council of Trent declare binding?
15284.e: The council declared the Latin Vulgate, which goes back to Jerome, the authoritative Bible for teaching, preaching and worship. It rejected the Reformers' translations such as the Luther Bible.
15284.m: Trent made the Latin Vulgate the binding Bible.

15285.q: Which institution was to be set up in every diocese after the Council of Trent to improve the education of the clergy?
15285.e: Badly trained priests were seen as one cause of abuses. The council therefore required every diocese to set up a seminary to train priests.
15285.m: Trent required a seminary in every diocese.

15286.q: Which abuse did the Council of Trent want to remedy by requiring bishops to reside in their dioceses?
a: That bishops did not live in their diocese
That bishops were elected by the people
15286.e: Many bishops held several benefices and lived far from their diocese. The residence requirement obliged them actually to live in and lead their diocese.
15286.m: The residence requirement tied bishops to their own diocese.

15287.e: In 1534 Ignatius of Loyola and his companions took their first vows in Paris. The order became a driving force of Catholic renewal.
15287.m: Ignatius of Loyola founded the Society of Jesus.

15288.q: In which year did Pope Paul III officially approve the Jesuit order?
15288.e: With the bull Regimini militantis ecclesiae the Society of Jesus was recognised in 1540. After that it spread quickly in Europe and around the world.
15288.m: The Jesuit order was approved by the Pope in 1540.

15289.q: What sets the Jesuits apart from many other orders with their fourth vow?
a: Special obedience to the Pope regarding missions
A ban on all missionary work
15289.e: Besides poverty, chastity and obedience, Jesuits promise the Pope special obedience when he sends them on a task. This made them especially flexible in the service of the Church.
15289.m: Jesuits vow special obedience to the Pope regarding missions.

15290.q: Which work appeared in 1566 as a result of the Council of Trent to teach the Catholic faith in a uniform way?
15290.e: The Roman Catechism of 1566 was aimed mainly at parish priests. In 1570 the standardised missal, the Missale Romanum, followed as well.
15290.m: The Catechismus Romanus of 1566 made Catholic teaching uniform.

15291.q: Why do many historians use the term ‘Catholic Reform’ as well as ‘Counter-Reformation’?
a: It stresses the Church's inner renewal, not just its reaction
It describes only the time before Luther
It means only the Jesuit mission in Asia
It refers to the Reformation in England
15291.e: The term Counter-Reformation puts the fight against Protestantism in the foreground. Historians such as Hubert Jedin used ‘Catholic Reform’ to make the Church's own forces of reform visible too.
15291.m: Catholic Reform stresses the inner renewal of the Catholic Church.

15292.q: Which artistic period did the Catholic Church use heavily after the Council of Trent to impress believers?
15292.e: Magnificent Baroque churches, painting, theatre and music were meant to appeal to believers' emotions. Art thus also became a way of promoting the faith.
15292.m: The Catholic Church used the Baroque to promote the faith.

15293.q: What happened in France on St Bartholomew's Night, 24 August 1572?
a: The Edict of Nantes was proclaimed
The Jesuits were driven out of France
15293.e: Many Huguenots were murdered in Paris and then in other cities. The event intensified the French Wars of Religion.
15293.m: Many Huguenots were murdered on St Bartholomew's Night in 1572.

15294.q: Which edict ended the French Wars of Religion in 1598 and gave the Huguenots rights?
15294.e: With the Edict of Nantes the Huguenots received limited freedom of religion in 1598. It was revoked in 1685 by the Edict of Fontainebleau.
15294.m: The Edict of Nantes of 1598 granted the Huguenots toleration.

15295.q: Which event led to the introduction of the Reformation in Bern in 1528?
15295.e: After the Bern Disputation of 1528, Bern decided to introduce the Reformation throughout its territory. This gave the Reformation a powerful ally in the Confederacy.
15295.m: After the Bern Disputation of 1528, Bern became Reformed.

15296.q: Which Reformer shaped the Reformation in Basel, which won through in 1529?
15296.e: Oecolampadius worked as a preacher and theologian in Basel. In February 1529 the Reformation won through there after unrest and an outbreak of image-breaking.
15296.m: Johannes Oecolampadius was the Reformer of Basel.

15297.q: Which humanist and mayor introduced the Reformation in St Gallen?
a: Joachim von Watt, known as Vadian
15297.e: Joachim von Watt became mayor of St Gallen in 1526. Under his leadership the city joined the Reformation.
15297.m: Vadian brought the Reformation to St Gallen.

15298.q: What does the ‘Kappel milk soup’ of 1529 stand for?
a: The peaceful settlement of the First War of Kappel
A famine after the Second War of Kappel
Zurich's victory over the five cantons
The first Reformed Lord's Supper in Zurich
15298.e: In the First War of Kappel in 1529 there was no battle. According to tradition, soldiers from both sides ate a milk soup together, which became a symbol of Swiss understanding.
15298.m: The Kappel milk soup is a symbol of reconciliation among the Swiss.

15299.q: What did the First Peace of Kappel of 1529 lay down for the common lordships?
a: The municipalities could vote on their own faith
All municipalities had to stay Catholic
All municipalities had to become Reformed
The municipalities were handed over to Austria
15299.e: After the bloodless First War of Kappel, the Glarus Landammann Hans Aebli negotiated the peace. In the common lordships the majority of a municipality now decided on its faith.
15299.m: The First Peace of Kappel let municipalities decide on their faith.

15300.q: Which power did the five Catholic cantons ally with in the Christian Union of 1529?
15300.e: As a counterweight to the Reformed Christian Civic Union, Lucerne, Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden and Zug made an alliance with Austria. This increased tensions within the Confederacy.
15300.m: In 1529 the Catholic cantons sought support from Austria.

15301.q: What consequence did the Second Peace of Kappel of 20 November 1531 have?
a: The spread of the Reformation in German-speaking Switzerland was stopped
Zurich took over leadership of the Diet
The Catholic cantons left the Confederacy
15301.e: After Zurich's defeats at Kappel and on the Gubel, the Reformation came to a standstill in German-speaking Switzerland. The religious division of the Confederacy became fixed.
15301.m: The Second Peace of Kappel halted the Reformation in German-speaking Switzerland.

15302.q: Which territory did Bern conquer from Savoy in 1536 and introduce the Reformation to?
15302.e: In 1536 Bern and its allies conquered Vaud from Savoy and introduced the Reformation there. In the same year Geneva also became Reformed.
15302.m: Bern conquered Vaud in 1536 and made it Reformed.

15303.q: Which Reformed confession of faith of 1566 did Heinrich Bullinger write?
15303.e: The Second Helvetic Confession has 30 articles. It became one of the most important confessional documents of the Reformed churches in Europe.
15303.m: Bullinger's Confessio Helvetica posterior of 1566 united many Reformed Christians.

15304.q: What was the Golden League, concluded in 1586?
a: An alliance of the Catholic cantons to preserve the old faith
A trade agreement between Basel and Zurich
An alliance of the Reformed cities with England
15304.e: On 5 October 1586 the Catholic cantons pledged to keep the old faith and support one another. After its patron saint Charles Borromeo it is also called the Borromean League.
15304.m: In the Golden League of 1586 the Catholic cantons joined together.

15305.q: Which institution did Charles Borromeo open in Milan in 1579 to train Swiss priests?
15305.e: At the Collegium Helveticum priests for Catholic Switzerland were trained according to the decisions of Trent. Borromeo also encouraged the Capuchins to settle in Catholic areas.
15305.m: Charles Borromeo founded the Collegium Helveticum in Milan in 1579.

15306.q: Which canton was split into two half-cantons in 1597 for religious reasons?
15306.e: The division of 1597 created Catholic Innerrhoden and Reformed Ausserrhoden. The split shows how strongly religion shaped political life.
15306.m: In 1597 Appenzell was split into two parts by religion.

15307.q: Who won the First War of Villmergen in 1656?
15307.e: On 24 January 1656 the Catholic cantons defeated the Bernese at Villmergen. The Third Peace that followed confirmed Catholic supremacy.
15307.m: The Catholic cantons won the First War of Villmergen in 1656.

15308.q: What consequence did the Second War of Villmergen of 1712 have?
a: The supremacy of the Catholic cantons ended
The Reformation was reversed in Zurich
15308.e: Bern and Zurich won at Villmergen on 25 July 1712. The Fourth Peace of Aarau ended Catholic dominance in the Confederacy.
15308.m: After 1712 the Reformed cantons had the upper hand in the Confederacy.

15309.q: Which order contributed especially to Catholic renewal in Switzerland with colleges in Lucerne and Fribourg?
15309.e: The Jesuits founded colleges in Lucerne in 1574 and in Fribourg in 1582. Peter Canisius, a pioneer of Catholic renewal, also worked in Fribourg.
15309.m: The Jesuits shaped the Counter-Reformation in Switzerland.

15310.q: Which event of 23 May 1618 is considered the trigger of the Thirty Years' War?
a: The election of Ferdinand II as emperor
15310.e: On 23 May 1618 Protestant nobles threw two imperial governors and a secretary out of a window of Prague Castle. All survived, but the uprising of the Bohemian estates grew into a great war.
15310.m: The Defenestration of Prague in 1618 started the Thirty Years' War.

15311.q: In which battle was the army of the Bohemian estates decisively defeated in 1620?
a: At the Battle of White Mountain
15311.e: On 8 November 1620 imperial and League troops under Bucquoy and Tilly defeated the Bohemians near Prague. Strict re-Catholicisation followed in Bohemia.
15311.m: The Bohemian uprising was crushed at White Mountain in 1620.

15312.q: Why was Frederick V of the Palatinate called the ‘Winter King’?
a: Because he was King of Bohemia for only about one winter
Because he only waged war in winter
Because he grew up in Sweden
Because he was crowned in the winter of 1648
15312.e: Frederick V was elected king by the Bohemian estates in 1619. After the defeat at White Mountain in 1620 he had to flee; his reign lasted hardly longer than a winter.
15312.m: Frederick V was King of Bohemia only briefly and so was called the Winter King.

15313.q: What is the last phase of the Thirty Years' War usually called?
15313.e: Researchers usually divide the war into four phases. After the Bohemian-Palatine, the Danish-Lower Saxon and the Swedish War came the Swedish-French War from 1635.
15313.m: The last phase of the Thirty Years' War was the Swedish-French War.

15314.q: What did Emperor Ferdinand II's Edict of Restitution of 1629 demand?
a: The return of Church property that Protestants had seized since 1555
The recognition of the Calvinists in the Empire
The withdrawal of all Spanish troops
The dissolution of the Catholic League
15314.e: The edict was meant to restore the Catholic Church to its former possessions. It marked the high point of imperial power and revived Protestant resistance.
15314.m: The Edict of Restitution of 1629 demanded Church property back from the Protestants.

15315.q: In which year did the Swedish king Gustavus Adolphus enter the Thirty Years' War by landing on Usedom?
15315.e: Gustavus Adolphus landed with his army on the island of Usedom in the summer of 1630. He wanted to help the Protestants and secure Sweden's power on the Baltic.
15315.m: Sweden entered the war in 1630 when Gustavus Adolphus landed.

15316.q: Which city was captured and destroyed by League troops under Tilly in May 1631, with over 20,000 people dying?
15316.e: After a siege of several months Magdeburg was taken and burned down. It was the largest massacre of the war and shocked people all over Europe.
15316.m: The destruction of Magdeburg in 1631 became a symbol of the horrors of war.

15317.q: In which battle was Gustavus Adolphus killed in November 1632?
a: At the Battle of White Mountain
15317.e: The Swedish king was killed at Lützen on 16 November 1632. His death was a heavy loss for the Protestant side.
15317.m: Gustavus Adolphus was killed at Lützen in 1632.

15318.q: Where was the imperial general Albrecht von Wallenstein murdered in 1634?
15318.e: Wallenstein had lost the emperor's trust because he negotiated on his own. On 25 February 1634 he was killed in Eger by officers loyal to the emperor.
15318.m: Wallenstein was murdered in Eger in 1634.

15319.q: What was the significance of the Battle of Nördlingen in September 1634?
a: It brought Sweden a heavy defeat and weakened its position in the Empire
It was the Bohemians' first victory
It led to the coronation of Frederick V
15319.e: At Nördlingen the Swedes were crushingly defeated. Their power in southern Germany collapsed, which paved the way for the Peace of Prague.
15319.m: The defeat at Nördlingen in 1634 shook Swedish power.

15320.q: What happened in the Peace of Prague of 1635?
a: Most Protestant imperial estates made peace with the emperor
Sweden and France left the war
Switzerland became independent of the Empire
15320.e: Led by Saxony, many Protestant estates left the alliance with Sweden. In return the Edict of Restitution was suspended for 40 years.
15320.m: In the Peace of Prague in 1635 many Protestants made peace with the emperor.

15321.q: What does Catholic France's open entry into the war against the Habsburgs in 1635 show?
a: That power politics had become more important than religion
That the Pope forced France to do it
15321.e: Catholic France fought alongside Lutheran Sweden against the Catholic Habsburgs. The war thus finally turned into a European power struggle.
15321.m: France's entry in 1635 shows that power interests outweighed religion.

15322.q: How badly were some areas of southern Germany depopulated by the Thirty Years' War?
a: In places only about a third of the population survived
About two per cent of people died
15322.e: War, hunger and epidemics led to enormous losses. Some regions needed more than a century to recover.
15322.m: The Thirty Years' War dramatically depopulated some regions.

15323.q: Which denomination was not explicitly protected by the Peace of Augsburg of 1555, which later fuelled conflicts?
15323.e: The religious peace of 1555 only protected Catholics and followers of the Augsburg Confession. The unclear position of the Reformed was one of the tensions that led to war in 1618.
15323.m: The Peace of Augsburg left the position of the Calvinists unclear.

15324.q: On which day were the treaties of the Peace of Westphalia signed?
15324.e: On 24 October 1648 the treaties with France and Sweden were signed in Münster. This ended the Thirty Years' War.
15324.m: The Peace of Westphalia was signed on 24 October 1648.

15325.q: In which two cities was the Peace of Westphalia negotiated?
15325.e: In Osnabrück the emperor negotiated mainly with Sweden and the Protestant estates, in Münster with France. Both cities are in Westphalia.
15325.m: The Peace of Westphalia was negotiated in Münster and Osnabrück.

15326.q: With which power did the emperor and the Empire make peace in Osnabrück in 1648?
15326.e: The Treaty of Osnabrück settled relations between the emperor, the Empire and Sweden. The Treaty of Münster concerned the emperor and France.
15326.m: In Osnabrück the emperor and the Empire made peace with Sweden.

15327.q: What did the Swiss Confederacy achieve in the Peace of Westphalia?
a: Legal separation from the Holy Roman Empire
Admission to the council of electors
15327.e: Article VI of the Treaty of Osnabrück recognised the Confederacy as independent of the Empire. In practice it had been independent for some time, but now this was confirmed in international law.
15327.m: Since 1648 the Confederacy has been legally separate from the Empire.

15328.q: Which mayor of Basel represented the Confederacy at the peace congress of Westphalia?
15328.e: Wettstein travelled to Westphalia in 1646. He made sure that the exemption of Basel and the Confederacy from the Empire was included in the peace treaty.
15328.m: Johann Rudolf Wettstein of Basel won the Confederacy's exemption in 1648.

15329.q: Which denomination was given equal legal status with the Lutherans in the Empire in the Peace of Westphalia?
15329.e: The Peace of Augsburg of 1555 had recognised only Catholics and Lutherans. In 1648 the Reformed, the followers of Calvin and Zwingli, were also recognised as having equal rights.
15329.m: From 1648 the Reformed had equal status with the Lutherans in the Empire.

15330.q: What did the so-called normal year in the Peace of Westphalia lay down?
a: Which denomination Church property belongs to, based on its state in a reference year
In which year the next war is allowed
From when the calendar is counted anew
How long an emperor may rule
15330.e: Religious property was to stay or be restored as it had been in the reference year 1624. This was meant to end disputes over churches and monasteries.
15330.m: The normal year 1624 set the Church property holdings after 1648.

15331.q: Which territory did Sweden receive in the Peace of Westphalia?
15331.e: Sweden received, among other things, Western Pomerania with Stettin, Wismar, and Bremen and Verden. These territories remained imperial fiefs, giving Sweden a seat and a vote in the Imperial Diet.
15331.m: In 1648 Sweden gained Western Pomerania, among other territories.

15332.q: Which bishoprics were finally awarded to France in the Peace of Westphalia?
15332.e: France received the three bishoprics of Metz, Toul and Verdun as well as rights in Alsace. This moved its border towards the Rhine.
15332.m: In 1648 France secured Metz, Toul and Verdun.

15333.q: Which two powers became guarantors of the Peace of Westphalia?
15333.e: France and Sweden were to guarantee that the treaties were kept. This gave them a say in the affairs of the Empire.
15333.m: France and Sweden guaranteed the Peace of Westphalia.

15334.q: What special right did the prince-electors have in the Holy Roman Empire?
a: They were the only ones allowed to mint coins
15334.e: The electors chose the King of the Romans, who could then become emperor. In the Peace of Westphalia a new, eighth electorate was created for the Palatinate.
15334.m: The electors chose the king; in 1648 an eighth electorate was added.

15335.q: Which country was finally recognised as independent of Spain in the Peace of Münster in 1648?
15335.e: In connection with the Westphalian peace congress, Spain and the Netherlands made peace in 1648. After eighty years of war Spain thus recognised the independence of the Netherlands.
15335.m: In 1648 Spain recognised the independence of the Netherlands.

15336.q: Which ruling house did the emperor who made the Peace of Westphalia in 1648 come from?
15336.e: Emperor Ferdinand III of the House of Habsburg made the peace in 1648. The Habsburgs provided the emperors of the Empire almost without interruption.
15336.m: The Habsburg Ferdinand III made the Peace of Westphalia in 1648.

15337.q: Which principle of international order is often linked with the Peace of Westphalia in political science?
a: The world rule of the Pope
The founding of the United Nations
15337.e: The term ‘Westphalian system’ describes an order of sovereign states that do not interfere in the internal affairs of others. Historians stress, however, that this picture greatly simplifies the treaty of 1648.
15337.m: The Peace of Westphalia is a symbol of an order of sovereign states.

15338.q: Which Latin expression does the term ‘absolutism’ go back to?
a: princeps civitatis, ‘first citizen of the state’
15338.e: The absolute ruler was seen as ‘legibus absolutus’, that is, not bound by the laws he himself had made. The name of the era comes from this.
15338.m: The absolute ruler claimed to stand above the laws.

15339.q: Which 16th-century French political theorist defined sovereignty as the highest power over citizens and subjects, released from the laws?
15339.e: With his ‘Six Books of the Commonwealth’ Jean Bodin provided a theoretical basis for absolutism. But he demanded that the sovereign, too, respect natural law and God's commandments.
15339.m: Jean Bodin is an important theorist of sovereignty.

15340.q: Against what background did Thomas Hobbes publish his ‘Leviathan’ in 1651?
a: Against the background of the English Civil War
After the end of the Hundred Years' War
15340.e: The experience of civil war shaped Hobbes's belief that only a strong sovereign can prevent the war of all against all. People hand over their power to him in a contract.
15340.m: In ‘Leviathan’ Hobbes justified strong rule by the fear of civil war.

15341.q: How did absolute rulers such as Louis XIV mainly justify their power?
15341.e: The rulers claimed to hold their power ‘by the grace of God’. According to their claim, they were therefore answerable only to God.
15341.m: Divine right placed the king under God alone.

15342.q: Which period is traditionally called the age of absolutism?
a: From the Peace of Westphalia in 1648 to the French Revolution in 1789
From the Reformation in 1517 to the Peace of Westphalia in 1648
From the Congress of Vienna in 1815 to the revolution of 1848
From the discovery of America in 1492 to 1600
15342.e: The era is usually placed between the end of the wars of religion and the revolutions of the late 18th century. In research, however, the boundaries are fluid.
15342.m: Absolutism shaped Europe mainly between 1648 and 1789.

15343.q: Which ruler called himself the ‘first servant of the state’ and is seen as a representative of enlightened absolutism?
15343.e: Frederick II saw his rule as a duty to the state and abolished torture in most criminal trials in 1740. But he did not allow a constitution to limit his power.
15343.m: In enlightened absolutism the ruler wanted to push through reforms from above.

15344.q: What did Emperor Joseph II issue in 1781 as a typical measure of enlightened absolutism?
a: A Patent of Toleration for non-Catholic Christians
15344.e: With the Patents of Toleration of 1781 and 1782 Joseph II gave Lutherans, Reformed, Orthodox and Jews more rights in the Habsburg lands. The reforms came from above, without the people having a say.
15344.m: Joseph II promoted religious toleration through Patents of Toleration.

15345.q: How does more recent historical research judge the term ‘absolutism’?
a: It stresses that in practice rulers never ruled without limits
It considers it the most precise description of the early modern period
It now uses it only for ancient Rome
It equates it with modern dictatorship
15345.e: Historians such as Nicholas Henshall speak of the ‘myth of absolutism’ because kings remained dependent on the nobility, officials and regional elites. Claim and practice of rule were often far apart.
15345.m: Absolute rulers claimed more power than they actually had.

15346.q: How old was Louis XIV when he became King of France in 1643?
15346.e: Louis XIV was born in 1638 and came to the throne as a small child in 1643. At first his mother Anne of Austria and Cardinal Mazarin ruled.
15346.m: Louis XIV became king as a small child.

15347.q: Which event in 1661 marks the start of Louis XIV's personal rule?
15347.e: After Mazarin's death in 1661 Louis XIV did without a chief minister and ruled himself. This personal rule lasted until his death in 1715.
15347.m: From 1661 Louis XIV ruled without a chief minister.

15348.q: Which experience from his youth shaped Louis XIV's mistrust of the nobility and the Paris Parlement?
15348.e: The Fronde (1648 to 1653) was a series of uprisings by the nobility and the Parlement against the Crown. The young king even had to flee Paris.
15348.m: The Fronde taught Louis XIV to control the nobility.

15349.q: What political purpose did the court's move to Versailles in 1682 serve?
a: The high nobility was tied to the court and watched
The king wanted to live closer to the Spanish border
Versailles was to be the seat of an elected parliament
The court wanted to avoid taxes in Paris
15349.e: At the court of Versailles the nobility depended on the king's favour and was far from its regional power base. Court ceremony made the king's position visible.
15349.m: Versailles made the nobility dependent on the king.

15350.q: What consequence did the Edict of Fontainebleau of 1685 have?
a: It revoked the Edict of Nantes and drove many Huguenots into exile
It granted the Huguenots full religious freedom
It ended the War of the Spanish Succession
It created the first French parliament
15350.e: With the Edict of Fontainebleau Louis XIV revoked the rights of the Protestants. Many Huguenots fled, among other places to Switzerland, Prussia and the Netherlands.
15350.m: With the Edict of Fontainebleau the Huguenots lost their rights.

15351.q: How long did Louis XIV's reign last in total?
15351.e: Louis XIV was king from 1643 to 1715, that is 72 years. It is one of the longest reigns in European history.

15352.q: Which peace of 1713 largely ended the War of the Spanish Succession for France, Great Britain and Spain?
15352.e: In the Peace of Utrecht Philip of Anjou was recognised as King of Spain but was not allowed to unite France and Spain. The Nine Years' War had already been ended in 1697 by the Peace of Ryswick.
15352.m: The Peace of Utrecht in 1713 prevented a union of France and Spain.

15353.q: Who succeeded Louis XIV on the throne in 1715?
a: His son Louis, the Grand Dauphin
15353.e: Because his son and grandson died before him, his great-grandson inherited the crown as a small child. Philippe II d'Orléans became regent.
15353.m: Louis XV was the great-grandson of Louis XIV.

15354.q: What does source criticism say about the sentence ‘L'État c'est moi’ (‘I am the state’) attributed to Louis XIV?
a: It is not recorded at the time and is thought to have been attributed to him later
It is in his handwritten will
It was printed in the Edict of Fontainebleau
It survives as an inscription at Versailles
15354.e: The sentence sums up the absolutist self-image well but is not recorded as something Louis said. Such famous quotations must always be checked against their source.
15354.m: ‘L'État c'est moi’ was probably never said in that form.

15355.q: What was the most important aim of mercantilist economic policy?
a: A trade surplus with more exports than imports
Completely free trade without customs duties
15355.e: Mercantilism wanted to export as many finished goods as possible and import few. This was meant to bring money, especially gold and silver, into the country.
15355.m: Mercantilism wanted to export more than it imported.

15356.q: After which minister of Louis XIV is the French form of mercantilism named?
15356.e: As Controller-General of Finances, Jean-Baptiste Colbert steered the French economy. He founded state manufactories and promoted trade and transport, which is why people speak of Colbertism.

15357.q: Which customs policy is typical of mercantilism?
a: High duties on imported finished goods, low ones on raw materials
High duties on imported raw materials, none on finished goods
15357.e: Home industries were to be protected from foreign competition and get raw materials cheaply. Internal customs duties were reduced to create a single market.
15357.m: Mercantilists protected home industry with import duties on finished goods.

15358.q: What role did mercantilism give to the colonies?
a: Suppliers of raw materials and markets for the mother country's goods
Equal trading partners with their own industry
15358.e: Colonies were to supply cheap raw materials and buy the mother country's finished goods. England even partly banned its colonies from making certain finished goods.
15358.m: Under mercantilism colonies mainly served the mother country.

15359.q: What is the German version of mercantilism, strongly focused on state finances, called?
15359.e: Cameralism arose after the Thirty Years' War and aimed at tax revenue, agriculture, trade and population growth. The name comes from the prince's chamber, which managed the finances.
15359.m: Cameralism was the German form of mercantilism.

15360.q: What did the English Navigation Act of 1651 lay down?
a: Goods could only be brought to England on English ships or ships of the country of origin
All English ports were opened to foreign ships
15360.e: Only English ships could bring goods from overseas, and European goods only on English ships or ships of the producing country. This was aimed mainly against Dutch carrying trade and strengthened the English merchant fleet.
15360.m: The Navigation Act protected English shipping.

15361.q: Which economist criticised mercantilism in 1776 in his work on ‘The Wealth of Nations’?
15361.e: Adam Smith thought it was wrong to equate wealth with gold and silver. He relied on the division of labour and free trade.
15361.m: Adam Smith is seen as a critic of mercantilism and founder of classical economics.

15362.q: Which French school of thought countered mercantilism with the motto ‘Laissez faire, laissez passer’?
15362.e: The Physiocrats saw land as the source of wealth and criticised the neglect of agriculture. They rejected state control of the economy.
15362.m: The Physiocrats called for less state interference in the economy.

15363.q: In which town was Nicolaus Copernicus born in 1473?
15363.e: Copernicus was born on 19 February 1473 in Thorn (Toruń), which then belonged to Royal Prussia under the Polish crown. He later studied in Kraków and Italy.
15363.m: Copernicus came from Thorn on the Vistula.

15364.q: When and where did Copernicus's main work ‘De revolutionibus orbium coelestium’ appear?
15364.e: The work was printed in 1543 by Johannes Petreius in Nuremberg. Copernicus died in the same year.
15364.m: Copernicus's main work appeared in 1543, the year of his death.

15365.q: What is the core of the Copernican view of the world?
a: The Earth and the planets orbit the Sun
The Sun orbits the Earth, which stands still
The Earth is a disc at the centre of the universe
All heavenly bodies orbit the Moon
15365.e: Copernicus replaced Ptolemy's geocentric view of the world with a heliocentric one. The Earth thus became one planet among others.
15365.m: The Copernican view of the world puts the Sun at the centre.

15366.q: Which discovery of Galileo's later supported Copernicus's view of the world?
a: The curve of the Earth during a lunar eclipse
The discovery of the planet Uranus
Galaxies moving away from each other
15366.e: In 1610 Galileo saw through his telescope moons orbiting Jupiter. This made it clear that not everything revolves around the Earth.
15366.m: Galileo's moons of Jupiter supported the heliocentric view of the world.

15367.q: Why did Copernicus only have his main work printed shortly before his death?
a: He feared mockery and opposition to his new teaching
The Church had banned him from writing
Printing had not yet been invented
He had only started the work shortly before
15367.e: Copernicus worked on his theory for decades but hesitated to publish it. Only his student Rheticus persuaded him to have the work printed in 1543.
15367.m: Copernicus hesitated for a long time to publish his teaching.

15368.q: What did Andreas Osiander's anonymous preface in ‘De revolutionibus’ claim?
a: That the model was only a mathematical hypothesis for calculations
That Copernicus had withdrawn his theory
That the Pope had expressly approved the work
That the Earth really stood still
15368.e: Osiander added the preface without Copernicus's agreement, probably to avoid conflict. It weakened the work's claim to truth.
15368.m: Osiander's preface presented the work as just a calculation model.

15369.q: Which office did Copernicus hold for most of his life?
a: Canon in the Prince-Bishopric of Warmia
15369.e: Copernicus was a canon in Frombork, did administrative work and also worked as a doctor. He studied astronomy alongside these duties.
15369.m: Copernicus was a canon and did astronomy alongside his office.

a: The work was put on the Index until certain passages were corrected
It became the Church's official teaching
It was translated into German for the first time
15370.e: In the course of the dispute over Galileo, the Church put the book on the Index of Forbidden Books in 1616 until certain passages were corrected. Before that it had caused hardly any offence for decades.
15370.m: Only in 1616 did the Church object to Copernicus's work.

15371.q: In which city was Galileo Galilei born in 1564?
15371.e: Galileo was born in Pisa on 15 February 1564. He later taught there too and studied the pendulum.
15371.m: Galileo Galilei was born in Pisa.

15372.q: Which work made Galileo suddenly famous in 1610 with his telescope observations?
15372.e: In the ‘Starry Messenger’ Galileo described the rough surface of the Moon, the many stars of the Milky Way and the moons of Jupiter. The work caused a stir throughout Europe.
15372.m: The ‘Sidereus Nuncius’ of 1610 made Galileo famous.

15373.q: Why were the moons of Jupiter discovered by Galileo an argument against the geocentric view of the world?
a: They showed that not all heavenly bodies orbit the Earth
They proved that the Moon is bigger than the Earth
They showed that Jupiter orbits the Moon
They proved that there are no planets
15373.e: The four large moons of Jupiter visibly orbit a body other than the Earth. So the Earth was no longer the only centre of motion.
15373.m: The moons of Jupiter showed that not everything orbits the Earth.

15374.q: Which observation by Galileo at the end of 1610 contradicted the Ptolemaic view of the world especially clearly?
15374.e: Like the Moon, Venus shows all phases and changes its apparent size. This is impossible in the Ptolemaic model, but possible if Venus orbits the Sun.
15374.m: The phases of Venus suggest that Venus orbits the Sun.

15375.q: Why did Galileo write his ‘Dialogo’, published in 1632, in Italian rather than Latin?
a: He wanted to reach a wider educated audience
Latin was banned in Italy at the time
The Church required Italian for works on astronomy
15375.e: By using the everyday language Galileo also reached readers outside the universities. The dialogue defended the Copernican system and led to his trial.
15375.m: Galileo wrote the ‘Dialogo’ in Italian to reach many people.

15376.q: How did Galileo's trial end in 1633?
a: He had to recant and then lived under house arrest
He was acquitted and made a cardinal
15376.e: The Inquisition accused Galileo of ignoring the ban of 1616. He recanted, and his prison sentence was changed to house arrest in his villa in Arcetri.
15376.m: Galileo spent his last years under house arrest in Arcetri.

15377.q: When did Pope John Paul II declare Galileo's condemnation a mistake?
15377.e: On 31 October 1992 John Paul II acknowledged the wrong done to Galileo. This ended a centuries-long conflict over his sentence.
15377.m: The Catholic Church only rehabilitated Galileo in 1992.

15378.q: With what did Galileo study the laws of falling bodies in his ‘Discorsi’ of 1638?
a: With balls on an inclined plane
15378.e: On the inclined plane balls rolled slowly enough to measure their acceleration. Galileo also showed that the paths of thrown objects are parabolas.
15378.m: Galileo studied the laws of falling with the inclined plane.

15379.q: What does source criticism say about the sentence ‘And yet it moves’, which Galileo is said to have spoken after recanting?
a: It is not recorded at the time and is considered a legend
It appears word for word in the trial record of 1633
It is the title of his last book
It comes from a letter to Kepler
15379.e: Neither the trial records nor the early biography by Vincenzo Viviani mention the saying. It only appears in print in 1757 and is part of the legend that grew up around Galileo.
15379.m: The sentence ‘And yet it moves’ is probably a legend.

15380.q: In which year did Newton's main work ‘Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica’ appear?
15380.e: The Principia appeared in Latin in 1687. In it Newton set out the laws of motion and the law of gravitation.

15381.q: What was new about Newton's law of gravitation?
a: The same force explains the fall of an apple and the orbit of the Moon
It applied only to bodies on Earth
It showed that the planets move in circles around the Earth
15381.e: Newton united earthly and heavenly mechanics. The attraction between masses decreases with the square of the distance.
15381.m: Newton explained heaven and Earth with the same force of gravity.

15382.q: What does Newton's first law of motion, the principle of inertia, say?
a: A body stays at rest or in uniform motion as long as no force acts on it
Every force produces an equal opposing force
Heavy bodies fall faster than light ones
15382.e: The principle of inertia describes the state without any outside force. The other statements are the second and third laws or an ancient error.
15382.m: Without a force, a body does not change its motion.

15383.q: With whom did Newton argue about who first invented calculus?
15383.e: Newton and Leibniz developed calculus independently of each other. The priority dispute began in 1699, peaked in 1712 and lasted until Leibniz's death in 1716.
15383.m: Newton and Leibniz invented calculus independently of each other.

15384.q: What did Newton show in his work on optics, published in 1704 as ‘Opticks’?
a: White light is made up of the colours of the spectrum
Colours only arise in the eye
The prism creates the colours itself
15384.e: With prisms Newton split white light into colours and put it back together again. In this way he disproved the view that the prism colours the light.
15384.m: According to Newton, white light consists of all the colours of the spectrum.

15385.q: Which scientific society did Newton preside over from 1703 until his death?
a: The Académie des sciences in Paris
The Accademia dei Lincei in Rome
15385.e: Newton became President of the Royal Society in 1703 after the death of his rival Robert Hooke. He shaped it for over two decades.
15385.m: Newton led the Royal Society from 1703.

15386.q: Why does one find both 1642 and 1643 for Newton's birth?
a: England was still using the Julian calendar at the time
He himself gave two dates of birth
He was born on New Year's Eve
15386.e: According to the Julian calendar Newton was born on 25 December 1642, according to the Gregorian calendar on 4 January 1643. England only introduced the Gregorian calendar in 1752.
15386.m: Different calendars lead to different dates for the same event.

15387.q: Where was Isaac Newton buried in 1727?
15387.e: Newton was buried with great honours in Westminster Abbey in London. This shows the enormous respect he already enjoyed in his lifetime.
15387.m: Newton is buried in Westminster Abbey.

15388.q: According to John Locke, which natural rights must the state above all protect?
a: Voting rights, press freedom and asylum
15388.e: Locke saw the protection of life, liberty and property as the purpose of the state. People have these rights even before any government exists.
15388.m: For Locke the state protects life, liberty and property.

15389.q: Which work by Locke appeared after the Glorious Revolution and bases government on the consent of the governed?
15389.e: The ‘Two Treatises of Government’ appeared anonymously, dated 1690. They justified a limited government based on consent.

15390.q: According to Locke, what may citizens do if a government violates their natural rights?
a: They may resist and remove the government
They must still put up with the government without conditions
They must ask the Pope for help
15390.e: Unlike Hobbes, Locke believed the contract of government could be ended. A government that betrays its purpose loses its legitimacy.
15390.m: Locke justified a right of resistance against unjust rulers.

15391.q: What does Locke's image of the ‘tabula rasa’ in his ‘Essay Concerning Human Understanding’ of 1690 stand for?
a: The mind is empty at birth and is filled by experience
Humans have inborn ideas of God
15391.e: Locke rejected inborn ideas; all knowledge comes from experience. He is therefore seen as an important representative of empiricism.
15391.m: According to Locke, all knowledge comes from experience.

15392.q: Where did John Locke flee into exile in 1683?
15392.e: Locke fled to the Netherlands for political reasons. After the Glorious Revolution he returned to England at the beginning of 1689.
15392.m: Locke spent his years of exile in the Netherlands.

15393.q: Which three powers of the state did John Locke distinguish?
15393.e: Locke separated the law-making power from the executive power and named the federative power for foreign relations. Only Montesquieu stressed the judiciary as a separate power.
15393.m: Locke did not yet have a separate judicial power.

15394.q: Which wording replaced Locke's term ‘property’ in the American Declaration of Independence of 1776?
15394.e: Instead of property, the Declaration of Independence names ‘the pursuit of happiness’ as an unalienable right. This shows Locke's great influence on the American Founding Fathers.
15394.m: The American Declaration of Independence builds on Locke's theory of natural law.

15395.q: Which group did Locke expressly exclude from toleration in his ‘Letter Concerning Toleration’?
15395.e: Locke believed that someone who did not believe in God could not be bound by any oath. His idea of toleration was progressive but still limited.
15395.m: Locke's toleration had limits and did not apply to atheists.

15396.q: When did Montesquieu's main work ‘The Spirit of the Laws’ appear?
