15837.q: What is the idea called that Europeans had to bring “civilisation” to other peoples, which was used to justify colonial rule?
15837.e: The civilising mission (French “mission civilisatrice”) presented conquest as a kindness. It was based on the assumption that one's own culture was superior.
15837.m: The civilising mission served as a justification for colonial rule.

15838.q: With which slogan did the German state secretary Bernhard von Bülow demand German colonies in 1897?
15838.e: On 6 December 1897 Bülow told the Reichstag that Germany also demanded its “place in the sun”. The phrase became a slogan for Germany's claim to colonies and world standing.
15838.m: With the “place in the sun”, Germany demanded colonies of its own.

15839.q: Which economic motive played a central role in imperialism?
a: Access to raw materials and markets
Abolishing all customs duties in Europe
15839.e: Industrialisation increased the demand for raw materials such as cotton, rubber or copper. Colonies were also meant to serve as markets for industrial goods.
15839.m: Raw materials and new markets were important motives of imperialism.

15840.q: What is the policy called that Wilhelm II pursued at the end of the 19th century to make Germany a world power with colonies and a navy?
15840.e: Wilhelm II broke away from Bismarck's cautious alliance policy and strove for world standing. This included colonies and a large naval build-up, which worsened tensions with Great Britain.
15840.m: German Weltpolitik worsened tensions with Great Britain.

15841.q: Which state acquired the Philippines in 1898 after the war against Spain?
15841.e: After the Spanish-American War, Spain ceded the Philippines to the USA in the Treaty of Paris in 1898. The USA thereby became a colonial power in Asia itself.
15841.m: From 1898 the USA was a colonial power in Asia.

15842.q: Which consequence of imperialism is seen as one of the long-term causes of the First World War?
a: the sharper rivalry between the great powers
the founding of the League of Nations
15842.e: Competition for colonies led to crises such as Fashoda or the Moroccan Crises. These tensions hardened the alliance systems before 1914.
15842.m: Colonial rivalry contributed to the tensions before the First World War.

15843.q: Which domestic aim did governments in the German Empire also pursue with colonial successes?
a: To distract from social tensions at home
To raise taxes for the rich
15843.e: Successes abroad were meant to stir pride and distract from conflicts between workers and property owners. Historians call this social imperialism.
15843.m: Colonial successes were meant to distract from internal conflicts.

15844.q: What is the basic difference between colonialism and imperialism?
a: Colonialism means direct rule over colonies, imperialism any form of expanding power
Colonialism means any form of expanding power, imperialism only rule over settler colonies
Colonialism means only trade with colonies, imperialism only their military conquest
Colonialism means the time before 1800, imperialism the same policy after 1800 with no real difference
15844.e: Colonialism means rule over a territory with a foreign population by a foreign power. Imperialism is broader and also includes indirect domination without colonies.
15844.m: Imperialism is the broader term, colonialism means direct rule.

15845.q: What do you call a colony to which many people from the mother country emigrated permanently?
15845.e: Many Europeans settled in settler colonies such as Australia or Canada. The local population was often pushed out or decimated.
15845.m: Many people from Europe settled in settler colonies.

a: a territory with its own government that is under the control of a foreign protecting power
a colony without a local population
a trading post on the coast
an independent state without an army
15846.e: In a protectorate, local rulers formally stay in office, but the protecting power decides above all foreign and military policy. Examples are Tunisia under France or Zanzibar under Great Britain.
15846.m: A protectorate is under the influence of a foreign protecting power.

15847.q: Which principle of British colonial administration used local rulers and structures to govern a territory?
15847.e: Under indirect rule, the British governed for example Nigeria through local rulers. This saved staff and costs.
15847.m: Under indirect rule, the colonial power governed through local rulers.

15848.q: Which colonial policy did France officially pursue by trying to turn local people into “Frenchmen”?
15848.e: The assimilation policy was meant to spread France's language, culture and law in the colonies. In practice, however, only a small minority received full civil rights.
15848.m: France officially pursued an assimilation policy in its colonies.

15849.q: Which Swiss missionary society was founded in 1815 and worked, among other places, on the Gold Coast (today Ghana)?
15849.e: The Basel Mission was founded in 1815 and worked on the Gold Coast from 1828 and in southern India from 1834. Through its own trading company it also traded in cocoa and palm oil.
15849.m: The Basel Mission worked in Africa and India from the 19th century.

15850.q: In which colonial army did around 8,000 Swiss mercenaries serve between 1815 and the First World War?
a: in the Dutch army in the Dutch East Indies
15850.e: Many Swiss signed up for the Dutch colonial army in what is now Indonesia. This shows that Switzerland took part in colonialism even without colonies of its own.
15850.m: Swiss men also fought as mercenaries in colonial wars.

15851.q: How did Swiss trading houses profit from colonialism in the 19th century, although Switzerland had no colonies?
a: They traded in raw materials from colonies such as cotton and coffee
They bought their own islands in the Caribbean
15851.e: Firms such as Gebrüder Volkart from Winterthur imported cotton and coffee from India and exported industrial goods. In this way Switzerland was closely tied into colonial world trade.
15851.m: Swiss trading houses profited from colonial world trade.

15852.q: How is Switzerland's involvement in colonialism often described by researchers?
15852.e: Switzerland never had colonies of its own. But Swiss firms, banks, missions, scientists and mercenaries were closely tied into colonial structures.
15852.m: Switzerland took part in colonialism without having colonies of its own.

15853.q: What were “human zoos”, which also took place in Swiss cities around 1900?
a: Shows in which people from other continents were put on display
15853.e: In human zoos, people from Africa or Asia, for example, were presented as “exotic” in zoos or at fairs. They spread racist ideas among the European population.
15853.m: Human zoos spread racist images of people from other continents.

15854.q: Which problem have the borders drawn by colonial powers in Africa caused up to today?
a: They split groups that belonged together and united rival ones
They were only temporary for a few years
15854.e: Many borders were drawn at the negotiating table, often as straight lines. They took little account of settlement areas, languages or political units.
15854.m: Colonial borders still have effects in Africa today.

15855.q: What is the process called in which colonies gained their independence after the Second World War?
15855.e: Decolonisation mainly covered the period from about 1945 into the 1970s. Many states in Asia and Africa became independent in this phase.
15855.m: After 1945 many colonies became independent through decolonisation.

15856.q: Which year is called the “Year of Africa” because a particularly large number of African states became independent then?
15856.e: In 1960, 18 colonies in Africa gained independence; because two of them immediately united to form Somalia, people usually speak of 17 new states. The year is seen as the high point of Africa's decolonisation.
15856.m: In the Year of Africa, 1960, a particularly large number of states became independent.

15857.q: What is the economic dependence of former colonies on industrial nations after formal independence called?
15857.e: The term neocolonialism describes influence through loans, trade conditions or corporations. It was spread, among others, by the Ghanaian president Kwame Nkrumah.
15857.m: Neocolonialism describes dependence despite formal independence.

15858.q: Which French scholar described the nation in 1882 as a “daily plebiscite”?
15858.e: In his lecture “What is a Nation?” at the Sorbonne, Renan stressed the shared will rather than language, religion or descent.
15858.m: For Ernest Renan, the nation was based on a shared will.

15859.q: Why is Switzerland often called a “nation by will” (Willensnation)?
a: because it is based not on a common language but on the will to live together
because it was founded through a war
because all its inhabitants have the same religion
because it was united by a king
15859.e: Switzerland brings together several languages and denominations. Its unity is based on shared history, institutions and the will to be one state.
15859.m: Switzerland is seen as a nation by will with several languages.

15860.q: Which philosopher gave the “Addresses to the German Nation” in 1807 and 1808?
15860.e: Fichte gave the addresses in Berlin while it was occupied by Napoleon. He called for a national education and strengthened German national consciousness.
15860.m: Fichte's addresses boosted German national consciousness under Napoleon's rule.

15861.q: Which thinker shaped the idea that every people has its own “national spirit” (Volksgeist), shown in its language and songs?
15861.e: Herder stressed the distinct character of every language and folk culture. His ideas were taken up by many national movements in the 19th century.
15861.m: Herder's idea of the Volksgeist influenced many national movements.

15862.q: In which year was the Kingdom of Italy proclaimed?
15862.e: In 1861 Victor Emmanuel II was proclaimed King of Italy. Rome was only added in 1870 and then became the capital.
15862.m: The Kingdom of Italy was created in 1861.

15863.q: Where was the German Empire proclaimed on 18 January 1871?
a: in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles
in St Paul's Church in Frankfurt
15863.e: After the victory over France, Wilhelm I was proclaimed German Emperor in the Palace of Versailles. This location humiliated France and strained relations between the two countries.
15863.m: The German Empire was proclaimed at Versailles in 1871.

15864.q: Which Italian revolutionary founded the secret society “Young Italy” in 1831?
15864.e: Mazzini aimed for a united, republican Italy. He also spent years in exile, including in Switzerland.
15864.m: Giuseppe Mazzini was a leading thinker of Italian unification.

15865.q: What do you call an exaggerated, aggressive nationalism that looks down on other nations?
15865.e: The term goes back to the figure of the French soldier Nicolas Chauvin. Chauvinism combines a feeling of superiority with hostility towards others.

15866.q: How did nationalism change in the late 19th century compared with the period around 1830?
a: It became increasingly conservative, aggressive and linked to imperialism
It was completely banned by the monarchies
It disappeared after the founding of the nation states
It was directed mainly against colonies
15866.e: At first, nationalism was closely linked to liberal demands for freedom. Later, governments used it to support power politics and colonial expansion.
15866.m: Nationalism changed from a liberal movement into an often aggressive one.

15867.q: In which Swiss city did the First Zionist Congress take place in 1897?
15867.e: Theodor Herzl called the congress in Basel in 1897. Zionism was a Jewish national movement that aimed for a homeland in Palestine.
15867.m: The First Zionist Congress met in Basel in 1897.

15868.q: Which 19th-century movement aimed for the unity of all Slavic peoples, often under Russia's leadership?
15868.e: Pan-Slavism stressed the bond between the Slavic peoples. It sharpened tensions in the Balkans between Russia and Austria-Hungary.
15868.m: Pan-Slavism increased tensions in the Balkans.

15869.q: Which German interest group called for an aggressive colonial and power policy from 1891?
15869.e: The association was founded in 1891 and took the name Pan-German League in 1894. It demanded colonies and naval armament and held ethnic nationalist and antisemitic views.
15869.m: The Pan-German League combined nationalism with imperial demands.

15870.q: Which affair involving a Jewish officer divided France from 1894 and showed the link between nationalism and antisemitism?
15870.e: Alfred Dreyfus was wrongly convicted of treason in 1894. He was only cleared years later; Émile Zola had stood up for him with “J'accuse”.
15870.m: The Dreyfus affair showed the link between nationalism and antisemitism.

15871.q: Which people fought for independence from the Ottoman Empire from 1821 and was supported by many Europeans?
15871.e: The Greek struggle for independence began in 1821 and was supported by European “philhellenes”. An independent Greek state was created around 1830.
15871.m: The Greek fight for freedom from 1821 inspired many Europeans.

15872.q: Who invited participants to the Berlin Conference on Africa (Congo Conference) in 1884?
15872.e: The conference lasted from 15 November 1884 to 26 February 1885. Bismarck wanted to settle conflicts between the colonial powers in Africa.
15872.m: Bismarck called the Berlin Congo Conference in 1884.

15873.q: Which principle for territorial claims in Africa was laid down at the Berlin Congo Conference?
15873.e: Under the principle of effective occupation, a colonial power had to actually take possession of a territory and control it. This sped up the Scramble for Africa.
15873.m: The principle of effective occupation sped up the Scramble for Africa.

15874.q: Were African representatives involved in the Berlin Congo Conference?
a: No, no African state was represented
Yes, with their own right of veto
15874.e: European states, the USA and the Ottoman Empire took part in the conference. The future of Africa was negotiated without Africans.
15874.m: In Berlin, decisions about Africa were made without Africans.

15875.q: Who owned the Congo Free State from 1885 to 1908?
a: King Leopold II of Belgium personally
15875.e: The Congo Free State was a private colony of Leopold II. Only in 1908, after international criticism, did it pass to the Belgian state as the Belgian Congo.
15875.m: The Congo Free State was Leopold II's private colony.

15876.q: Which raw material was at the centre of exploitation in the Congo Free State?
15876.e: Demand for rubber for tyres and cables rose sharply. The population was forced to collect it through forced labour and brutal punishments.
15876.m: In the Congo Free State, rubber was obtained through forced labour.

15877.q: Which British consul confirmed the atrocities in the Congo Free State in an investigation report published in 1904?
15877.e: Roger Casement investigated the conditions in 1903 on behalf of the British government. His report supported Edmund Dene Morel's campaign against Leopold's rule.
15877.m: Roger Casement's report made the Congo atrocities known around the world.

15878.q: Which two African states were not under European colonial rule around 1914?
15878.e: Ethiopia successfully defended itself against Italy in 1896. Liberia had been founded in the 19th century as a settlement area for freed slaves from the USA and remained formally independent.
15878.m: Around 1914, only Ethiopia and Liberia were independent in Africa.

15879.q: In which year did the Fashoda Crisis between Great Britain and France occur?
15879.e: In Sudan, French troops under Marchand and British troops under Kitchener met. France gave way, and the peaceful solution paved the way for the Entente Cordiale of 1904.
15879.m: The Fashoda Crisis of 1898 ended with France's withdrawal.

15880.q: Which colonial aim clashed at Fashoda with the British plan for a north-south link?
a: France's plan for an east-west axis across Africa
Germany's plan for a railway to Baghdad
Portugal's plan to link Angola with Mozambique
15880.e: France wanted to connect its territories from West to East Africa. Great Britain aimed for a line from Cairo to Cape Town; both plans crossed in Sudan.
15880.m: At Fashoda the British and French plans for Africa crossed.

15881.q: Which territory became the first German colony in Africa in 1884?
15881.e: The starting point was the land bought by the Bremen merchant Adolf Lüderitz. In 1884 the German Empire placed the territory in present-day Namibia under its “protection”.
15881.m: German South West Africa, in present-day Namibia, became a German colony in 1884.

15882.q: In which years did German colonial troops commit the genocide of the Herero and Nama?
15882.e: After the Herero uprising in 1904, the Schutztruppe waged a war of annihilation. Tens of thousands of Herero and Nama died in the desert or in camps.
15882.m: The genocide of the Herero and Nama took place from 1904 to 1908.

15883.q: Which general issued the so-called extermination order against the Herero in October 1904?
15883.e: Lothar von Trotha issued the order on 2 October 1904. It is regarded as a key document of the genocide of the Herero.
15883.m: Lothar von Trotha ordered the extermination of the Herero in 1904.

15884.q: In which year did the German Foreign Office first officially call the crimes against the Herero and Nama genocide?
15884.e: On 10 July 2015 the Foreign Office spoke of genocide for the first time. Before that, the federal government had long avoided this term.
15884.m: Germany only called the crimes against the Herero and Nama genocide in 2015.

15885.q: Which North African country did Great Britain occupy militarily in 1882, partly to secure the Suez Canal?
15885.e: Great Britain occupied Egypt in 1882 after a nationalist uprising. The Suez Canal was very important for the sea route to India.
15885.m: Great Britain occupied Egypt in 1882 because of the Suez Canal.

15886.q: What share of the Earth's land area did the British Empire cover at its greatest extent around 1922?
15886.e: Around 1922 the Empire covered about 33.7 million square kilometres. This made it the largest empire in history.
15886.m: Around 1922 the British Empire covered about a quarter of the world's land area.

15887.q: Which saying described the worldwide reach of the British Empire?
a: “The empire on which the sun never sets”
15887.e: Because British territories lay on every continent, it was always daytime somewhere in the Empire. The saying had earlier been applied to the Spanish Empire.
15887.m: In the British Empire, as the saying went, the sun never set.

15888.q: In which year was the English East India Company founded?
15888.e: The East India Company received a royal trading charter in 1600. In the 18th and 19th centuries it ruled large parts of India with its own army.
15888.m: The English East India Company was founded in 1600.

15889.q: What happened to the rule of the East India Company after the Indian uprising of 1857?
a: The British Crown took over direct rule of India in 1858
India was handed over to France
15889.e: With the Government of India Act of 1858, the administration passed to the Crown. This began the period of the “British Raj”.
15889.m: After the 1857 uprising, the British Crown took over India directly.

15890.q: In which year did Queen Victoria take the title “Empress of India”?
15890.e: At the urging of Prime Minister Disraeli, Victoria became Empress of India in 1876. The title stressed India's importance as the “jewel in the crown” of the Empire.
15890.m: Queen Victoria became Empress of India in 1876.

15891.q: In which year did Great Britain buy Egypt's shares in the Suez Canal?
15891.e: In 1875 Prime Minister Disraeli bought the shares of the indebted Egyptian ruler for about 4 million pounds. In this way Great Britain secured influence over the route to India.
15891.m: Great Britain bought Egypt's Suez Canal shares in 1875.

15892.q: In which year was the Suez Canal opened?
15892.e: The canal was built under the direction of the Frenchman Ferdinand de Lesseps and opened in 1869. It greatly shortened the sea route from Europe to Asia.

15893.q: What was a “dominion” in the British Empire?
a: a largely self-governing settler colony such as Canada or Australia
a trading area run by the Company
15893.e: Dominions such as Canada, Australia, New Zealand or South Africa had their own parliaments and governments. But Great Britain kept responsibility for their foreign policy for a long time.
15893.m: Dominions were self-governing parts of the British Empire.

15894.q: Which 1931 law made the dominions legally equal to Great Britain?
15894.e: The Statute of Westminster gave the dominions full legislative independence. It is seen as an important step towards today's Commonwealth of Nations.
15894.m: The Statute of Westminster of 1931 strengthened the independence of the dominions.

15895.q: In which year did the Australian colonies join together to form a federation?
15895.e: The Commonwealth of Australia was created on 1 January 1901. Australia had originally been settled as a British penal colony from 1788.
15895.m: Australia became a federation within the British Empire in 1901.

15896.q: Which British businessman and politician dreamt of a railway line “from the Cape to Cairo”?
15896.e: Cecil Rhodes was a diamond businessman and Prime Minister of the Cape Colony. The colony of Rhodesia was named after him.
15896.m: Cecil Rhodes pursued the plan of a British line from the Cape to Cairo.

15897.q: In which years did the Second Boer War take place in South Africa?
15897.e: Great Britain fought against the Boer republics of the Transvaal and the Orange Free State. The Treaty of Vereeniging of 31 May 1902 brought both into the Empire.
15897.m: The Second Boer War lasted from 1899 to 1902.

15898.q: Which controversial measure did the British use against civilians in the Second Boer War?
a: Internment camps in which tens of thousands died
15898.e: To break the guerrilla war, the British burned down farms and interned women and children. More than 26,000 people died of hunger and disease in the camps, plus many Black internees.
15898.m: In the Boer War, many civilians died in British internment camps.

15899.q: Which territory did Great Britain return to China in 1997?
15899.e: Hong Kong had been British since the First Opium War. In 1997 it went to the People's Republic of China; Macau followed from Portugal in 1999.
15899.m: Hong Kong was returned to China in 1997.

15900.q: Which law abolished slavery in most parts of the British Empire?
15900.e: The law came into force in 1834. Former slave owners received compensation, but the freed people did not.
15900.m: Great Britain abolished slavery by law in 1833.

15901.q: Which agreement ended the First Opium War in 1842?
15901.e: The Treaty of Nanking of 29 August 1842 is seen as the first of the so-called Unequal Treaties. Among other things, China had to cede the island of Hong Kong and pay a large indemnity.
15901.m: The Treaty of Nanking ended the First Opium War in 1842.

15902.q: What triggered the First Opium War?
a: China's action against the British opium trade
a British ban on Chinese tea
15902.e: In 1839 the Chinese special commissioner Lin Zexu had large amounts of opium destroyed in Canton. Great Britain responded with war to force the trade.
15902.m: Great Britain went to war to force the opium trade on China.

15903.q: How many Chinese ports had to be opened to foreign trade after the Treaty of Nanking?
15903.e: Canton, Xiamen, Fuzhou, Ningbo and Shanghai were opened. China also had to pay a large indemnity in silver.
15903.m: After the Treaty of Nanking, China opened five ports.

15904.q: Why does Chinese history speak of “Unequal Treaties”?
a: because China signed them under pressure and had to grant one-sided advantages
because they were signed by only one side
because they were translated unequally into different languages
because China gained more territory through them
15904.e: The treaties forced China to cede territory, open ports and grant special rights to foreigners. In China they are a symbol of a “century of humiliation”.
15904.m: The Unequal Treaties were forced on China by foreign powers.

15905.q: Which Chinese territory did the German Empire lease for 99 years in 1898?
15905.e: After two German missionaries were murdered, Germany occupied the bay in 1897. Its main town was Tsingtao, which was lost to Japan in 1914.
15905.m: Germany leased Kiautschou, with its main town Tsingtao, in 1898.

15906.q: How many powers joined together to crush the Boxer Rebellion in China in 1900?
15906.e: The alliance included Germany, Great Britain, France, Russia, Japan, the USA, Italy and Austria-Hungary. The Boxer Protocol of 1901 forced China to pay large indemnities.
15906.m: Eight powers crushed the Boxer Rebellion together.

15907.q: Which notorious speech did Wilhelm II give in 1900 when sending troops off to China?
a: the place in the sun speech
15907.e: On 27 July 1900 in Bremerhaven, Wilhelm II demanded that no mercy be shown. He compared the soldiers to the Huns, which caused outrage around the world.
15907.m: In the Hun speech, Wilhelm II called for ruthless harshness.

15908.q: Which present-day countries belonged to the colony of French Indochina?
15908.e: The Indochinese Union was created in 1887, and Laos was added in 1893. It lasted until decolonisation after the Second World War.
15908.m: French Indochina covered Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia.

15909.q: Which battle ended French colonial rule in Indochina in 1954?
15909.e: The Viet Minh defeated the French army in May 1954. The Geneva Conference on Indochina then confirmed the independence of Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia.
15909.m: With Dien Bien Phu, France's rule in Indochina ended in 1954.

15910.q: Which country in Southeast Asia was the only one spared from colonial rule?
15910.e: Siam lay as a buffer state between British and French territories. Through skilful diplomacy and reforms it kept its independence, but had to give up territory.
15910.m: Siam was the only country in Southeast Asia to stay independent.

15911.q: Which European power ruled present-day Indonesia in the 19th century?
15911.e: The Dutch East Indies grew out of the possessions of the Dutch East India Company. In the Aceh War from 1873 to 1904, the Netherlands extended their rule to northern Sumatra.
15911.m: Present-day Indonesia was a Dutch colony as the Dutch East Indies.

15912.q: How did Japan respond from 1868 to the threat from Western powers?
a: with rapid modernisation on the Western model
by completely shutting itself off from abroad
15912.e: In the Meiji Restoration, Japan modernised its army, industry and administration. As a result it became an imperialist power in Asia itself.
15912.m: Japan modernised from 1868 and became a colonial power itself.

15913.q: Which event in 1905 shook the image of European powers as superior in Asia?
a: Japan's victory in the war against Russia
15913.e: Japan defeated Russia in the Russo-Japanese War of 1904 to 1905. For the first time in the modern era, an Asian state won a major war against a European great power.
15913.m: Japan's victory over Russia in 1905 encouraged anti-colonial movements.

15914.q: Which country did Japan annex in 1910?
15914.e: Japan had already made Korea a protectorate and annexed it in 1910. Japanese colonial rule lasted until 1945.

15915.q: Which battle did Ethiopia win against Italy on 1 March 1896?
15915.e: The Ethiopian army defeated the Italian invasion force at Adwa. As a result, Ethiopia stayed independent and became a symbol of African resistance.
15915.m: With the victory at Adwa in 1896, Ethiopia kept its independence.

15916.q: Which ruler led Ethiopia to victory at Adwa in 1896?
15916.e: Menelik II was Emperor of Ethiopia and had equipped his army with modern rifles. After the defeat, Italy had to recognise Ethiopia's independence in the Treaty of Addis Ababa in 1896.
15916.m: Emperor Menelik II led Ethiopia to victory over Italy.

15917.q: Who began the great uprising against British rule in India in 1857?
a: Indian soldiers in British service, the sepoys
British settlers against their own government
15917.e: Indian soldiers (sepoys) mutinied at Meerut on 10 May 1857 and marched to Delhi. The uprising then spread across large parts of northern India.
15917.m: The Indian uprising of 1857 began as a mutiny of the sepoys.

15918.q: Which rumour helped spark the Indian uprising in 1857?
a: that rifle cartridges were greased with cow and pig fat
that the British wanted to close all temples
that India would be sold to Russia
that the soldiers would be sent to Africa
15918.e: The cartridges had to be bitten open. Fat from cows and pigs broke the religious rules of Hindus and Muslims.
15918.m: Rumours about greased cartridges helped trigger the Indian uprising of 1857.

15919.q: What was Gandhi's Salt March of 1930 directed against?
a: the British salt tax and salt monopoly
the introduction of the English language
15919.e: From 12 March 1930, Gandhi marched about 385 kilometres to Dandi on the Arabian Sea, arriving on 5 April. The next morning he symbolically gathered salt and so broke British law.
15919.m: With the Salt March of 1930, Gandhi protested non-violently against the salt tax.

15920.q: What is Gandhi's method of non-violent resistance called?
15920.e: Satyagraha means roughly “holding on to truth”. Gandhi first developed the method in South Africa and then used it in India; Swaraj, by contrast, means self-rule.
15920.m: Gandhi called his non-violent resistance Satyagraha.

15921.q: In which year was the Indian National Congress founded?
15921.e: The founding meeting took place in Bombay in December 1885. The Congress became the most important organisation of the Indian independence movement.
15921.m: The Indian National Congress was founded in 1885.

15922.q: What does the Swahili word “maji” in the name of the Maji Maji Rebellion in German East Africa mean?
15922.e: A blessed water was supposed to protect the fighters from bullets. The uprising against German colonial rule lasted from 1905 to 1907.
15922.m: In the Maji Maji Rebellion, the fighters believed in protective water.

15923.q: Which way of waging war by German troops caused the most deaths in the Maji Maji Rebellion?
a: burning villages and fields, which caused a famine
15923.e: The Schutztruppe followed a scorched earth policy. Estimates range from 75,000 to 300,000 dead, most of whom died of hunger.
15923.m: Most victims of the Maji Maji War died in a deliberately caused famine.

15924.q: Who led the resistance against the French conquest of Algeria from 1832 to 1847?
15924.e: Abd el-Kader was elected emir in 1832 and fought until his surrender in 1847. He later lived in Damascus, where in 1860 he saved thousands of Christians from a massacre.
15924.m: Abd el-Kader led the Algerian resistance against France.

15925.q: Which army did Abd el-Krim defeat at the Battle of Annual in 1921?
15925.e: In the Rif War in northern Morocco, Abd el-Krim won a great victory over Spain in 1921 and proclaimed a Rif Republic. In 1926 he surrendered to the superior forces of Spain and France.
15925.m: Abd el-Krim defeated the Spanish army at Annual in 1921.

15926.q: Which Ashanti symbol sparked the uprising led by Yaa Asantewaa against the British in 1900?
15926.e: The British governor demanded the handing over of the Golden Stool, the most sacred symbol of the Ashanti. After the uprising, Yaa Asantewaa was exiled to the Seychelles.
15926.m: The demand for the Golden Stool sparked the Ashanti uprising in 1900.

15927.q: Which people defeated a British army at Isandlwana on 22 January 1879?
15927.e: Under King Cetshwayo, the Zulu beat a British force. A few months later, however, the British defeated the Zulu at Ulundi.
15927.m: The Zulu defeated a British army at Isandlwana in 1879.

15928.q: Which Filipino writer and critic of Spanish colonial rule was executed in 1896?
15928.e: In his 1887 novel “Noli me tangere”, Rizal criticised Spanish colonial rule. His execution on 30 December 1896 made him the national hero of the Philippines.
15928.m: José Rizal became the national hero of the Philippines.

15929.q: Which Nama leader fought against German colonial rule in South West Africa from 1904?
15929.e: Hendrik Witbooi joined the war against the Germans in 1904 and was killed in 1905. Samuel Maharero, on the other hand, was the leader of the Herero.
15929.m: Hendrik Witbooi led the Nama resistance against the Germans.

15930.q: Which two states formed the Dual Alliance in 1879?
15930.e: In October 1879 the German Empire and Austria-Hungary allied in the Dual Alliance. It remained a separate treaty even after it was expanded into the Triple Alliance.
15930.m: The Dual Alliance of 1879 tied the German Empire closely to Austria-Hungary.

15931.q: Which state joined the Dual Alliance in 1882, turning it into the Triple Alliance?
15931.e: Italy joined the Dual Alliance on 20 May 1882. Among other things, it hoped for support for its colonial plans in Africa.
15931.m: With Italy joining in 1882, the Dual Alliance became the Triple Alliance.

15932.q: What was the consequence of the German Empire not renewing the Reinsurance Treaty with Russia in 1890?
15932.e: After Bismarck's dismissal, Berlin let the 1887 treaty expire. Russia then looked for a new partner and found it in France.
15932.m: The end of the Reinsurance Treaty in 1890 opened the way to an alliance between France and Russia.

15933.q: In which year was the Franco-Russian Alliance concluded, from which the Triple Entente later grew?
15933.e: The Franco-Russian Alliance of 1894 was the core of the later Triple Entente. For Germany it meant the danger of a war on two fronts.
15933.m: From 1894 France and Russia were allies, which made Germany fear a war on two fronts.

15934.q: What did Great Britain and France settle in the Entente Cordiale of 1904?
a: The resolution of their conflicting colonial interests
A mutual assistance pact with Russia
15934.e: In the Entente Cordiale the two powers settled their disputes, above all in Africa. It was not a formal military alliance, but an important coming together.
15934.m: The Entente Cordiale of 1904 ended old colonial disputes between Great Britain and France.

15935.q: Which 1907 treaty completed the Triple Entente?
a: The Anglo-Russian Convention of St Petersburg
The Treaty of London between Italy and France
The Reinsurance Treaty between Russia and Germany
15935.e: In 1907 Great Britain and Russia agreed on their interests in Asia in the Convention of St Petersburg. This closed the triangle of Great Britain, France and Russia.
15935.m: The Anglo-Russian agreement of 1907 created the Triple Entente.

15936.q: Why did Italy switch to the side of the Entente in 1915 despite the Triple Alliance?
a: It was promised territorial gains in the secret Treaty of London
15936.e: In 1914 Italy at first declared itself neutral. In the Treaty of London of 26 April 1915, the Entente promised it territory, after which Italy left the Triple Alliance and entered the war.
15936.m: In 1915 Italy was persuaded to change sides by the Entente's promises of territory.

15937.q: Which term describes Germany's fear before 1914 of being surrounded by hostile alliances?
15937.e: Many Germans saw the Entente as a deliberate “encirclement” of the Empire. This feeling increased the readiness to strike first in a crisis.
15937.m: The fear of encirclement shaped German policy before the First World War.

15938.q: Which movement saw Russia as the protector of all Slavic peoples, including the Serbs?
15938.e: Pan-Slavism aimed for the unity of the Slavic peoples. It explains why Russia got so strongly involved in the conflict over Serbia.
15938.m: Pan-Slavism made Russia the self-appointed protector of Serbia.

15939.q: Which territory did France want to win back before 1914 as revenge for its defeat in 1871?
15939.e: After the Franco-Prussian War of 1870/71, France had to give up Alsace-Lorraine. The desire for revenge burdened relations with Germany for a long time.
15939.m: The loss of Alsace-Lorraine in 1871 fuelled the idea of revenge in France.

15940.q: Which event in 1908 greatly increased tensions between Austria-Hungary and Serbia?
a: The annexation of Bosnia and Herzegovina
The founding of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia
The murder of the Serbian king
15940.e: In 1908 Austria-Hungary annexed Bosnia and Herzegovina, which it had previously only administered. Serbian nationalists saw the territory as part of a future Greater Serbia.
15940.m: The annexation of Bosnia in 1908 made the Balkans even more explosive.

15941.q: Why was the Balkans often called the “powder keg of Europe” before 1914?
a: Because of its many national conflicts and the interests of the great powers
Because of the large explosives factories in the region
Because most warships were built there
Because the region was the strongest economically
15941.e: After the Ottoman Empire withdrew, young nation states fought over territory, for example in the Balkan Wars of 1912 and 1913. Russia and Austria-Hungary pursued opposing aims there.
15941.m: In the Balkans, national conflicts and great power interests clashed dangerously.

15942.q: Which conflict above all strained relations between Germany and Great Britain before 1914?
15942.e: Under Admiral Tirpitz, the German Empire built up a large navy. Great Britain saw its control of the seas threatened and responded with modern battleships such as the “Dreadnought”.
15942.m: The naval arms race drove Great Britain and Germany apart before 1914.

15943.q: Why was nationalism especially dangerous for Austria-Hungary?
a: Because it was a multinational state with many nationalities
Because it had no army of its own
Because it consisted only of German speakers
15943.e: The Danube Monarchy was home to Germans, Hungarians, Czechs, Poles, Croats and Serbs, among others. National independence movements threatened the unity of the state.
15943.m: For the multinational state of Austria-Hungary, nationalism was an explosive force from within.

15944.q: What is the policy called under which the German parties, including the SPD, put aside their conflicts for the duration of the war in August 1914?
15944.e: On 4 August 1914 the SPD voted for the war credits. Kaiser Wilhelm II declared that he no longer knew any parties, only Germans.
15944.m: With the Burgfrieden, the German parties put aside their differences in 1914.

15945.q: What does recent research show about the so-called “spirit of August” in 1914?
a: Enthusiasm for war was mainly found in towns and among the middle classes, less in the countryside and among workers
The whole population was enthusiastic without exception
Nobody in Europe was surprised when the war began
15945.e: Pictures of cheering crowds long shaped the idea of general enthusiasm for war. Looked at critically, the sources also show much worry, fear and indifference.
15945.m: Enthusiasm for war in 1914 was less general than propaganda pictures suggested.

15946.q: On which day was the Austrian heir to the throne Franz Ferdinand assassinated in Sarajevo?
15946.e: On 28 June 1914, Gavrilo Princip shot the heir to the throne and his wife. The assassination set off a diplomatic crisis that led to war.
15946.m: The assassination in Sarajevo on 28 June 1914 triggered the First World War.

15947.q: Who died together with Franz Ferdinand in the Sarajevo assassination?
15947.e: Sophie Chotek, Duchess of Hohenberg, was hit by the first shot. Both died shortly after the attack.
15947.m: Franz Ferdinand and his wife Sophie were killed in Sarajevo.

15948.q: Which nationalist group did the assassin Gavrilo Princip belong to?
15948.e: Princip was a member of Mlada Bosna, which fought against Austria-Hungary's rule over Bosnia. The attack was prepared with the support of the Serbian secret society “Black Hand”.
15948.m: Gavrilo Princip belonged to the nationalist movement Mlada Bosna.

15949.q: What role did the Serbian secret society “Black Hand” play in the Sarajevo assassination?
a: It helped plan the attack and arm the assassins
It protected the heir as a bodyguard
It sentenced the assassins in court
15949.e: The Black Hand under Colonel Dragutin Dimitrijević, known as “Apis”, supplied the young assassins with weapons and helped them cross the border. Apis was also an officer in the Serbian intelligence service.
15949.m: The secret society “Black Hand” around Colonel Apis was also behind the assassination.

15950.q: Why did many Serbs see the date of the heir's visit to Sarajevo in 1914 as a provocation?
a: It was the anniversary of the Battle of Kosovo of 1389
It was the founding day of the Serbian state
It was the anniversary of the annexation of Bosnia
It was the day the Balkan Wars ended
15950.e: The visit fell on Vidovdan, St Vitus's Day. On this day Serbs remembered the Battle of Kosovo of 1389, seen as a symbol of the struggle against foreign rule.
15950.m: Vidovdan commemorates the Battle of Kosovo of 1389.

15951.q: What happened during the visit to Sarajevo before the fatal shots at Franz Ferdinand?
a: Another assassin threw a bomb at the motorcade
15951.e: Nedeljko Čabrinović threw a bomb, which bounced off the heir's car and exploded behind the third vehicle. Several members of the party and spectators were injured, but the visit went on anyway.
15951.m: The first bomb attack in Sarajevo failed, but the visit continued.

15952.q: Which coincidence made Princip's fatal shots possible?
a: The driver took a wrong turn and stopped right next to him while turning round
The heir walked into the crowd on foot
Princip was disguised as a bodyguard
The car broke down in front of the town hall
15952.e: The driver had not been told about the changed route and turned wrongly at the Latin Bridge. When it stopped to reverse, the car was only just over two metres from Princip.
15952.m: A driving mistake at the Latin Bridge brought the heir within Princip's reach.

15953.q: Why was Gavrilo Princip not sentenced to death?
a: He was still a minor at the time of the crime
The death penalty had been abolished in Austria
15953.e: Princip was only 19 and under Austrian law at the time counted as a minor. He received 20 years of hard imprisonment and died of bone tuberculosis in Theresienstadt in 1918.
15953.m: Because Princip was a minor, he escaped the death penalty.

15954.q: What is meant by Germany's “blank cheque” of July 1914?
a: Germany's unconditional promise of support to Austria-Hungary
15954.e: On 5 and 6 July 1914, the German Empire promised Austria-Hungary full support for action against Serbia. This encouraged Vienna to take a hard line.
15954.m: The blank cheque gave Austria-Hungary a free hand against Serbia in July 1914.

15955.q: How long did Austria-Hungary give Serbia to answer in the ultimatum of 23 July 1914?
15955.e: The ultimatum contained harsh demands, including the involvement of Austrian officials in the investigation in Serbia. The short deadline was meant to make a diplomatic solution harder.
15955.m: The ultimatum to Serbia of 23 July 1914 allowed only 48 hours.

15956.q: When did Austria-Hungary declare war on Serbia?
15956.e: Although Serbia accepted many demands, Austria-Hungary declared war on 28 July 1914. After that, the alliance obligations kicked in one after another.
15956.m: The war began with Austria-Hungary's declaration of war on Serbia on 28 July 1914.

15957.q: Which declaration of war was made on 1 August 1914?
15957.e: After Russia's general mobilisation, the German Empire declared war on Russia on 1 August 1914. The declaration of war on France followed on 3 August.
15957.m: On 1 August 1914 Germany declared war on Russia.

15958.q: What led to Great Britain entering the war on 4 August 1914?
a: The German invasion of neutral Belgium
15958.e: Great Britain was a guarantor of Belgian neutrality. When German troops occupied Belgium according to the Schlieffen Plan, London declared war on the German Empire.
15958.m: The violation of Belgian neutrality brought Great Britain into the war.

15959.q: What is the diplomatic crisis between the Sarajevo assassination and the start of the war called?
15959.e: In the July Crisis of 1914, all attempts at mediation failed. Ultimatums, mobilisations and declarations of war followed one another within a few weeks.
15959.m: The July Crisis of 1914 led from the Sarajevo assassination to the great war.

15960.q: Why did the conflict between Austria-Hungary and Serbia turn into a European war so quickly?
a: Because of the great powers' alliance obligations and mobilisation plans
Because the League of Nations ordered the war
Because all the states were already at war
15960.e: Russia supported Serbia, Germany stood behind Austria-Hungary, and France was allied with Russia. Rigid mobilisation plans left little time for negotiations.
15960.m: In 1914, alliances and rigid mobilisation plans turned a regional conflict into a world war.

15961.q: Which alliance did Germany, Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire and Bulgaria form in the First World War?
15961.e: The Central Powers were so called because of their position in the middle of Europe. They were opposed by the Entente and its allies.
15961.m: Germany, Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire and Bulgaria formed the Central Powers.

15962.q: What was the basic idea of the Schlieffen Plan?
a: Defeat France quickly first, then turn the troops against Russia
Only defend and wait for peace
Attack Great Britain directly with the navy
15962.e: The plan was meant to avoid a war on two fronts by defeating France before Russia had fully mobilised. The well-known memorandum dates from December 1905.
15962.m: The Schlieffen Plan relied on a quick victory in the west before fighting in the east.

15963.q: Who was Chief of the German General Staff at the start of the war and was replaced after the Battle of the Marne in September 1914?
15963.e: Moltke had altered the Schlieffen Plan and directed the advance in the west. After the failure on the Marne, he was replaced by Erich von Falkenhayn on 14 September 1914.
15963.m: After the failure on the Marne, Chief of Staff Moltke had to go in 1914.

15964.q: Which battle stopped the German advance on Paris in September 1914?
15964.e: From 5 to 12 September 1914, French and British troops halted the German advance on the Marne. This meant the Schlieffen Plan had failed.
15964.m: With the Battle of the Marne in 1914, the plan for a quick victory in the west failed.

15965.q: When did the Battle of Verdun begin?
15965.e: The Battle of Verdun lasted from 21 February to 19 December 1916. It became a symbol of mass death in trench warfare.
15965.m: The Battle of Verdun raged from February to December 1916.

15966.q: What did the German Chief of Staff Erich von Falkenhayn intend with the attack on Verdun?
a: To weaken the French army by attrition
To capture Paris within a week
15966.e: According to his own later account, Falkenhayn mainly wanted to weaken France through heavy losses. But the German army also lost hundreds of thousands of soldiers.
15966.m: Verdun stands for a strategy of attrition that bled both sides dry.

15967.q: What was the road from Bar-le-Duc to Verdun called, along which France brought up troops and supplies in 1916?
15967.e: Lorries rolled non-stop to Verdun along the “Sacred Way”, about 57 kilometres long. In the first month of the battle alone, more than a quarter of a million soldiers were brought up this way.
15967.m: The Voie Sacrée was the lifeline of France's defence of Verdun.

15968.q: When did the Battle of the Somme begin?
15968.e: The British and French offensive on the Somme lasted from 1 July to 18 November 1916. It was also meant to relieve Verdun.
15968.m: The Battle of the Somme began on 1 July 1916 and lasted into November.

15969.q: Why is 1 July 1916 seen as the “blackest day in British military history”?
a: About 20,000 British soldiers were killed on the first day of the Battle of the Somme
The British fleet was completely sunk
The British king was taken prisoner
15969.e: The British attacked after days of artillery fire, but the German positions were hardly destroyed. Machine guns inflicted huge losses on the attackers.
15969.m: On the first day of the Somme, the British army suffered its heaviest losses in a single day.

15970.q: When did the Armistice of Compiègne, which ended the fighting on the Western Front, come into force?
15970.e: The armistice was signed in a railway carriage in the Forest of Compiègne. On 11 November 1918 at 11 o'clock, the guns fell silent.
15970.m: 11 November 1918 marks the end of the fighting in the First World War.

15971.q: What is typical of trench warfare?
a: The front lines hardly move and the troops dig themselves into trenches
The armies advance many kilometres every day
Fighting takes place only with ships
The fighting takes place only in towns
15971.e: After the German advance failed in autumn 1914, the Western Front froze. Both sides built trench systems from which they could hardly drive each other out.
15971.m: In trench warfare the fronts froze and the soldiers lived in trenches.

15972.q: What was the area between the opposing trenches called?
15972.e: No man's land was often covered with shell craters, barbed wire and bodies. Anyone crossing it was exposed to enemy fire without protection.
15972.m: No man's land between the trenches was a deadly zone.

15973.q: Roughly where did the frozen Western Front begin and end from late 1914?
a: From the Belgian North Sea coast to the Swiss border
From the Baltic Sea to the Black Sea
15973.e: After the so-called Race to the Sea, the front stretched from the coast in Flanders to the Swiss border in the Jura. Switzerland therefore bordered directly on the end of the Western Front.
15973.m: The Western Front stretched from the North Sea to the Swiss border.

15974.q: Why was defence usually stronger than attack in trench warfare?
a: Machine guns, barbed wire and trenches made attacks very costly
15974.e: Attacking infantry had to cross open ground and got caught in the barbed wire. A few machine guns could stop entire waves of attack.
15974.m: In trench warfare, weapons technology clearly favoured the defender.

15975.q: What does the term “battle of materiel” (Materialschlacht) mean?
a: A battle in which huge amounts of ammunition and war materiel are used
A dispute over raw materials between factories
15975.e: Battles such as Verdun or the Somme were marked by days of artillery fire with millions of shells. The outcome depended heavily on industrial production.
15975.m: In the battles of materiel of the First World War, industry helped decide the war.

a: Non-stop artillery fire before an attack
A fire to heat the trenches
15976.e: Shelling for hours or days was meant to destroy the enemy positions. For the soldiers in the trenches it meant extreme physical and mental strain.
15976.m: Drumfire was meant to destroy the enemy trenches before the assault.

15977.q: Which psychological consequence of trench warfare was seen in many soldiers?
a: Shell shock, today understood as trauma
15977.e: After constant shelling, many soldiers suffered from shaking, paralysis or loss of speech. At the time people spoke of “war tremblers” or “shell shock”; today we would speak of a trauma-related disorder.
15977.m: Constant shelling in trench warfare left many soldiers with severe mental damage.

15978.q: What happened on some sections of the Western Front at Christmas 1914?
a: Soldiers from both sides spontaneously agreed a ceasefire
The biggest offensive of the war took place
15978.e: In the so-called Christmas Truce, soldiers in some places left their trenches, sang and exchanged gifts. The army commands then banned such fraternisation.
15978.m: The Christmas Truce of 1914 showed that soldiers on both sides did not have to hate each other.

15979.q: Which weapon did the German army first use on a large scale at Ypres in April 1915?
15979.e: On 22 April 1915, German engineers released about 150 tonnes of chlorine gas from thousands of steel cylinders. The heavy gas sank into the Allied trenches.
15979.m: Large-scale gas warfare began at Ypres in April 1915.

15980.q: Which German chemist played a leading role in developing gas warfare?
15980.e: Fritz Haber organised Germany's use of poison gas and is called the “father of chemical warfare”. He later received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for the synthesis of ammonia.
15980.m: Fritz Haber combined scientific fame with responsibility for gas warfare.

15981.q: When were tanks first used in a battle?
15981.e: British Mark I tanks were first used at Flers on the Somme. Many broke down because of technical problems, but the new weapon was meant to overcome trench warfare.
15981.m: The first tanks rolled on the Somme in September 1916.

15982.q: What did the “unrestricted submarine warfare” that Germany waged from 1 February 1917 mean?
a: Even neutral merchant ships were sunk without warning
Submarines only sailed in the Baltic
15982.e: Germany wanted to cut Great Britain off from supplies and force it to make peace. The attacks on neutral ships played a decisive part in the USA entering the war.
15982.m: Unrestricted submarine warfare turned the USA against Germany.

15983.q: Which British passenger ship was sunk by a German submarine in 1915, killing many Americans too?
15983.e: The Lusitania sank off Ireland on 7 May 1915, and about 1,200 people died. The sinking outraged the public in the USA.
15983.m: The sinking of the Lusitania in 1915 weakened American sympathy for Germany.

15984.q: What did Germany propose to Mexico in the Zimmermann Telegram of 1917?
a: An alliance against the USA with the prospect of Texas, New Mexico and Arizona
15984.e: British intelligence intercepted and decoded the telegram. Its publication on 1 March 1917 strengthened the mood for war in the USA.
15984.m: The Zimmermann Telegram offered Mexico lost territories for an alliance against the USA.

a: A heavy German 42 cm mortar made by Krupp
A German airship for attacks on London
15985.e: “Big Bertha” was a siege gun made by the Krupp company. In August 1914 it shelled the forts around Liège in Belgium, which were thought to be impregnable.
15985.m: With giant guns like “Big Bertha”, the German army destroyed Belgian fortresses in 1914.

15986.q: What were aircraft mainly used for at the start of the First World War?
15986.e: At first, aircraft watched enemy troop movements and directed artillery fire. Fighter planes and bombers only appeared as the war went on.
15986.m: In the First World War, aircraft were first used mainly for reconnaissance.

15987.q: Why is the First World War called an industrialised war?
a: Mass production of weapons and ammunition and the mobilisation of the whole of society helped decide it
Because factories were the infantry's main targets
Because the war began in industrial areas
15987.e: States switched their economies to war production, and more women worked in arms factories. Modern technology made killing possible on a scale never seen before.
15987.m: In the First World War, not just armies but whole industrial societies fought.

15988.q: Whom did the Federal Assembly elect as General of the Swiss Army on 3 August 1914?
15988.e: Ulrich Wille was elected commander-in-chief on 3 August 1914. On the same day, the general mobilisation ordered by the Federal Council began.
15988.m: In the First World War, General Ulrich Wille led the Swiss Army.

15989.q: Roughly how large was the Swiss field army at mobilisation in August 1914?
15989.e: The active field army numbered about 250,000 men and around 77,000 horses. On top of that came about 200,000 members of the auxiliary service.
15989.m: In 1914 Switzerland called up about a quarter of a million soldiers to protect its borders.

15990.q: What does the “Graben” (rift) in Switzerland during the First World War refer to?
a: The split between pro-German German-speaking Switzerland and the pro-French Romandy
A trench on the border with Italy
The conflict between town and country over taxes
The border between Catholic and Protestant cantons
15990.e: German-speaking Switzerland mostly sympathised with the German Empire, the Romandy with France. Affairs such as the Colonels' Affair deepened this rift.
15990.m: The First World War opened a rift between German-speaking Switzerland and the Romandy.

15991.q: What happened in the Colonels' Affair of 1915/16?
a: Two General Staff officers passed secret bulletins to the military attachés of Germany and Austria-Hungary
Two colonels fled abroad with the army's funds
A colonel became general against the will of parliament
15991.e: Colonels Karl Egli and Friedrich Moritz von Wattenwyl passed the General Staff's intelligence bulletin on to the Central Powers. Western Switzerland saw this as favouring the Central Powers and reacted with outrage.
15991.m: The Colonels' Affair made the Romandy doubt the neutrality of the army leadership.

15992.q: Why did Federal Councillor Arthur Hoffmann have to resign in 1917?
a: His attempt to arrange a separate peace between Germany and Russia was seen as a breach of neutrality
He had taken bribes from France
He had organised the general strike
He wanted Switzerland to join the Entente
15992.e: In the Grimm-Hoffmann Affair, Hoffmann supported a peace mediation attempt that would have helped Germany. The Entente and western Switzerland protested, and Hoffmann resigned.
15992.m: The Grimm-Hoffmann Affair of 1917 showed how delicate peace mediation was for a neutral state.

15993.q: Which financial innovation did the federal war tax of 1915 bring?
a: It was the first direct federal tax
15993.e: In 1915 the people approved a one-off tax on income and wealth to pay for the mobilisation. This was the first time the Confederation levied a direct tax.
15993.m: With the war tax of 1915, the Confederation levied a direct tax for the first time.

15994.q: Which humanitarian task did Switzerland take on from 1916 for wounded and sick prisoners of war from both sides?
a: It took in about 68,000 of them to recover (internment)
It sent Swiss doctors to all the fronts
It built hospital ships for the Entente
It ran prison camps for Germany
15994.e: Wounded and sick prisoners of war were interned in Swiss health resorts. This strengthened Switzerland's image as a humanitarian state.
15994.m: By interning sick prisoners of war, Switzerland gave important humanitarian help.

15995.q: What did the International Committee of the Red Cross receive the Nobel Peace Prize for in 1917?
a: For its work for prisoners of war, including a central agency in Geneva
For founding the League of Nations
15995.e: From October 1914 the ICRC ran a central agency for prisoners of war in Geneva. Its card files hold details on more than 4.8 million prisoners.
15995.m: In the First World War the ICRC in Geneva helped millions of prisoners of war and their families.

15996.q: Why did many families of Swiss soldiers fall into hardship during the First World War?
a: There was no compensation for lost wages during service
The soldiers had to buy their own weapons
The families had to pay the war tax twice
The soldiers were never allowed home
15996.e: A soldier served about 500 days on average, without compensation for lost earnings. Together with rising prices, this led to great social hardship.
15996.m: The lack of wage compensation for soldiers worsened social hardship in the First World War.

15997.q: What triggered the February Revolution in Petrograd in 1917?
a: The signing of the Treaty of Versailles
15997.e: Supply shortages and heavy war losses led to mass strikes and demonstrations. When soldiers joined the rebels, the tsar's rule collapsed.
15997.m: Hunger and war-weariness brought down the tsar's rule in 1917.

15998.e: Nicholas II abdicated on 15 March 1917 (2 March in the Julian calendar). This ended more than 300 years of Romanov rule.
15998.m: With the abdication of Nicholas II in 1917, the age of the tsars in Russia ended.

15999.q: What is meant by “dual power” in Russia in 1917?
a: The co-existence of the Provisional Government and the workers' and soldiers' councils (soviets)
The joint rule of two tsars
The division of Russia into east and west
The government of Lenin and Stalin together
15999.e: After the February Revolution, the Provisional Government formally ruled. But the soviets had great influence over workers and soldiers.
15999.m: Under dual power in 1917, the Provisional Government and the soviets shared power.

16000.q: Which politician led the Provisional Government from July 1917, which was overthrown by the Bolsheviks?
16000.e: Kerensky continued the war, and an offensive in summer 1917 failed. This weakened his government and strengthened the Bolsheviks.
16000.m: Kerensky's insistence on the war paved the Bolsheviks' way to power.

16001.q: Why is the Bolshevik seizure of power called the “October Revolution”, although by our calendar it took place in November?
a: Russia was still using the Julian calendar at that time
The revolution lasted from October to November
The name was only invented later
16001.e: In the Julian calendar it was 25 October 1917, in the Gregorian calendar 7 November. Soviet Russia only introduced the Gregorian calendar in 1918.
16001.m: By our calendar, the October Revolution took place on 7 November 1917.

16002.q: What did the Bolsheviks do with the freely elected Constituent Assembly in January 1918?
a: They dissolved it as soon as it met
They made it the Supreme Soviet
16002.e: In the elections of November 1917, the Bolsheviks won only about a quarter of the votes. That is why they dissolved the assembly in January 1918.
16002.m: The dissolution of the Constituent Assembly in 1918 showed the Bolsheviks' undemocratic course.

16003.q: With which treaty did Soviet Russia leave the First World War in March 1918?
16003.e: In the peace of 3 March 1918, Russia lost large territories, such as Poland, the Baltic states, Finland and Ukraine. After Germany's defeat in November 1918, the treaty was cancelled.
16003.m: In the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk, Soviet Russia paid for leaving the war with large losses of territory.

16004.q: When was the Soviet Union (USSR) founded after the civil war?
16004.e: After the civil war between Reds and Whites, which cost millions of lives, the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics was founded at the end of 1922.
16004.m: The Soviet Union was founded at the end of 1922.

16005.q: What was Lenin's real family name?
16005.e: Lenin was born in Simbirsk in 1870 as Vladimir Ilyich Ulyanov. He used the alias “Lenin” from about 1900.
16005.m: Lenin's real name was Vladimir Ilyich Ulyanov.

16006.q: Which event in 1887 had a strong effect on the young Lenin?
a: The execution of his brother Alexander for a planned attack on the tsar
The founding of the Soviet Union
16006.e: Alexander Ulyanov was executed on 20 May 1887 for taking part in a planned attack on Tsar Alexander III. This radicalised Lenin.
16006.m: His brother's execution in 1887 drove Lenin into the revolutionary movement.

16007.q: Which idea of a party did Lenin set out in 1902 in his pamphlet “What Is to Be Done?”?
a: A tightly organised party of professional revolutionaries
A loose mass party without leadership
16007.e: Lenin called for a small, disciplined cadre party as the vanguard of the working class. This idea later shaped the Bolsheviks.
16007.m: In “What Is to Be Done?”, Lenin called for a party of professional revolutionaries.

16008.q: What were the two wings called into which Russian social democracy split in 1903?
16008.e: At the 1903 party congress in London, Lenin's group won a vote and therefore called itself “Bolsheviks” (those of the majority). Their opponents were called “Mensheviks” (those of the minority).
16008.m: In 1903 Russian social democracy split into Bolsheviks and Mensheviks.

16009.q: Where did Lenin live in Swiss exile from February 1916?
a: In Geneva on the Quai du Mont-Blanc
16009.e: Lenin lived in Switzerland during the war, last in Zurich at Spiegelgasse 14. From there he travelled to Russia in April 1917.
16009.m: Shortly before the revolution, Lenin lived in Zurich on the Spiegelgasse.

16010.q: Why did the German Empire let Lenin travel by train from Switzerland to Russia in April 1917?
a: Because it hoped Russia would be weakened
Because Lenin was friends with the Kaiser
Because the tsar had called Lenin back
16010.e: The Swiss socialist Fritz Platten organised the journey through Germany. Germany hoped Lenin would weaken Russia and take it out of the war.
16010.m: Germany let Lenin travel from Switzerland to Russia in 1917 to weaken Russia.

16011.q: What did Lenin demand in his April Theses of 1917?
a: No support for the Provisional Government and all power to the soviets
Free elections on the British model
16011.e: After his return, Lenin called for a break with the Provisional Government, an end to the war and the seizure of power by the soviets.
16011.m: With the April Theses, Lenin steered towards a second revolution in 1917.

16012.q: Whom did Lenin warn against in his political testament around the turn of 1922/23?
16012.e: In an addition to his letter to the party congress in January 1923, Lenin criticised Stalin as too rude and suggested removing him as General Secretary. After Lenin's death on 21 January 1924, Stalin still won out.
16012.m: Lenin warned against Stalin, who nevertheless took power after Lenin's death.

16013.q: When and where was the Treaty of Versailles signed?
a: On 28 June 1919 in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles
On 11 November 1918 in the Forest of Compiègne
16013.e: The signing deliberately took place in the Hall of Mirrors, where the German Empire had been proclaimed in 1871. For France this was a symbolic act of redress.
16013.m: The Treaty of Versailles was signed in the Hall of Mirrors on 28 June 1919.

16014.q: What did Article 231 of the Treaty of Versailles state?
a: Germany and its allies are responsible for the war damage
Germany must hand over Kaiser Wilhelm II
Germany remains a member of the League of Nations
16014.e: The so-called war guilt clause formed the legal basis for reparations. In Germany it was felt to be humiliating.
16014.m: Article 231 made Germany responsible for the war damage.

16015.q: What was the maximum size of the German army under the Treaty of Versailles?
16015.e: Germany was only allowed a professional army of 100,000 men without general conscription. Tanks, submarines and an air force were banned.
16015.m: The Treaty of Versailles limited the German army to 100,000 men.

16016.q: What happened to the Saar region after the Treaty of Versailles?
a: It came under League of Nations administration for 15 years
16016.e: France received the coal mines, and the region was under League of Nations administration. In 1935 the population voted to return to Germany.
16016.m: After 1920 the Saar region was under League of Nations administration for 15 years.

16017.q: What status did Danzig receive through the Treaty of Versailles?
a: Free city under the supervision of the League of Nations
16017.e: Danzig was separated from the German Empire and became a free city. Through the so-called corridor, Poland gained access to the Baltic Sea.
16017.m: The Treaty of Versailles made Danzig a free city.

16018.q: Why did many Germans call the Treaty of Versailles a “dictated peace” (Diktat)?
a: Germany was not allowed to take part in the negotiations, only to comment in writing
16018.e: The victorious powers set the terms largely on their own and gave Germany an ultimatum. Nationalists later used the slogan against the Weimar Republic.
16018.m: Because Germany was not allowed to negotiate, people spoke of a “dictated peace”.

16019.q: What did the so-called stab-in-the-back myth claim?
a: The German army had been undefeated in the field and had been betrayed by the home front
France had attacked Germany with poison
Austria had deliberately dragged Germany into the war
The USA had won the war alone
16019.e: The myth blamed democrats, socialists and Jews for the defeat. It was a deliberate falsification of history and poisoned the political climate of the Weimar Republic.
16019.m: The stab-in-the-back myth was a lie that badly damaged democracy in Germany.

16020.q: Which international organisation was founded with the Treaty of Versailles and had its seat in Geneva?
16020.e: The League of Nations was meant to prevent future wars. Despite President Wilson's initiative, the USA did not join, and Germany only joined in 1926.
16020.m: The League of Nations, based in Geneva, grew out of the Treaty of Versailles.

16021.q: With which state did the victorious powers conclude the Treaty of Saint-Germain in 1919?
16021.e: The Treaty of Saint-Germain of 10 September 1919 settled peace with Austria. The Treaty of Trianon was concluded with Hungary, and that of Neuilly with Bulgaria.
16021.m: Besides Versailles there were other Paris peace treaties, such as Saint-Germain with Austria.

16022.q: When did the Swiss general strike (Landesstreik) take place?
16022.e: The open-ended general strike began on 12 November 1918. On 14 November the strike leadership called it off.
16022.m: The general strike lasted from 12 to 14 November 1918.

16023.q: Which body led the general strike of 1918?
a: The International Committee of the Red Cross
16023.e: The Olten Action Committee was founded in February 1918 as a link between the Social Democratic Party and the trade unions. Its president was Robert Grimm.
16023.m: The Olten Action Committee under Robert Grimm led the general strike.

16024.q: Roughly how many people took part in the general strike?
16024.e: On 12 November 1918, about 250,000 workers and trade unionists stopped work. It was the biggest domestic crisis of the federal state.
16024.m: About a quarter of a million people went on strike in November 1918.

16025.q: How did the Federal Council and the army leadership react to the general strike?
a: They called up about 95,000 soldiers as troops to keep order
They immediately met all the demands
They asked France for military help
16025.e: General Wille had already warned of a revolution before the strike. Large numbers of troops were sent above all to Zurich and Bern.
16025.m: The state used about 95,000 soldiers against the general strike.

16026.q: What happened in Grenchen on 14 November 1918?
a: Soldiers shot dead three young watch workers
The strikers occupied the Federal Palace
The strike began there with a huge rally
16026.e: On the last day of the strike there was a confrontation with troops in Grenchen. Three watch workers aged 17 to 29 were killed.
16026.m: The deaths in Grenchen are the saddest event of the general strike.

16027.q: Which demand of the general strike was already put into practice in 1919?
a: The early re-election of the National Council by proportional representation
Paying off the national debt through the wealthy
16027.e: The people had already accepted proportional representation on 13 October 1918; the general strike demanded an immediate new election. It took place in autumn 1919 and broke the Free Democrats' majority of many decades.
16027.m: The early proportional election of the National Council in 1919 met a demand of the general strike.

16028.q: When was the AHV (old-age insurance), a demand of the general strike, finally introduced?
16028.e: The constitutional article was accepted in 1925, but the AHV only came into force in 1948. The 48-hour week, by contrast, was already achieved in 1919/20.
16028.m: The AHV became reality 30 years after the general strike.

16029.q: How did the general strike end?
a: The Action Committee called it off after an ultimatum from the Federal Council
The strikers took over the government
16029.e: On 13 November the Federal Council and the middle-class majority in parliament issued an ultimatum. To avoid bloodshed, the Olten Action Committee ended the strike on 14 November.
16029.m: The general strike ended after three days when the strike leadership called it off.

16030.q: In which city did the League of Nations have its seat?
16030.e: The League of Nations began its work in 1920 and had its seat in Geneva. From the mid-1930s it moved into the newly built Palais des Nations in the Ariana Park.
16030.m: The League of Nations had its seat in Geneva.

16031.q: When did the League of Nations officially begin its work?
16031.e: The League of Nations began work when the Treaty of Versailles came into force on 10 January 1920. Its covenant was part of the Paris peace treaties.
16031.m: The League of Nations worked from 10 January 1920.

16032.q: Why did the USA never become a member of the League of Nations, although President Wilson had strongly promoted the idea?
a: The US Senate rejected the Treaty of Versailles
The League explicitly excluded the USA
The USA demanded the seat be in Washington
16032.e: The League's covenant was part of the Treaty of Versailles. Because the US Senate did not ratify this treaty, the USA never joined, which weakened the League from the start.
16032.m: Without the USA, the League of Nations lacked an important great power.

16033.q: How did the people and the cantons decide in 1920 on Switzerland joining the League of Nations?
a: They agreed, but very narrowly among the cantons
There was no vote; the Federal Council decided alone
16033.e: The people said yes with about 56 percent. Among the cantons the result was very close, at 11½ to 10½ cantonal votes.
16033.m: Switzerland joined the League of Nations in 1920 after a close popular vote.

16034.q: Which country left the League of Nations on 27 March 1933 after criticism of its actions in Manchuria?
16034.e: The League had condemned Japan's occupation of Manchuria. Japan then left the organisation in 1933.
16034.m: Japan left the League of Nations in 1933 over the Manchuria question.

16035.q: During which period was the German Empire a permanent member of the League of Nations Council?
16035.e: After the Locarno Treaties, Germany was admitted in 1926 and received a permanent seat on the Council. Under Hitler it left again in 1933.
16035.m: Germany had a permanent seat on the League of Nations Council from 1926 to 1933.

16036.q: Why were the League of Nations' sanctions against Italy in the Abyssinian War of 1935 largely ineffective?
a: Important goods such as oil were excluded
Italy was not a member of the League
The sanctions applied only to works of art
16036.e: The League condemned Italy as the aggressor and imposed economic sanctions. But oil and coal were excluded, and non-members such as the USA kept on supplying.
16036.m: The Abyssinian War showed the weakness of the League's sanctions.

16037.q: Why was the Soviet Union expelled from the League of Nations in 1939?
a: Because of its attack on Finland
Because of the Hitler-Stalin Pact alone
Because of the invasion of Manchuria
16037.e: The Soviet Union had joined in 1934. After its attack on Finland in the Winter War, it was expelled in December 1939.
16037.m: The Soviet Union was expelled from the League in 1939 because of the Winter War.

16038.q: When was the League of Nations formally dissolved?
16038.e: After the Second World War, the United Nations took over its tasks. The League officially dissolved itself on 18 April 1946.
16038.m: The League of Nations was dissolved in 1946 and replaced by the UN.

16039.q: Who proclaimed the “German Republic” from the balcony of the Reichstag on 9 November 1918?
16039.e: Philipp Scheidemann (SPD) proclaimed the republic from the Reichstag. A few hours later, Karl Liebknecht proclaimed a “free socialist republic”.
16039.m: Philipp Scheidemann proclaimed the German Republic on 9 November 1918.

16041.q: Which power did Article 48 of the Weimar Constitution give the Reich President?
a: Emergency decrees when security and order were in danger
The sole right to set taxes
Electing the judges of the Supreme Court
16041.e: Under Article 48, the Reich President could issue decrees in an emergency. From 1930 the presidential cabinets largely used it to govern without parliament.
16041.m: Article 48 made the Reich President a very powerful figure.

16042.q: How did the Kapp Putsch of March 1920 end?
a: It failed because of a general strike and civil servants refusing to cooperate
It was bloodily crushed by the Reichswehr
It led to Friedrich Ebert being removed
It ended with a compromise in the Reichstag
16042.e: Right-wing forces under Wolfgang Kapp occupied Berlin. A general strike and the refusal of the ministry officials made the putsch fail after a few days.
16042.m: The Kapp Putsch failed because of resistance from workers and the administration.

16043.q: Who murdered Foreign Minister Walther Rathenau in June 1922?
16043.e: Rathenau was murdered by members of the far-right Organisation Consul. The murder shows the violence against politicians of the young republic.
16043.m: Far-right terrorists murdered Walther Rathenau in 1922.

16044.q: What happened on 11 January 1923 at the start of the occupation of the Ruhr?
a: French and Belgian troops marched in because reparations were overdue
Polish troops advanced into Upper Silesia
The Reichswehr occupied the Saar region
16044.e: France and Belgium occupied the Ruhr to enforce reparations. The German government responded with passive resistance, which fuelled inflation even more.
16044.m: The occupation of the Ruhr in 1923 worsened hyperinflation.

16045.q: At what rate was the paper mark exchanged for the Rentenmark on 15 November 1923?
16045.e: The Rentenmark ended hyperinflation. One Rentenmark was worth one trillion (a million million) paper marks.
16045.m: The Rentenmark ended hyperinflation in November 1923.

16046.q: What was the main aim of the Locarno Treaties of 1925?
16046.e: In Locarno in Ticino, Germany recognised its western border with France and Belgium. With Poland and Czechoslovakia only arbitration treaties were signed, without guaranteeing their borders.
16046.m: The Locarno Treaties brought an easing of tensions with the West in 1925.

16047.q: Who was elected Reich President in 1925 after the death of Friedrich Ebert?
16047.e: The former Field Marshal Paul von Hindenburg beat Wilhelm Marx in 1925. He was critical of the republic.
16047.m: In 1925 Hindenburg, an opponent of the republic, became Reich President.

16048.q: What result did the Nazi Party (NSDAP) achieve in the Reichstag election of July 1932?
a: It became the largest party but missed an absolute majority
It failed and did not get into the Reichstag
It became the second-largest party behind the KPD
16048.e: The NSDAP became the largest party with 37.3 percent and 230 seats, but missed an absolute majority. In 1930 it had only had 107 seats.
16048.m: In July 1932 the NSDAP became the largest party without having a majority.

16049.q: On which day did prices on the New York Stock Exchange collapse on “Black Thursday”?
16049.e: On 24 October 1929 there was a great crash on Wall Street. It is seen as the trigger of the Great Depression.
16049.m: Black Thursday in 1929 marks the beginning of the Great Depression.

16050.q: Why did the crisis hit Germany especially hard?
a: The economy depended heavily on short-term US loans
Germany had no industry of its own
Germany was the only country to have left the gold standard
Reparations had already been paid off by 1929
