16050.e: Since the Dawes Plan, a lot of American capital had flowed into Germany. After the crash these loans were withdrawn, which put banks and firms in trouble.
16050.m: The withdrawal of American loans worsened the crisis in Germany.

16051.q: How many unemployed people were counted in Germany in February 1932?
16051.e: In February 1932 more than 6.1 million people were officially unemployed. On top of that came a large number of jobless people who were not recorded.
16051.m: At the start of 1932, more than six million people were unemployed in Germany.

16052.q: Which economic policy did Chancellor Heinrich Brüning pursue in the crisis?
a: An austerity policy with cuts in wages and spending
A debt-financed boost to the economy
The nationalisation of all big banks
The introduction of a basic income
16052.e: Brüning cut wages and public spending by emergency decree and raised taxes. This deflationary policy worsened the crisis without putting the budget on a sound footing for good.
16052.m: Brüning's austerity policy deepened the crisis in Germany.

16053.q: What happened in Germany in July 1931 during the Great Depression?
a: A banking crisis forced the banks to close for days
The Reichsmark was replaced by the dollar
The stock exchange was closed for ever
16053.e: After the collapse of the Danatbank on 13 July 1931, the banks stopped payments. Bank holidays and state control followed.
16053.m: The banking crisis of 1931 shook confidence in the German economy.

16054.q: What did Great Britain do with the pound in 1931 to fight the crisis?
a: It took the pound off gold
It replaced the pound with the dollar
It banned the export of pounds
It introduced a common currency with France
16054.e: Great Britain gave up the link to gold on 21 September 1931. The pound quickly lost about a quarter of its value against the dollar, which helped exports.
16054.m: Great Britain left the gold standard in 1931.

16055.q: What is US President Franklin D. Roosevelt's reform programme from 1933 called?
16055.e: With the New Deal, Roosevelt relied on public investment and social reforms, partly financed by debt. Full employment only came with the arms boom around 1941.
16055.m: Roosevelt fought the crisis with the New Deal.

16056.q: Why did Switzerland devalue the franc in 1936?
a: So that Swiss firms could sell more cheaply abroad again
So that Switzerland could join the European Union
Because the franc was replaced by the Reichsmark
Because Switzerland had lost its gold reserves
16056.e: Switzerland held on to the gold link and to austerity for a long time. Only the late devaluation of September 1936 made Swiss firms competitive on the world market again.
16056.m: Switzerland only devalued the franc in 1936.

16057.q: What result did the Lausanne Conference of 1932 bring for German reparations?
16057.e: In Lausanne in 1932 the states agreed on a greatly reduced final payment, which was never made. This meant reparations were effectively over.
16057.m: At the Lausanne Conference of 1932, reparations effectively ended.

16058.q: Where does the word “fascism” come from?
a: From the Italian “fascio”, league, and the Roman bundles of rods
16058.e: “Fascio” means league or bundle. The word is usually traced back to the “fasces”, the bundles of rods carried by Roman lictors as a sign of power.
16058.m: The word fascism goes back to the bundle of rods of the Roman lictors.

16059.q: Which feature belongs to Italian fascism under Mussolini?
a: The leader principle and one-party dictatorship
A federal structure of the state
16059.e: Fascism rejected liberalism and democracy. It relied on a leader, a state party, extreme nationalism and violence against opponents.
16059.m: Fascism replaced democracy with a leader cult and one-party rule.

16060.q: What were the uniformed fighting squads of the Italian fascists called?
16060.e: The fascist squadre wore black shirts. They used violence against socialists, trade unions and people who thought differently.
16060.m: The Italian fascists were called Blackshirts after their uniform.

16061.q: How do researchers often describe the authoritarian corporate state in Austria from 1933 to 1938?
16061.e: Under Engelbert Dollfuss and Kurt Schuschnigg, an authoritarian corporate state arose. The term Austrofascism is widely used, but is also debated by researchers.
16061.m: From 1933 to 1938 Austria was an authoritarian corporate state.

16062.q: What set off the so-called “Frontenfrühling” (spring of the Fronts) in Switzerland in 1933?
a: Switzerland joining the League of Nations
16062.e: After 30 January 1933, far-right “Fronts” in Switzerland gained momentum. The National Front was the most influential of these groups.
16062.m: The Frontenfrühling of 1933 was a short boom of far-right groups in Switzerland.

16063.q: What election success did the National Front achieve in the city of Zurich in 1933?
a: An absolute majority in the city executive
16063.e: In the Zurich city council elections of September 1933, the National Front won 10 seats. After that, however, its influence remained limited.
16063.m: The Fronts had notable election successes in Switzerland only for a short time.

16064.q: What happened in 1935 to the initiative for a total revision of the Federal Constitution, which the Fronts supported?
a: It was declared invalid by the Federal Supreme Court
16064.e: The initiative for a total revision of the Federal Constitution failed at the ballot box in 1935. Direct democracy proved to be a bulwark against authoritarian plans here.
16064.m: Swiss voters rejected the total revision of the constitution in 1935.

16065.q: How does the historian Roger Griffin define the core of fascism?
a: As populist ultranationalism with the idea of national rebirth
As a purely economic movement of the big banks
As a religious movement of the Catholic Church
As a form of direct democracy
16065.e: Griffin speaks of a “palingenetic” ultranationalism. This means the idea that the nation must be reborn from a supposed decline.
16065.m: Griffin sees the myth of national rebirth as the core of fascism.

16066.q: Why is it disputed whether the term “fascism” should also be applied to National Socialism?
a: Because racial antisemitism played a much more central role in Nazism
Because Mussolini had banned National Socialism
Because neither movement had a leader
16066.e: Some researchers use fascism as an umbrella term, others limit it to Italy. An important difference is the central place of racism and the policy of extermination in National Socialism.
16066.m: Whether National Socialism was a form of fascism is debated by researchers.

16067.q: In which decade was Benito Mussolini born?
16067.e: Mussolini was born on 29 July 1883 in Predappio in Romagna. When he became prime minister in 1922, he was only 39.
16067.m: Mussolini was born in 1883 and came to power at the age of 39.

16068.q: What link did the young Mussolini have with Switzerland?
a: He lived in Switzerland as an emigrant from about 1902 to 1904
He was Italy's envoy in Bern
He studied medicine in Basel until 1914
16068.e: Mussolini emigrated to Switzerland in 1902, worked there and was politically active as a socialist. At the end of 1904 he returned to Italy.
16068.m: The young Mussolini lived in Switzerland for a few years as an emigrant.

16069.q: Why was Mussolini expelled from the Italian Socialist Party at the end of 1914?
a: He called for Italy to enter the war
He wanted to work with the Church
He demanded the dissolution of the trade unions
16069.e: Mussolini was editor of the party newspaper “Avanti!”. Because he supported Italy entering the First World War, he was expelled and founded “Il Popolo d'Italia”.
16069.m: Mussolini broke with the socialists in 1914 over the question of war.

16070.q: Where were the “Fasci di combattimento” founded on 23 March 1919?
16070.e: The founding meeting took place in Milan. The Fascist Party later grew out of this movement.
16070.m: The fascist movement began in Milan in 1919.

16071.q: Which event in October 1922 led to Mussolini being appointed prime minister?
a: The founding of the Republic of Salò
The signing of the Lateran Treaties
16071.e: From 28 October 1922, fascist units moved towards Rome. King Victor Emmanuel III then asked Mussolini to form a government.
16071.m: After the March on Rome in 1922, Mussolini became prime minister.

16072.q: What was the consequence of the murder of the socialist Giacomo Matteotti in June 1924?
a: A crisis after which Mussolini expanded the dictatorship
The banning of the Fascist Party
New elections with a left-wing majority
16072.e: Matteotti had denounced electoral fraud and was murdered by squadristi. After the crisis, Mussolini took responsibility on 3 January 1925 and expanded the dictatorship.
16072.m: The Matteotti crisis led to the strengthening of the fascist dictatorship.

16073.q: Which conflict did the Lateran Treaties of 1929 end?
a: The dispute between the Italian state and the papacy
The war between Italy and Austria
The dispute over South Tyrol with Switzerland
The conflict over the colony of Libya
16073.e: With the Lateran Treaties, Vatican City was recognised as a sovereign state. This ended the so-called Roman Question.
16073.m: The Lateran Treaties of 1929 reconciled the Italian state with the Pope.

16074.q: Which war crime did Italy commit in the Abyssinian War from December 1935?
a: The systematic use of poison gas
Sinking British ships in the Suez Canal
16074.e: Italy used mustard gas, phosgene and arsenic compounds, including against civilians. Mussolini explicitly approved the use of gas.
16074.m: Italy used banned poison gas in the Abyssinian War.

16075.q: What happened to Mussolini on 28 April 1945?
a: He abdicated in favour of the king
16075.e: Mussolini was caught by communist partisans while fleeing and shot near Giulino di Mezzegra. Before that he had led the Republic of Salò, which depended on Germany.
16075.m: Mussolini was killed by partisans in April 1945.

16076.q: Which party did the NSDAP grow out of in 1920?
16076.e: The German Workers' Party, founded in Munich in 1919, renamed itself the National Socialist German Workers' Party in 1920.
16076.m: The NSDAP grew out of the German Workers' Party in 1920.

16077.q: What did Nazi ideology mean by “living space in the East” (Lebensraum)?
a: The conquest and Germanisation of Eastern European territories
Building new flats in East Berlin
16077.e: Hitler demanded the violent conquest of territories in Eastern Europe. The people living there were to be driven out, enslaved or murdered.
16077.m: The Lebensraum ideology aimed at a war of conquest in the East.

16078.q: What did the Nazi term “Volksgemeinschaft” (people's community) mean?
a: A community that excluded supposed “outsiders” and opponents
Equal rights for all people in the Reich
The merger of all trade unions
16078.e: The Volksgemeinschaft promised unity across classes. At the same time, it excluded and persecuted Jews, political opponents and other groups.
16078.m: The Volksgemeinschaft was based on inclusion and brutal exclusion.

16079.q: What did the “leader principle” (Führerprinzip) mean in National Socialism?
a: Orders from the top down without democratic control
The election of all leaders by the people
16079.e: Under the leader principle, all authority lay with the leader and was passed down from the top. Votes and controls disappeared.
16079.m: The leader principle replaced democracy with command and obedience.

16080.q: What role did the SA have in the period before 1933?
a: It was the NSDAP's thugs and meeting-hall guards
It was the army of the Weimar Republic
It was the police of the League of Nations
It was a church youth organisation
16080.e: The Sturmabteilung protected NSDAP meetings and used violence against political opponents. After 1933 it became an instrument of terror.
16080.m: The SA helped the NSDAP rise through violence on the streets.

16081.q: How did the SS develop after 1934?
a: Into the regime's central organisation of terror and extermination
Into a department of the railways
16081.e: Under Heinrich Himmler, the SS took over the police, the concentration camps and later the carrying out of genocide. It became the core of Nazi terror.
16081.m: Under Himmler, the SS became the most important instrument of Nazi terror.

16082.q: What role did racism play in the ideology of National Socialism?
a: It was a central core that divided people into “worthy” and “unworthy”
It only played a role in foreign policy
It was officially rejected by the NSDAP
16082.e: Nazi ideology divided people according to pseudo-scientific racial theories. This led to exclusion, persecution and finally mass murder.
16082.m: Racism was the core of National Socialist ideology.

16083.q: Against which political movements was National Socialism especially directed?
a: Against monarchy and the nobility alone
16083.e: The NSDAP fought parliamentary democracy, liberalism and the labour movement. Communists and Social Democrats were the first to be persecuted after 1933.
16083.m: National Socialism was anti-democratic, anti-liberal and anti-Marxist.

16084.q: Which statement about the Reichstag election of 5 March 1933 is correct?
a: Despite terror, the NSDAP missed an absolute majority
The NSDAP won more than two thirds of the votes
The KPD became the largest party
The election only took place after the Enabling Act
16084.e: Despite terror and restrictions on the opposition, the NSDAP won only 43.9 percent. Only together with the DNVP did the government reach a narrow majority.
16084.m: Even in March 1933, the NSDAP did not win an absolute majority of the votes.

16085.q: Where was Adolf Hitler born on 20 April 1889?
16085.e: Hitler was born in Braunau am Inn in Austria-Hungary. So he was originally an Austrian citizen.
16085.m: Hitler was born in Braunau am Inn in 1889.

16086.q: What did Hitler experience in Vienna between about 1907 and 1913?
a: He was rejected by the art academy and lived in poor conditions
He completed a degree in architecture
He was an officer in the Austrian army
He worked as a journalist for a big newspaper
16086.e: The Academy of Fine Arts did not accept him. At times he lived in a men's hostel and sold paintings and copies of postcards.
16086.m: Hitler failed with his artistic plans in Vienna.

16087.q: When did Hitler join the German Workers' Party (DAP)?
16087.e: Hitler attended a DAP meeting on 12 September 1919 and joined it shortly afterwards. He soon became its most important speaker.
16087.m: Hitler joined the German Workers' Party in 1919.

16088.q: How did Hitler's attempted putsch of 8 and 9 November 1923 in Munich end?
a: The police stopped the march at the Feldherrnhalle
Hitler took over the Bavarian government
The putsch was called off before it began
16088.e: The putsch began on the evening of 8 November in the Bürgerbräukeller. The next day the state police stopped the march at the Feldherrnhalle, and Hitler was arrested shortly afterwards.
16088.m: Hitler's putsch of 1923 failed at the Feldherrnhalle.

16089.q: What was partly written during Hitler's imprisonment in Landsberg?
16089.e: Hitler was sentenced to fortress imprisonment in 1924 but was released early. He wrote parts of “Mein Kampf” in Landsberg; the book appeared in 1925 and 1926.
16089.m: Hitler wrote parts of “Mein Kampf” in prison in Landsberg.

16090.q: To whom did Hitler lose the election for Reich President in 1932?
16090.e: In the second round on 10 April 1932, Hindenburg was confirmed in office. Hitler lost, but won many votes.
16090.m: Hindenburg beat Hitler in the presidential election of 1932.

16091.q: Who appointed Hitler Chancellor on 30 January 1933?
a: The Reichstag in a free vote
16091.e: Hindenburg appointed Hitler at the urging of conservative circles. They wrongly believed they could control him.
16091.m: Hindenburg appointed Hitler Chancellor on 30 January 1933.

16092.q: What did Hitler do after Hindenburg's death on 2 August 1934?
a: He combined the offices of Reich President and Chancellor
He called new elections for the presidency
16092.e: Hitler took over the powers of the Reich President and called himself “Führer and Reich Chancellor”. The Reichswehr had to swear an oath to him personally.
16092.m: After Hindenburg's death in 1934, Hitler combined all the top offices in himself.

16093.q: How and when did Adolf Hitler die?
a: By suicide on 30 April 1945 in Berlin
16093.e: Hitler took his own life in the bunker of the Reich Chancellery as the Red Army captured Berlin. A week later the Wehrmacht surrendered.
16093.m: Hitler took his own life in Berlin on 30 April 1945.

16094.q: What was the consequence of the Reichstag Fire Decree of 28 February 1933?
16094.e: After the Reichstag fire of 27 February, the decree suspended important basic rights. Thousands of communists and other opponents were arrested.
16094.m: The Reichstag Fire Decree did away with basic rights in 1933.

16095.q: What did the Enabling Act of 23 March 1933 allow Hitler's government to do?
a: Pass laws without the Reichstag's approval
Have the Reich President elected directly by the people
Change the constitution only by referendum
16095.e: By 444 votes to 94, the Reichstag handed its power to the government. Only the SPD voted against; the KPD members had been arrested or had fled.
16095.m: With the Enabling Act, Hitler could govern without parliament.

16096.q: Where did the Reichstag meet when it passed the Enabling Act?
a: In the Kroll Opera House in Berlin
In the National Theatre in Weimar
In St Paul's Church in Frankfurt
16096.e: The Reichstag building could not be used after the fire. So parliament met in the Kroll Opera House opposite.
16096.m: The Enabling Act was passed in the Kroll Opera House in Berlin.

16097.q: Which party, through Otto Wels, spoke the last free words in the Reichstag against the Enabling Act?
16097.e: Otto Wels said, among other things: “You can take our freedom and our lives, but not our honour.” Shortly afterwards the SPD was banned.
16097.m: As SPD leader, Otto Wels bravely defended democracy in 1933.

16098.q: What did the Law against the Formation of New Parties of 14 July 1933 mean?
a: The NSDAP became the only permitted party
New parties could be founded freely
16098.e: With this law, Germany was officially a one-party state. Other parties had already been banned or had dissolved themselves.
16098.m: From July 1933 Germany was a one-party state.

16099.q: Which organisation replaced the smashed free trade unions in 1933?
16099.e: The trade unions were smashed in May 1933. They were replaced by the German Labour Front under Robert Ley, which controlled the workers.
16099.m: The German Labour Front replaced the free trade unions in 1933.

a: Bringing the state and society into line with Nazi rule
16100.e: States, associations, clubs, the press and culture were placed under the NSDAP. Independent organisations were dissolved or taken over.
16100.m: Through Gleichschaltung, the states and associations lost their independence.

16101.q: Which concentration camp started operating near Munich in March 1933?
16101.e: Dachau was intended as a permanent facility and became the model for the later camp system. At first it mainly held political opponents.
16101.m: Dachau was one of the first concentration camps.

16102.q: What happened in the so-called “Röhm Putsch” (Night of the Long Knives) in summer 1934?
a: Hitler had SA leaders and other opponents murdered
The SA took power in the Reich
The Reichswehr staged a coup against Hindenburg
16102.e: On the pretext of an alleged putsch, Hitler had Ernst Röhm and many opponents killed without trial. Afterwards the killings were declared lawful after the event.
16102.m: With the killings of 1934, Hitler got rid of rivals without trial.

16103.q: Who headed the Reich Ministry of Public Enlightenment and Propaganda from 1933?
16103.e: The ministry was set up in March 1933. Joseph Goebbels headed it until 1945 and controlled the press, radio and film.
16103.m: Joseph Goebbels was the Nazi regime's propaganda minister.

16104.q: What was the task of the Reich Chamber of Culture, founded in 1933?
a: It controlled people working in the press, film, theatre and radio
It supported free art without rules
16104.e: Anyone who wanted to work in a cultural profession had to be a member. Unwanted artists, above all Jewish and politically disliked ones, were excluded.
16104.m: The Reich Chamber of Culture turned culture into a tool of propaganda.

16105.q: Why did the Nazi regime promote the cheap “people's receiver” (Volksempfänger)?
a: So that as many people as possible would hear propaganda on the radio
So that people could receive foreign stations
16105.e: The cheap radio set was meant to bring Nazi propaganda into every household. Listening to foreign stations was made a punishable offence during the war.
16105.m: The Volksempfänger brought Nazi propaganda into people's living rooms.

16106.q: What happened in many German university towns on 10 May 1933?
a: Books by unwanted authors were publicly burned
The first free student elections took place
16106.e: Students burned works by authors such as Heinrich Heine, Erich Kästner or Sigmund Freud. The action was meant to symbolically wipe out unwanted thinking.
16106.m: In the book burnings of 1933, works by banned authors were destroyed.

16107.q: Which propaganda film did Leni Riefenstahl make about the 1934 Nazi Party rally?
16107.e: “Triumph of the Will” came out in 1935 and staged Hitler and the party as a unity of leader and people. The film is seen as an example of the power of visual propaganda.
16107.m: Leni Riefenstahl's film “Triumph of the Will” glorified the 1934 party rally.

16108.q: What was the aim of the exhibition “Degenerate Art” in Munich in 1937?
a: To mock and outlaw modern art
To promote and sell modern art
To show the art of antiquity
16108.e: Works by artists such as Paul Klee, Ernst Ludwig Kirchner or Otto Dix were shown in a defamatory way. Many works were confiscated, sold or destroyed.
16108.m: With the exhibition “Degenerate Art”, the regime fought modern art.

16109.q: How did the Nazi regime use the 1936 Summer Olympics in Berlin?
a: To fake a peaceful and open-minded image for the world
To give special support to Jewish athletes
Not at all; they took place in Rome
16109.e: During the Games, antisemitic signs were temporarily removed. This was meant to deceive other countries about the true nature of the regime.
16109.m: The 1936 Olympic Games were a major propaganda event.

16110.q: Which question did Goebbels put to the audience in the Berlin Sportpalast on 18 February 1943?
16110.e: After the defeat at Stalingrad, Goebbels called for total war before a hand-picked party audience. The staged approval was broadcast on the radio.
16110.m: The Sportpalast speech of 1943 was meant to justify total war after Stalingrad.

16111.q: Why must photos and films from the Nazi era be examined critically as sources?
a: Many were deliberately staged and selected for propaganda
Because they were all faked in colour
Because there are no photos from this time
Because they all come from foreigners
16111.e: The regime controlled the press and the newsreels and showed only the pictures it wanted. Historians therefore always ask who made a picture and with what intention.
16111.m: With Nazi pictures, you must always ask who made them and why.

16112.q: What changed about antisemitism in Germany from about 1879?
a: It became the slogan of a political movement
It was directed only against the Jewish religion
It disappeared from public life for decades
16112.e: In 1879 Wilhelm Marr founded the “League of Antisemites”, and the Berlin antisemitism dispute began. The term spread quickly, and the first antisemitic parties appeared.
16112.m: From 1879 antisemitism formed as a political movement.

16113.q: How does modern racial antisemitism differ from older Christian anti-Judaism?
a: Jews were seen as a “race”, so even baptism changed nothing
It was directed only against the Jewish religion
16113.e: Christian anti-Judaism was directed against the faith. Racial antisemitism declared Jews an unchangeable “race”, so that even baptised Jews were excluded.
16113.m: Racial antisemitism made origin rather than religion the criterion.

16114.q: Why was the Berlin antisemitism dispute from 1879 especially far-reaching?
a: A respected historian made hatred of Jews acceptable in educated circles
It led to a ban on all Jewish newspapers
It ended with a law against Jews
It brought an end to antisemitism at the universities
16114.e: In 1879 Heinrich von Treitschke coined the phrase “The Jews are our misfortune”, which the Nazi hate paper “Der Stürmer” later adopted. Theodor Mommsen publicly contradicted him in 1880.
16114.m: Treitschke made antisemitism acceptable in educated circles.

16115.q: What are the so-called “Protocols of the Elders of Zion”?
a: An antisemitic forgery about an alleged Jewish world conspiracy
A genuine document from a Zionist congress
16115.e: The text was spread at the beginning of the 20th century and is a proven forgery. In Switzerland, the court in the Bern trial of 1935 also described the text as plagiarism and a forgery.
16115.m: The “Protocols of the Elders of Zion” are an antisemitic forgery.

16116.q: Which action against Jews took place throughout the German Reich on 1 April 1933?
a: A boycott of Jewish shops, doctors' surgeries and law offices
16116.e: The NSDAP called for a boycott, and SA men stood in front of Jewish shops and stopped customers from going in. It was the new regime's first nationwide anti-Jewish action.
16116.m: The boycott of 1 April 1933 was the first nationwide action against Jews.

16117.q: Which law of 7 April 1933 made it possible to dismiss Jewish civil servants?
a: The Law for the Restoration of the Professional Civil Service
16117.e: Through the so-called Aryan paragraph, Jewish and politically disliked civil servants were dismissed. At first there were still exceptions, for example for men who had fought at the front.
16117.m: Jewish civil servants were already dismissed by law in April 1933.

16118.q: What happened during the November pogroms of 1938?
a: Synagogues were destroyed and Jewish people were murdered and arrested
Jews got their right to vote back
Jewish shops were supported by the state
16118.e: About 1,400 synagogues and prayer rooms were destroyed, hundreds of Jews were murdered or driven to their deaths and about 30,000 Jewish men were taken to concentration camps. Nazi propaganda presented the violence as spontaneous “anger of the people”.
16118.m: The November pogroms of 1938 were a turning point towards open violence against Jews.

16119.q: What role did Switzerland play in the introduction of the “J stamp” in 1938?
a: It agreed with Germany that Jews' passports would be marked
It had the stamp banned by the League of Nations
16119.e: Switzerland wanted to recognise Jewish refugees at the border and threatened to require visas for all Germans. In autumn 1938 both states agreed on the red J; according to recent research, the idea of the stamp came from German officials.
16119.m: With its refugee policy, Switzerland contributed to the introduction of the J stamp.

16120.q: Why is the Swiss ban on kosher slaughter of 1893 seen as historically tainted?
a: The first popular initiative was accepted partly for antisemitic reasons
It was demanded by Hitler personally
It was demanded by the League of Nations
16120.e: In 1893 the ban on kosher slaughter (shechita) was the first federal popular initiative to be accepted. Besides animal protection, antisemitic motives also played a part in the debate.
16120.m: Switzerland's first accepted popular initiative also had antisemitic background.

16121.q: When were the Nuremberg Laws passed?
16121.e: The Reichstag was specially called to Nuremberg and passed the laws unanimously. They were published in the Reich Law Gazette on 16 September 1935.
16121.m: The Nuremberg Laws were passed in September 1935.

16122.q: On which occasion were the Nuremberg Laws announced?
a: At the NSDAP party rally, the “Rally of Freedom”
At a meeting of the League of Nations
16122.e: The laws were passed at the 7th party rally in Nuremberg. The regime called it the “Rally of Freedom”.
16122.m: The Nuremberg Laws were announced at an NSDAP party rally.

16123.q: What did the Reich Citizenship Law lay down?
a: Only people “of German or related blood” were to have full political rights
All inhabitants received the same right to vote
Women were no longer allowed to work
16123.e: The law separated nationals from “Reich citizens” with full rights. This made Jews citizens with fewer rights.
16123.m: The Reich Citizenship Law made Jews second-class people.

16124.q: What did the “Law for the Protection of German Blood and German Honour” forbid?
16124.e: The so-called Blood Protection Law banned marriages and relationships between Jews and non-Jews. Breaking it was prosecuted as “racial disgrace”.
16124.m: The Blood Protection Law banned marriages between Jews and non-Jews.

16125.q: Which third law is often counted among the Nuremberg Laws today?
16125.e: The Reich Flag Law declared the swastika flag the national flag. At the time it was not counted among them, but today it is often included.
16125.m: With the Reich Flag Law, the swastika flag became the national flag.

16126.q: By which criterion did the First Regulation to the Reich Citizenship Law of 14 November 1935 decide who counted as a “Jew”?
a: By the religion of the grandparents
16126.e: Anyone with at least three Jewish grandparents counted as a Jew. Although the laws spoke of “race”, they relied on the religion of the ancestors, which shows the pseudo-science of racial theory.
16126.m: The supposed “race” was decided by the religion of the grandparents.

16127.q: Whom did the Nazi authorities call a “Mischling of the first degree” under the Nuremberg Laws?
a: People who had converted to Judaism
16127.e: A “Mischling of the first degree” was someone with two Jewish grandparents who was not classed as a “Jew”. Someone with one Jewish grandparent counted as a “Mischling of the second degree”.
16127.m: The Nazi categories divided people arbitrarily by their grandparents.

16128.q: What was the immediate consequence of the Nuremberg Laws for Jews in Germany?
a: They lost the right to vote and could no longer hold public office
They got their own members in the Reichstag
They were all stripped of citizenship at once
They had to wear a star immediately
16128.e: Jews lost political rights, and Jewish civil servants had to leave at the end of 1935. The laws created the legal basis for further loss of rights and persecution.
16128.m: The Nuremberg Laws created the basis for stripping Jews of their rights.

16129.q: How were the Nuremberg Laws repealed after the Second World War?
a: By Control Council Law No. 1 of 20 September 1945
By a League of Nations decision in 1946
16129.e: With its first law, the Allied Control Council repealed the key unjust Nazi laws. These included the Nuremberg Laws.
16129.m: The Allies repealed the Nuremberg Laws in 1945.

16130.q: On which date did the Second World War in Europe begin with the German invasion of Poland?
16130.e: Early in the morning of 1 September 1939, the Wehrmacht attacked Poland without a declaration of war. This day is seen as the beginning of the Second World War in Europe.
16130.m: The Second World War in Europe began on 1 September 1939.

16131.q: Which staged incident on 31 August 1939 served Nazi propaganda as a pretext for the attack on Poland?
a: The faked attack on the Gleiwitz radio station
The sinking of a German ship off Danzig
An assassination of the German ambassador in Warsaw
The blowing up of a bridge over the Oder
16131.e: An SS unit under Alfred Naujocks attacked the Gleiwitz radio station and faked a Polish attack. Hitler used such staged incidents to present the war as defence.
16131.m: The attack on the Gleiwitz radio station was a deception staged by the SS.

16132.q: Which German warship opened fire on the Polish garrison on the Westerplatte near Danzig on 1 September 1939?
16132.e: From 4.45 am, the battleship and training ship Schleswig-Holstein shelled the Westerplatte. These shots are seen as one of the first acts of combat of the war.
16132.m: The Schleswig-Holstein shelled the Westerplatte on the first day of the war.

16133.q: What did the secret additional protocol to the Hitler-Stalin Pact of 23 August 1939 lay down?
a: The division of East Central Europe into German and Soviet spheres of interest
A joint declaration of war on France
The return of Alsace-Lorraine to Germany
A mutual assistance pact against Japan
16133.e: In the secret protocol, Germany and the Soviet Union divided Poland along the Narew, Vistula and San rivers. Finland, Estonia, Latvia and Bessarabia were assigned to the Soviet sphere, Lithuania at first to the German one.
16133.m: The Hitler-Stalin Pact secretly divided East Central Europe between two dictatorships.

16134.q: When did Great Britain and France declare war on Germany?
16134.e: Great Britain and France had given Poland guarantees. After Germany did not answer their ultimatum, they declared war on 3 September 1939.
16134.m: Great Britain and France declared war on Germany two days after the invasion of Poland.

16135.q: What happened in Poland on 17 September 1939?
a: The Red Army marched into eastern Poland
Poland signed an armistice with Germany
16135.e: In line with the agreements of the Hitler-Stalin Pact, the Soviet Union occupied eastern Poland from 17 September 1939. Poland was therefore attacked from two sides.
16135.m: In 1939 Poland was attacked by Germany and the Soviet Union at the same time.

16136.q: When did the Polish capital Warsaw surrender in 1939?
16136.e: After heavy bombing and shelling, Warsaw surrendered on 28 September 1939. The campaign was thus largely decided after a few weeks.
16136.m: Warsaw surrendered at the end of September 1939 after heavy shelling.

16137.q: Which decision did the Swiss Federal Assembly make on 30 August 1939, shortly before the war began?
a: It elected Henri Guisan General of the Army
It left the League of Nations
It closed the border to all refugees
It extended the Federal Council's term of office
16137.e: For active service, the Federal Assembly elects a general. On 30 August 1939 it chose Henri Guisan, who led the Swiss Army until 1945.
16137.m: Henri Guisan was elected General of the Swiss Army in 1939.

16138.q: Why do many historians consider the term “Blitzkrieg” misleading?
a: It was more a propaganda slogan than a military doctrine planned in advance
It actually comes from the Thirty Years' War
It was only invented by the Allies after 1945
It originally referred only to attacks at sea
16138.e: The historian Karl-Heinz Frieser shows that “Blitzkrieg” was not a technical term of the Wehrmacht. The myth arose mainly after the unexpectedly quick victory in the western campaign of 1940.
16138.m: Blitzkrieg was more a propaganda term than a concept planned in advance.

16139.q: Which aircraft became the symbol of the close cooperation between the air force and tank units in the Blitzkrieg?
16139.e: Stukas attacked targets ahead of the advancing tanks as flying artillery. Normal artillery often could not keep up with the fast advance.
16139.m: In the Blitzkrieg, Stukas supported the tanks as flying artillery.

16140.q: Which technical equipment particularly helped the quick command of German tank units in 1939 and 1940?
16140.e: German tanks were fitted with radios. This allowed units to be commanded in a mobile and coordinated way, while many opponents still relied on flags or messengers.
16140.m: Radios made the German tank units fast and mobile.

16141.q: Which German general is seen as one of the most important pioneers of the tank arm and Blitzkrieg warfare?
16141.e: Heinz Guderian argued early on for tank divisions that could operate independently. He led tank units in the Polish and western campaigns.
16141.m: Heinz Guderian shaped the building of the German tank arm.

16142.q: What was a typical aim of fast tank advances in the Blitzkrieg?
a: To encircle the enemy and cut off its supplies
To besiege enemy cities for a long time
16142.e: Tank units pushed deep into the enemy's rear, often without protecting their flanks. In this way enemy armies were to be trapped in pockets.
16142.m: Blitzkrieg advances aimed at encircling enemy armies.

16143.q: Which weakness of the Wehrmacht showed that it was not fully equipped for a fast war of movement?
a: Most of the troops depended on horses and marching on foot
16143.e: Only a small part of the army was motorised. Most infantry divisions marched on foot and moved equipment with horses.
16143.m: Despite its tanks, the Wehrmacht was mostly not motorised.

16144.q: Why did the Blitzkrieg principle fail in the Soviet Union in 1941?
a: The Red Army could not be destroyed in a short campaign, and the timetable collapsed
The Wehrmacht attacked only with infantry and no tanks
The Soviet Union surrendered before any fighting
Great Britain landed in Germany at the same time
16144.e: German planning counted on victory within a few months. Vast spaces, supply problems and unexpectedly strong Soviet reserves made this plan fail.
16144.m: In the Soviet Union, the hope of a short campaign failed.

16145.q: When did the German attack in the west on France, Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg begin?
16145.e: On 10 May 1940 the Wehrmacht attacked the neutral Benelux states and France. The period before is often called the “Phoney War”.
16145.m: The western campaign began on 10 May 1940.

16146.q: What was the aim of the German “sickle cut” plan in the western campaign of 1940?
a: To cut off and encircle the Allied troops in Belgium from the south
To break through the Maginot Line head-on
16146.e: Erich von Manstein suggested making the main thrust through the Ardennes to the Channel coast. This trapped the Allies who had advanced into Belgium.
16146.m: In 1940 the sickle cut encircled the Allies in Belgium.

16147.q: Through which area did the surprising main thrust of the German tanks go in May 1940?
a: Over the Maginot Line in Alsace
16147.e: The Allies thought the Ardennes were hardly passable for tanks. The breakthrough at Sedan on the Meuse made the advance to the Channel coast possible.
16147.m: The German main thrust in 1940 came as a surprise through the Ardennes.

16148.q: How many Allied soldiers were brought from Dunkirk to England in Operation Dynamo in 1940?
16148.e: From 26 May to 4 June 1940, 338,226 British and French soldiers were evacuated. Besides warships, many small civilian boats helped too.
16148.m: In 1940 more than 330,000 soldiers were rescued at Dunkirk.

16149.q: What happened in Rotterdam on 14 May 1940?
a: The city was bombed by the German Luftwaffe
The Netherlands declared war on Germany
The port was blockaded by British ships
16149.e: More than 800 civilians died in the bombing of Rotterdam's city centre. Shortly afterwards the Netherlands surrendered.
16149.m: The bombing of Rotterdam led to the Netherlands' quick surrender.

16150.q: Where was the Franco-German armistice signed on 22 June 1940?
16150.e: Hitler deliberately had the armistice signed at Compiègne, where Germany had had to sign the armistice of the First World War in 1918.
16150.m: The armistice of 1940 was signed at Compiègne, a place full of symbolism.

16151.q: Which operation came before the western campaign on 9 April 1940?
a: Operation Weserübung, the occupation of Denmark and Norway
Operation Sea Lion, the landing in England
Operation Barbarossa, the attack on the Soviet Union
Operation Citadel, the offensive at Kursk
16151.e: With Operation Weserübung, Germany occupied Denmark and attacked Norway. One aim was to secure the supply of iron ore from Sweden.
16151.m: In April 1940 Germany occupied Denmark and Norway.

16152.q: Which event took place on 25 July 1940, when Switzerland was almost completely surrounded by the Axis powers after the fall of France?
a: General Guisan's Rütli Report to the senior officers
The signing of an alliance with Germany
The disbanding of the Swiss Army
16152.e: On the Rütli meadow, Guisan confirmed the army's will to resist. Linked to this was the strategy of the Réduit (national redoubt) in the Alps.
16152.m: With the Rütli Report, General Guisan strengthened the will to defend the country in 1940.

16153.q: What was the main aim of the German Luftwaffe in the Battle of Britain in 1940?
a: To win control of the air for a planned invasion
To sink the British fleet in the Pacific
16153.e: Control of the air over the English Channel and southern England was a precondition for a German landing. The Royal Air Force prevented this.
16153.m: Without control of the air, a German landing in England was not possible.

16154.q: What was the German plan for an invasion of Great Britain called?
16154.e: Hitler ordered preparations on 16 July 1940. In September 1940 the operation was postponed indefinitely.
16154.m: Operation Sea Lion was never carried out.

16155.q: What was the German Luftwaffe's major offensive from “Eagle Day” in August 1940 meant to achieve?
a: To decisively weaken the Royal Air Force
To sink the US fleet in the Atlantic
16155.e: Eagle Day on 13 August 1940 was meant to decisively weaken the Royal Air Force. This did not succeed.
16155.m: Eagle Day in August 1940 opened the major German offensive.

16156.q: Which technology helped the Royal Air Force spot approaching German formations early?
a: The Chain Home radar network on the coast
16156.e: The Chain Home radar stations reported attacks early. This allowed the British fighters to be used where they were needed.
16156.m: Radar gave the Royal Air Force an important advantage.

16157.q: To whom was Churchill referring with the sentence “Never was so much owed by so many to so few”?
a: The pilots of the Royal Air Force
The sailors of the merchant navy
The ministers of his war cabinet
16157.e: In August 1940 Churchill paid tribute to the few fighter pilots who were defending the country. The sentence became one of the best-known quotations of the war.
16157.m: With this sentence, Churchill honoured the pilots of the Royal Air Force.

16158.q: Which day is commemorated in Great Britain as “Battle of Britain Day”?
16158.e: On 15 September 1940 the Royal Air Force fought off large German attacks on London. Shortly afterwards the planned landing in England was postponed.
16158.m: 15 September is seen as the turning point of the Battle of Britain.

16159.q: Which English city was badly destroyed by a German air raid on 14 November 1940?
16159.e: The raid on Coventry destroyed large parts of the city centre and the cathedral. The ruins of the cathedral are today a place of reconciliation.
16159.m: In 1940 Coventry became a symbol of destruction by air raids.

16160.q: Which change of strategy by the Luftwaffe from September 1940 took pressure off the British airfields?
a: The switch to attacks on London and other cities
The withdrawal of all aircraft to Africa
Concentrating on attacks on ships in the Atlantic
16160.e: At the start of September 1940, Hitler ordered attacks on London. This gave the Royal Air Force time to rebuild its bases and fighters.
16160.m: The switch to attacks on cities took pressure off the Royal Air Force.

16161.q: On which date did the German attack on the Soviet Union begin?
16161.e: With Operation Barbarossa, Germany broke the Hitler-Stalin Pact. About three million German soldiers crossed the border.
16161.m: On 22 June 1941 Germany attacked the Soviet Union.

16162.q: Into how many army groups was the German attack on the Soviet Union in 1941 divided?
a: Three army groups, North, Centre and South
Two army groups, East and West
16162.e: Army Group North aimed at Leningrad, Army Group Centre at Moscow and Army Group South at Ukraine.
16162.m: Three army groups attacked the Soviet Union in 1941.

16163.q: Why do historians call the war against the Soviet Union a “war of annihilation”?
a: Because from the start it was designed for murder, starvation and expulsion of the population
Because only weapons were to be destroyed
Because both sides took no prisoners
Because it lasted only a few days
16163.e: The Nazi leadership planned racially motivated mass murder and the starvation of millions of people. Rules of international law were deliberately ignored.
16163.m: The war against the Soviet Union was planned as a racist war of annihilation.

16164.q: What did the “Commissar Order” of 6 June 1941 command?
a: To murder captured political commissars of the Red Army immediately
To treat Soviet commissars as allies
To give German officers political training
To treat prisoners of war according to the Geneva Convention
16164.e: The order deliberately broke the laws of war. It shows that the Wehrmacht leadership took part in criminal orders.
16164.m: The Commissar Order was an order to murder that broke international law.

16165.q: Roughly how many Soviet prisoners of war died in German captivity?
16165.e: Of almost six million Soviet prisoners of war, about three million died, mainly from hunger, cold and disease. Their deaths were deliberately accepted.
16165.m: About half of the Soviet prisoners of war did not survive German captivity.

16166.q: How long did the siege of Leningrad by German troops last?
16166.e: The siege lasted from 8 September 1941 to 27 January 1944. According to most estimates, about 1.1 million civilians died, most of them of hunger.
16166.m: The siege of Leningrad cost about a million civilians their lives.

16167.q: What was the “Road of Life” during the siege of Leningrad?
a: A supply route across the frozen Lake Ladoga
A secret tunnel under the Neva
16167.e: In winter, an ice road ran across Lake Ladoga into the city. Food came in along it, and civilians were evacuated.
16167.m: The Road of Life across Lake Ladoga supplied the besieged city of Leningrad.

16168.q: Which Soviet operation encircled the 6th Army at Stalingrad in November 1942?
16168.e: Operation Uranus began on 19 November 1942. Within a few days the 6th Army under Friedrich Paulus was surrounded.
16168.m: With Operation Uranus, the Red Army encircled the 6th Army at Stalingrad.

16169.q: Of the roughly 90,000 to 110,000 German prisoners from Stalingrad, about how many returned home after the war?
16169.e: The last parts of the 6th Army surrendered on 2 February 1943. Most of the prisoners died of exhaustion, hunger and disease in captivity.
16169.m: Only a small number of the prisoners from Stalingrad came back.

16170.q: On which date did Japan attack the US base at Pearl Harbor in Hawaii?
16170.e: On the morning of 7 December 1941, Japanese carrier aircraft attacked the US Pacific Fleet. After that, the USA entered the war.
16170.m: The attack on Pearl Harbor on 7 December 1941 brought the USA into the war.

16171.q: Which Japanese admiral is seen as the author of the plan to attack Pearl Harbor?
16171.e: Yamamoto was commander-in-chief of the Combined Fleet and developed the idea. Vice Admiral Nagumo led the attack force.
16171.m: Admiral Yamamoto planned the attack on Pearl Harbor.

16172.q: Which US measure in summer 1941 greatly sharpened the conflict with Japan?
a: A complete oil embargo against Japan
The declaration of war on Germany
16172.e: Japan depended heavily on imported oil. The embargo threatened its warfare in China and Southeast Asia and contributed to the decision to attack.
16172.m: The American oil embargo of 1941 sharpened the conflict with Japan.

16173.q: Roughly how many Americans died in the attack on Pearl Harbor?
16173.e: In total, 2,403 military personnel and civilians died. Almost half of them died on the battleship USS Arizona.
16173.m: About 2,400 Americans died in the attack on Pearl Harbor.

16174.q: Why was the attack on Pearl Harbor not a complete military success for Japan?
a: The US aircraft carriers were not in the harbour
All the Japanese aircraft were shot down
The battleships had been moved away beforehand
The attack took place at night and missed all its targets
16174.e: The carriers Enterprise and Lexington were at sea, and the Saratoga was on the US west coast. In the Pacific War, aircraft carriers became more important than battleships.
16174.m: The American aircraft carriers escaped the attack on Pearl Harbor.

16175.q: Which battleship, now a memorial, was destroyed at Pearl Harbor by an explosion in its ammunition magazines?
16175.e: A bomb set off the Arizona's ammunition, and more than 1,100 sailors died. The wreck still lies in the harbour today and is a memorial.
16175.m: The USS Arizona is today a memorial to the victims of Pearl Harbor.

a: Germany and Italy declared war on the USA
The USA declared war on the Soviet Union
16176.e: Four days after Pearl Harbor, Germany and Italy declared war on the USA. This finally turned the war into a world war.
16176.m: With Germany's declaration of war on the USA, the war became global.

16177.q: How did President Roosevelt describe 7 December 1941 in his speech to Congress?
a: As “a date which will live in infamy”
16177.e: In his speech on 8 December 1941, Roosevelt called the day a date which will live in infamy. Congress then declared war on Japan.
16177.m: Roosevelt called the day of Pearl Harbor a date which will live in infamy.

16178.q: How many European Jews were murdered in the Holocaust?
16178.e: Researchers give figures of 5.6 to 6.3 million murdered Jews. That was about two thirds of the Jews living in Europe at the time.
16178.m: About six million Jews were murdered in the Holocaust.

16179.q: What does the Hebrew word “Shoah”, often used for the Holocaust, mean?
16179.e: In Hebrew, Shoah means the catastrophe or the great disaster. Many prefer this term because “Holocaust” originally referred to a religious burnt offering.
16179.m: Shoah is the Hebrew word for the catastrophe.

16180.q: What was discussed at the Wannsee Conference of 20 January 1942?
a: The organisation and coordination of the murder of the European Jews
16180.e: Under the leadership of Reinhard Heydrich, senior officials coordinated the carrying out of the so-called “Final Solution of the Jewish Question”. Adolf Eichmann took the minutes.
16180.m: At the Wannsee Conference, the genocide of the Jews was coordinated organisationally.

16181.q: What was the task of the Einsatzgruppen of the Security Police and the SD in the Soviet Union from 1941?
a: They carried out mass shootings, above all of Jews
They built roads for the Wehrmacht
They supplied the civilian population with food
They only guarded prisoners of war
16181.e: Einsatzgruppen A to D followed behind the front and murdered hundreds of thousands of people. They were supported by the Wehrmacht, police and local helpers.
16181.m: The Einsatzgruppen committed mass murder behind the Eastern Front.

16182.q: When did the November pogroms take place, in which synagogues were destroyed and Jews persecuted in Germany?
16182.e: In the night of 9 to 10 November 1938, synagogues were set on fire and Jewish shops destroyed. Hundreds of people were murdered or died as a result.
16182.m: The November pogroms of 1938 were a step towards open violence against Jews.

16183.q: What did the Nuremberg Laws of 1935 lay down?
a: They took away Jews' civic rights and banned marriages with non-Jews
They set out the punishment of war criminals
16183.e: The Nuremberg Laws made Jews second-class citizens in law. They were the basis for further exclusion and persecution.
16183.m: The Nuremberg Laws of 1935 turned discrimination against Jews into law.

16184.q: When did the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising begin?
16184.e: Jewish fighters under Mordechai Anielewicz put up armed resistance against the deportations. The SS crushed the uprising by mid-May 1943.
16184.m: The Warsaw Ghetto Uprising of 1943 was an act of Jewish resistance.

16185.q: Which Swiss diplomat in Budapest saved tens of thousands of Jews from deportation with protective letters?
16185.e: Carl Lutz was vice-consul in Budapest and saved more than 60,000 people with protective letters and safe houses. Yad Vashem honoured him as Righteous Among the Nations.
16185.m: The Swiss Carl Lutz saved tens of thousands of Jews in Budapest.

16186.q: Which measure did Switzerland agree with Germany in autumn 1938?
a: Marking the passports of German Jews with a “J”
Opening the borders to all refugees
16186.e: Switzerland wanted to recognise Jewish refugees at the border and threatened to require visas for all Germans. Both countries then agreed on the J stamp, which made it easier for Swiss officials to turn Jewish refugees away.
16186.m: The J stamp made it easier for Switzerland to turn Jewish refugees away.

16187.q: What do many Roma call the genocide of the Sinti and Roma in the Nazi era?
16187.e: In Romani, Porajmos means roughly “the devouring”. Several hundred thousand Sinti and Roma were murdered.
16187.m: Sinti and Roma were also victims of a Nazi genocide.

16188.q: Which St Gallen police commander let Jewish refugees into Switzerland in 1938 and 1939 against instructions?
16188.e: Paul Grüninger backdated the entry of many refugees to before the border closure and so saved several hundred people. He was dismissed, convicted in 1940 and only cleared by a court in 1995; Yad Vashem honoured him in 1971 as Righteous Among the Nations.
16188.m: Paul Grüninger defied the rules to save Jewish refugees.

16189.q: Which camp was set up in March 1933 as one of the first permanent concentration camps and later served as a model?
16189.e: Dachau concentration camp opened on 22 March 1933. Its organisation served as a model for other camps in the Reich.
16189.m: Dachau concentration camp was a model for the whole camp system.

16190.q: Who was mainly imprisoned in the first concentration camps in 1933?
a: Political opponents such as communists and social democrats
16190.e: The first camps served to eliminate and intimidate political opponents. Later Jews, Sinti and Roma, homosexuals and many other groups were added.
16190.m: The first concentration camps were directed mainly against political opponents.

16191.q: What does the term “extermination through labour” mean in the concentration camp system?
a: The deliberate death of prisoners through forced labour, hunger and disease
16191.e: In concentration camps, many prisoners died of exhaustion, malnutrition and disease. Their deaths during forced labour were deliberately accepted.
16191.m: In the concentration camps, forced labour was used deliberately as a means of extermination.

16192.q: When was Dachau concentration camp liberated by US troops?
16192.e: Soldiers of the US 7th Army liberated Dachau on 29 April 1945. In total more than 200,000 people were imprisoned in the camp, and about 41,500 died.
16192.m: Dachau concentration camp was liberated at the end of April 1945.

16193.q: How did extermination camps such as Treblinka differ from most concentration camps?
a: They served mainly to murder the deported people immediately
Only prisoners of war were held there
They were all in Western Europe
16193.e: In extermination camps, most people were murdered straight after they arrived. Only a few had to work to keep the camp running.
16193.m: Extermination camps were places of immediate mass murder.

16194.q: Which three extermination camps belonged to “Operation Reinhard”?
16194.e: Operation Reinhard began in March 1942 and aimed to murder the Jews in the General Government. Belzec, Sobibor and Treblinka were built for this purpose.
16194.m: Belzec, Sobibor and Treblinka were the camps of Operation Reinhard.

16195.q: Roughly how many people were murdered in the Auschwitz camp complex?
16195.e: About 1.1 million people were murdered in the Auschwitz camp complex, the great majority of them Jews. Auschwitz became the symbol of the Holocaust.
16195.m: Auschwitz was the largest site of murder in the Holocaust.

16196.q: Which army liberated the Auschwitz camp on 27 January 1945?
16196.e: Soviet troops reached Auschwitz on 27 January 1945. This day is now International Holocaust Remembrance Day.
16196.m: 27 January commemorates the liberation of Auschwitz.

16197.q: What happened from December 1941 in the Kulmhof (Chelmno) camp in occupied Poland?
a: The systematic mass murder of Jews with gas vans began there
Only prisoners of war were made to work there
Jews were gathered there to leave for Switzerland
Arms were made there for the Wehrmacht
16197.e: In Kulmhof in the annexed Wartheland, systematic murder with gas vans began in December 1941. It is regarded as the first extermination camp; others followed later.
16197.m: Kulmhof was the first extermination camp.

16198.q: Which lone assassin carried out a bomb attack on Hitler in the Bürgerbräukeller in Munich on 8 November 1939?
16198.e: The carpenter Georg Elser built a time bomb into a pillar on his own. Hitler left the hall about 13 minutes before the explosion and survived.
16198.m: Georg Elser acted alone in 1939 and only narrowly missed Hitler.

16199.q: Where was Georg Elser arrested on the evening of his assassination attempt?
a: In Konstanz, just before the Swiss border
On the French border near Strasbourg
16199.e: Elser wanted to flee to Switzerland and was stopped by customs in Konstanz. He was murdered in Dachau concentration camp in April 1945.
16199.m: Georg Elser was arrested at the border with Switzerland.

16200.q: How did the resistance group “White Rose” in Munich mainly act?
a: It distributed leaflets against the Nazi regime
It carried out bomb attacks on barracks
It spied for the Soviet Union
16200.e: The group around Hans and Sophie Scholl wrote and spread six leaflets. They called for resistance against Hitler and the war.
16200.m: The White Rose resisted with leaflets.

16201.q: When were Hans Scholl, Sophie Scholl and Christoph Probst executed?
16201.e: After the Scholls were arrested on 18 February 1943, the three were sentenced to death by the People's Court. The sentence was carried out on the same day, 22 February 1943.
16201.m: Hans and Sophie Scholl were executed in February 1943.

16202.q: Where did Claus Schenk Graf von Stauffenberg set off his bomb on 20 July 1944?
a: At the Wolf's Lair headquarters in East Prussia
16202.e: Stauffenberg put the briefcase with explosives down in a briefing hut. The case was moved, and the heavy map table shielded Hitler.
16202.m: The assassination attempt of 20 July 1944 took place at the Wolf's Lair.

16203.q: What was “Operation Valkyrie” in connection with 20 July 1944?
a: A plan for internal unrest that the conspirators wanted to use for a coup
The German plan to attack England
A plan to free prisoners of war
16203.e: Valkyrie was an official plan of the Replacement Army in case of internal unrest. The conspirators adapted it to take power after Hitler's death.
16203.m: The conspirators of 20 July wanted to use Operation Valkyrie for the coup.

16204.q: Which Catholic bishop publicly denounced the murders of sick and disabled people in 1941?
16204.e: The Bishop of Münster made the so-called euthanasia public in his sermons. The centrally organised Aktion T4 was then officially stopped, but the murders continued in other ways.
16204.m: Bishop von Galen made the murders of patients publicly known.

16205.q: How did the protest by non-Jewish wives in Berlin's Rosenstrasse in 1943 end?
a: Their arrested Jewish husbands were released
The women were allowed to leave for Switzerland
16205.e: For days the women gathered in front of the building where their Jewish husbands were being held. The men were released; how far this was due to the protest is disputed among historians.
16205.m: The Rosenstrasse protest is a rare example of public protest in the Nazi state.

16206.q: On which date did the Allies land in Normandy?
16206.e: On D-Day, 6 June 1944, the largest amphibious landing in history began. On the first day, about 170,000 soldiers went ashore.
16206.m: The Normandy landings began on 6 June 1944.

16207.q: Who was commander-in-chief of the Allied forces in Operation Overlord?
16207.e: As Supreme Allied Commander, General Eisenhower led the invasion. Montgomery commanded the land forces in the first phase.
16207.m: Eisenhower was commander-in-chief of the invasion of Normandy.

16208.q: On which landing beaches did the American troops go ashore on D-Day?
16208.e: The Americans landed at Utah and Omaha. The British landed at Gold and Sword, and the Canadians at Juno.
16208.m: The Americans landed on the Utah and Omaha beaches.

16209.q: Because of the deception operation “Fortitude”, where did the German leadership expect the main Allied landing?
16209.e: With an invented army group under Patton, the Allies faked a landing in the Pas-de-Calais. German reserves were kept back there.
16209.m: The Fortitude deception drew the Germans' attention to the Pas-de-Calais.

16210.q: What were the “Mulberry harbours” in the invasion of Normandy?
a: Artificial harbours built off the coast for supplies
16210.e: Because no large port had been captured, the Allies built two artificial harbours. Troops and materiel were landed through them.
16210.m: Artificial Mulberry harbours secured supplies after the landing.

16211.q: Which German field marshal was responsible for strengthening the coastal defences in northern France in 1944?
16211.e: Rommel took over Army Group B at the start of 1944. He had the Atlantic Wall strengthened with obstacles and mines.
16211.m: Erwin Rommel strengthened the Atlantic Wall in 1944.

16212.q: When was Paris liberated after the Normandy landings?
16212.e: After the breakout from Normandy, Allied and French troops reached Paris. The city was liberated on 25 August 1944.

16213.q: What was the second Allied landing in France, on the Mediterranean coast on 15 August 1944, called?
16213.e: In Operation Dragoon, Allied troops landed between Toulon and Cannes. They then pushed quickly north through the Rhône valley.
16213.m: With Operation Dragoon, the Allies also landed in southern France.

16214.q: When did the unconditional surrender of the Wehrmacht come into force?
16214.e: The surrender was signed in Reims and Berlin-Karlshorst. It came into force on all fronts on 8 May 1945 at 23:01 Central European Time.
16214.m: The war in Europe ended on 8 May 1945.

16215.q: Why is victory celebrated in Russia on 9 May rather than 8 May?
a: Because of the time difference, it came into force on 9 May in Moscow
Because the Soviet Union only surrendered a month later
Because Stalin saw 8 May as an unlucky day
Because the surrender was only signed in Moscow
16215.e: At 23:01 Central European Time it was already after midnight in Moscow. In addition, the surrender was only announced there after the signing in Karlshorst.
16215.m: Because of the time difference, 9 May is Victory Day in Russia.

16216.q: Who signed the first instrument of surrender for the Wehrmacht in Reims in the night before 7 May 1945?
16216.e: Jodl had been authorised by Grand Admiral Dönitz. In Berlin-Karlshorst the surrender was signed again by Wilhelm Keitel and other representatives.
16216.m: Alfred Jodl signed the surrender in Reims.

16217.q: Whom did Hitler name in his political testament as his successor at the head of the state?
16217.e: After Hitler's suicide on 30 April 1945, Grand Admiral Dönitz led a caretaker government based in Flensburg. It was removed in May 1945.
16217.m: After Hitler's death, Karl Dönitz briefly became head of state.

16218.q: Where did American and Soviet troops meet on 25 April 1945, an event known as “Elbe Day”?
16218.e: The first contacts were at Strehla and Torgau. The meeting on the Elbe cut the German Reich in two. It became a symbol of Allied victory.
16218.m: Americans and Soviets met at Torgau on the Elbe.

16219.q: What did the Berlin Declaration of 5 June 1945 lay down?
a: The four victorious powers took over supreme authority in Germany
Germany became a sovereign state again
Berlin became the capital of the UN
16219.e: The USA, the Soviet Union, Great Britain and France took over governmental authority. Germany was divided into occupation zones.
16219.m: After the war, the four victorious powers took power in Germany.

16220.q: According to estimates, how many people died in total in the Second World War?
16220.e: Estimates give more than 65 million dead, and up to 80 million if all the effects of the war are included. Most of the victims were civilians.
16220.m: The Second World War was the deadliest war in history.

16221.q: What happened in Switzerland on 1 April 1944?
a: American bombers bombed Schaffhausen by mistake
16221.e: US bombers mistook Schaffhausen for a German target. 40 people died in the attack.
16221.m: Even neutral Switzerland was hit by a mistaken bombing raid in 1944.

16222.q: On which date was the atomic bomb dropped on Hiroshima?
16222.e: On the morning of 6 August 1945 at 8.15 local time, a US bomber dropped the bomb. Nagasaki followed three days later.
16222.m: Hiroshima was destroyed by an atomic bomb on 6 August 1945.

16223.q: What were the atomic bombs of Hiroshima and Nagasaki called, and which fissile material did they use?
a: Little Boy with uranium and Fat Man with plutonium
Fat Man with uranium and Little Boy with plutonium
Trinity with hydrogen and Gadget with uranium
Little Boy and Fat Man, both with hydrogen
16223.e: Little Boy was a uranium bomb and fell on Hiroshima. Fat Man was a plutonium bomb and fell on Nagasaki.
16223.m: Little Boy contained uranium, Fat Man contained plutonium.

16224.q: What was the name of the bomber that dropped the atomic bomb on Hiroshima?
16224.e: The B-29 “Enola Gay” was flown by Paul Tibbets. The bomb on Nagasaki was dropped by “Bockscar”.
16224.m: The Enola Gay dropped the bomb on Hiroshima.

16225.q: Why did the second atomic bomb fall on Nagasaki on 9 August 1945?
a: Clouds and smoke blocked the view over the actual main target
Nagasaki was the capital of Japan
The emperor's headquarters were in Nagasaki
The bomb was accidentally released too early
16225.e: The main target was the city of Kokura. Because clouds and smoke prevented an aimed drop, the crew flew to the alternative target, Nagasaki.
16225.m: On 9 August 1945, Nagasaki was only the alternative target.

16226.q: What was the American research programme in which the first atomic bombs were developed called?
16226.e: From 1942, researchers worked on the Manhattan Project under the scientific leadership of Robert Oppenheimer. The first test, Trinity, took place on 16 July 1945.
16226.m: The atomic bomb was developed in the Manhattan Project.

16227.q: According to estimates, how many people had died as a result of both atomic bombings by the end of 1945?
16227.e: About 100,000 people died immediately, and more than 100,000 more by the end of 1945 from injuries and the effects of radiation. Most of the victims were civilians.
16227.m: By the end of 1945, the atomic bombs had killed more than 200,000 people.

16228.q: What are the survivors of the atomic bombings called in Japan?
16228.e: Hibakusha means roughly “explosion-affected people”. Many suffered all their lives from radiation damage and social exclusion.
16228.m: The survivors of the atomic bombs are called hibakusha.

16229.q: When did Japan sign the surrender that ended the Second World War?
a: On 2 September 1945 aboard the USS Missouri
16229.e: Emperor Hirohito announced the surrender on the radio on 15 August 1945. The document was signed in Tokyo Bay on 2 September 1945.
16229.m: The Second World War ended with Japan's surrender on 2 September 1945.

16230.q: In which treaty did the European powers recognise Switzerland’s permanent neutrality on 20 November 1815?
a: In the Second Peace of Paris
16230.e: On 20 November 1815 in Paris, the signatory powers recognised and guaranteed the permanent neutrality and the inviolability of Swiss territory. The groundwork had been laid at the Congress of Vienna.
16230.m: Switzerland’s permanent neutrality was recognised internationally in 1815.

16231.q: In which set of treaties were the rights and duties of neutral states in war laid down in 1907?
a: In the Charter of the United Nations
16231.e: The law of neutrality was codified in the Hague Conventions in 1907. It also applied to Switzerland in the Second World War.
16231.m: The law of neutrality comes from the Hague Conventions of 1907.

16232.q: What duty does a neutral state have under the law of neutrality?
a: It may provide neither troops nor its territory to parties at war
It must stop all trade with parties at war
It may not keep an army of its own
It must supply all parties at war with the same number of weapons
16232.e: A neutral state may not take part militarily in a war, provide troops or open its territory to parties at war. Private trade, however, remained allowed in principle, which raised tricky questions during the war.
16232.m: A neutral state does not take part militarily in any war.

16233.q: What did Switzerland’s return to “integral neutrality” in 1938 mean?
a: It no longer took part in League of Nations sanctions
It made an alliance with France
16233.e: Since joining the League of Nations in 1920, Switzerland had followed a “differential” neutrality that included taking part in economic sanctions. In 1938 it returned to full, integral neutrality and no longer joined in sanctions.
16233.m: From 1938 Switzerland no longer took part in League of Nations sanctions.

16234.q: What does the term “armed neutrality” mean?
a: Switzerland defends its neutrality with its own army
Switzerland supplies weapons only to neutral states
Switzerland lets foreign armies into the country for protection
Switzerland does without any arms industry
16234.e: Swiss neutrality is self-chosen, permanent and armed. The state intends to defend its independence with its own army if necessary.
16234.m: Switzerland protects its neutrality with its own army.

16235.q: What was Switzerland’s geographical situation from the summer of 1940?
a: It was surrounded by the Axis powers and territories they controlled
It bordered an unoccupied, Allied France
It had free access to the Mediterranean
It was completely surrounded by Allied states
16235.e: After France’s defeat in 1940, Switzerland was enclosed by Germany, Italy and territories they controlled. From the end of 1942 it was completely surrounded.
16235.m: From 1940 Switzerland was surrounded by the Axis powers.

16236.q: Which President of the Confederation gave a radio speech on 25 June 1940 that many saw as adapting to a Nazi-ruled Europe?
16236.e: Shortly after France surrendered, Pilet-Golaz spoke of an “inner rebirth”. Terms such as armed neutrality and independence were missing, which many interpreted as adapting to the new situation.
16236.m: Pilet-Golaz’s speech in June 1940 was criticised as adapting to Nazi Germany.

16237.q: Which meeting held by Federal Councillor Pilet-Golaz in September 1940 caused fierce criticism?
a: Receiving leaders of the Frontist National Movement of Switzerland
16237.e: Pilet-Golaz received representatives of the pro-Nazi National Movement of Switzerland. The movement was banned in November 1940.
16237.m: Pilet-Golaz receiving Frontists in 1940 caused outrage.

16238.q: Which diplomatic task did Switzerland take on for many states in the Second World War?
a: As a protecting power, it represented the interests of states at war with each other
It led the negotiations on Germany’s surrender
It provided peacekeeping troops for the Allies
It chaired the League of Nations Council in Geneva
16238.e: Especially after the USA entered the war, Switzerland took on many protecting power mandates. It represented the interests of states that no longer had direct relations with each other.
16238.m: As a protecting power, Switzerland represented the interests of many states in the war.

16239.q: Which political and cultural movement from the 1930s was meant to strengthen Swiss values against totalitarian ideologies?
16239.e: Spiritual National Defence stressed multilingualism, democracy and freedom as a defence against Nazism and fascism. It shaped culture and politics into the 1960s.
16239.m: Spiritual National Defence strengthened Swiss identity against dictatorships.

16240.q: Which event is considered the most powerful expression of Spiritual National Defence?
a: The National Exhibition of 1939 in Zurich
The World Exhibition of 1937 in Paris
The 1928 Olympic Games in St Moritz
16240.e: The “Landi” of 1939 in Zurich gave a strong sense of national independence shortly before the war began. People therefore speak of the “Landi spirit”.
16240.m: The Landi of 1939 became a symbol of Switzerland’s will to stand firm.

16241.q: What is the name of the form of government in which the Federal Council governed largely without parliament during the war, using extraordinary powers?
16241.e: The Federal Assembly gave the Federal Council extraordinary full powers on 30 August 1939. After the popular initiative “Return to direct democracy” was accepted in 1949, the regime of full powers was completely lifted by the end of 1952.
16241.m: During the war the Federal Council governed with extraordinary full powers.

16242.q: What did General Guisan do on the Rütli on 25 July 1940?
a: He called on the officers to resist and presented the Réduit
He signed a treaty with Germany
He announced his resignation as general
He announced the end of active service
16242.e: At the Rütli Report, Guisan gathered the senior officers at the symbolic place. He made it clear that Switzerland would defend itself, if necessary from the Alpine Réduit.
16242.m: With the Rütli Report in 1940, Guisan strengthened the will to resist.

16243.q: Shortly before which event was Henri Guisan elected general in 1939?
a: Before the German attack on Poland
Before the attack on Pearl Harbor
16243.e: The United Federal Assembly elected Guisan on 30 August 1939, two days before the German attack on Poland.
16243.m: Guisan became general shortly before the war began in 1939.

16244.q: Which body elects the general in Switzerland?
16244.e: The general is elected jointly by the National Council and the Council of States, that is, by the United Federal Assembly. This is also what happened with Henri Guisan in 1939.
16244.m: The general is elected by the United Federal Assembly.

16245.q: What was the result of Henri Guisan’s election as general in 1939?
a: A clear majority of the Federal Assembly
A narrow lead of one vote
Drawing lots because of a tie
No election, appointment by the Federal Council
16245.e: Guisan received 204 of 229 valid votes. The clear result showed broad support in parliament.
16245.m: Guisan was elected general with a clear majority.

16246.q: What is special about the rank of “general” in the Swiss Army?
a: A general is only elected in times of serious threat or war
The general is elected directly by the people
The general is also President of the Confederation
16246.e: In peacetime the Swiss Army has no general. Only when a large number of troops are called up to protect the country does the Federal Assembly elect a commander-in-chief.
16246.m: Switzerland only has a general in times of serious threat.

16247.q: Which canton did Henri Guisan come from?
16247.e: Guisan was born in Mézières in the canton of Vaud in 1874. He later lived on the Verte Rive estate in Pully.

16248.q: What job did Guisan do before his military career?
16248.e: Guisan worked as a farmer, among other places in Chesalles-sur-Oron, and took over an estate in Pully in 1902. As was usual in the militia army, he pursued a military career alongside.
16248.m: Guisan was a farmer and a militia officer.

16249.q: After which event did Guisan hold the Rütli Report in July 1940?
a: After the end of the war
After the Allied landings in Normandy
After the German attack on the Soviet Union
16249.e: After the fall of France, Switzerland was almost completely surrounded by the Axis powers. On 25 July 1940 Guisan wanted to strengthen the army’s will to resist.
16249.m: The Rütli Report followed the fall of France in 1940.

16250.q: What did Guisan announce at the Rütli Report?
a: The will to resist and the new Réduit strategy
16250.e: Guisan called for resistance and announced defence in the Alpine region, the Réduit. The report was seen as a counterpart to Pilet-Golaz’s speech, which was felt to be timid.
16250.m: On the Rütli in 1940, Guisan called for resistance.

16251.q: Why did Guisan choose the Rütli meadow for his report in 1940?
a: It is the symbolic place of the founding tradition of the Confederation
It was at the centre of the Gotthard fortress
He had started his military service there himself
16251.e: According to tradition, which is partly legend, the first Confederates swore their alliance on the Rütli. The place was meant to express unity and the will to be free.
16251.m: Guisan used the Rütli as a symbol of freedom and unity.

16252.q: When did Henri Guisan’s time as general end?
a: After the end of the war in summer 1945
In 1943 after the landings in Italy
16252.e: Active service ended on 20 August 1945. With that, Guisan stepped down as general.
16252.m: Guisan’s time as general ended in August 1945.

16253.q: How does Switzerland still remember General Henri Guisan today?
a: With monuments and streets and squares named after him
With a national holiday of its own
With his picture on all coins
With a permanent seat for his family on the Federal Council
16253.e: Guisan died in 1960, and his funeral was a great national event. Many places have an Avenue Général-Guisan or a General-Guisan-Quai.
16253.m: Many streets and monuments recall General Guisan.

16254.q: How does more recent historical research judge Guisan’s role?
a: It questions the myth that he alone saved Switzerland from occupation
It considers him a supporter of Nazism
It denies that he was ever general
It sees him as the founder of neutrality
16254.e: People who lived through the time often saw Guisan as the saviour of the country. More recent historians also stress other factors such as economic relations and put the myth around him into perspective.
16254.m: Research today sees Guisan’s role in a more nuanced way than before.

16255.q: Which troops did the Federal Council call up at the end of August 1939, even before general mobilisation?
16255.e: On 28 August 1939 the Federal Council ordered the mobilisation of the border guard with about 80,000 men; the border troops reported on 29 August. General mobilisation only followed after the German attack on Poland.
16255.m: The border troops were the first to be called up at the end of August 1939.

16256.q: When did the general war mobilisation of the Swiss Army begin?
16256.e: After the German attack on Poland on 1 September 1939, the whole army was called up. The first day of mobilisation was 2 September 1939, and a second general mobilisation followed on 10 May 1940.

16257.q: Roughly how many soldiers were called up in the general mobilisation of 1939?
16257.e: In the general mobilisation about 430,000 combat troops reported for duty. Over the whole war, about 450,000 soldiers were called up.
16257.m: About 430,000 soldiers reported for duty in the general mobilisation of 1939.

16258.q: Which group also supported the regular troops in large numbers in 1939?
a: about 200,000 men in the auxiliary service
16258.e: In the general mobilisation, about 200,000 men liable for auxiliary service reported alongside the combat troops; over the whole war about 250,000 were called up. They took on guard, transport and medical duties, for example.
